Foreword
Water management in agriculture is increasingly critical as the world faces escalating challenges
from climate change, water scarcity, and the demands of an increasing global population. The FAO
Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 56, “Crop Evapotranspiration—Guidelines for Computing
Crop Water Requirements”, has been a cornerstone of agricultural water management since its
first edition in 1998. The standardization of methodologies and the adoption of the Penman-Monteith ETo equation
for computing the reference evapotranspiration and then estimating crop evapotranspiration
enabled agronomists, researchers, policymakers, and farmers to effectively manage water resources,
optimize irrigation practices, and promote sustainable agricultural systems. Its influence is globally
reflected in thousands of citations and numerous studies validating its overall accuracy. In response to significant progress in both science and technology over the past two decades,
FAO, in collaboration with key partners, has revised these guidelines. The revamped version
not only reaffirms the value of the original guidelines but also integrates cutting-edge techniques
such as remote sensing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and improved energy balance methods. These tools enhance the accuracy and applicability of the methods included in the guidelines,
addressing the dynamic and complex needs of today’s agricultural systems. Moreover, the new
version includes new approaches and datasets, making it adaptable to diverse regional conditions,
especially in arid and semi-arid areas. The revised guidelines are also key for addressing the pressing challenges posed by climate
change. Rising temperatures and shifting precipitation patterns reinforce the need for more
precise information on crop water requirements and more efficient water use in agriculture. This
revamped version introduces refined methodologies for optimizing water allocation, incorporating
water-saving strategies, and advancing crop coefficient estimation and irrigation scheduling. These
enhancements enable stakeholders to tailor their irrigation practices to local conditions, preserve
water, and support food security while minimizing environmental impacts. By integrating the latest scientific knowledge with practical tools, the revised guidelines remain an
indispensable resource for agriculture to effectively respond to changing climate and water availability
conditions, and to become more efficient, inclusive, resilient and sustainable in the future. Lifeng Li
Director, FAO Land and Water Division

1. Introduction to evapotranspiration
Introduction to evapotranspiration
This chapter introduces the evapotranspiration process and explains the concepts
of and the differences between reference crop evapotranspiration (ETo) and crop
evapotranspiration under standard conditions (ETc) and various management and
environmental conditions (ETc act). It examines the factors that affect evapotranspiration,
the units in which it is normally expressed and the way in which it can be determined. It
also describes the field methods used to determine the ETc act, as well as the main remote
sensing ET methods. 1.1 EVAPOTRANSPIRATION PROCESS
The combination of two separate processes whereby water is transferred to the
atmosphere, on the one hand from the soil surface by evaporation and, on the other
hand, from the crop by transpiration, is referred to as evapotranspiration (ET). 1.1.1 Evaporation
Evaporation is the process whereby liquid water is converted to water vapour
(vaporization) and removed from the evaporating surface (vapour removal). Water
evaporates from a variety of surfaces, such as lakes, rivers, pavements, soils and vegetation. Energy is required to change the state of the molecules of water from liquid to vapour. Direct solar radiation and, to a lesser extent, the ambient temperature of the air provide
this energy. The driving force to remove water vapour from the evaporating surface is
the difference between the water vapour pressure at the evaporating surface and that
of the surrounding atmosphere. As evaporation proceeds, the surrounding air becomes
gradually saturated and the process will slow down, and might stop if the wet air is
not transferred to the atmosphere. The replacement of the saturated air with drier air
depends greatly on wind speed. Hence, solar radiation, air temperature, air humidity
and wind speed are the essential climatological parameters to consider when assessing
the evaporation process. Where the evaporating surface is the soil surface, the degree of shading by the crop
canopy and the amount of water available at the evaporating surface are other factors that
affect the evaporation process. Frequent rains, irrigation and water transported upwards
in a soil from a shallow water table wet the soil surface. Where the soil is able to supply
water fast enough to satisfy the evaporation demand, the evaporation from the soil is
determined only by the meteorological conditions. However, where the interval between
rains and irrigation becomes large and the ability of the soil to conduct moisture to near
the surface is small, the water content in the topsoil drops and the soil surface dries out. Under these circumstances, the limited availability of water exerts a controlling influence
on soil evaporation. In the absence of any supply of water to the soil surface, evaporation
decreases rapidly and may cease almost completely within a few days. 1.1.2 Transpiration
Transpiration consists of the vaporization of liquid water contained in plant tissues
and the vapour removal to the atmosphere. Crops predominately lose their water
through stomata. These are small openings on the plant leaf through which gases and

the roots and transported through the plant. The vaporization occurs within the leaf,
namely in the intercellular spaces, and the vapour exchange with the atmosphere is
controlled by the stomatal aperture. Nearly all water taken up is lost by transpiration
and only a tiny fraction is used within the plant. FIGURE 1.1

Transpiration, like direct evaporation, depends on the energy supply, vapour pressure
gradient and wind. Hence, radiation, air temperature, air humidity and wind terms
should be considered when assessing transpiration. The soil water content and the
ability of the soil to conduct water to the roots also determine the transpiration rate,
as do waterlogging and soil water salinity. The transpiration rate is also influenced by
crop characteristics, environmental aspects and cultivation practices. Different kinds
of plants may have different transpiration rates. Not only the type of crop, but also
the crop development stage, environment and management should be considered when
assessing transpiration. 1.1.3 Evapotranspiration (ET)
Evaporation and transpiration occur simultaneously and there is no easy way of
distinguishing between the two processes unless specific instruments are used. Apart
from the water availability in the topsoil, the evaporation from a cropped soil is
mainly determined by the fraction of the solar radiation reaching the soil surface. This fraction decreases over the growing period as the crop develops and the crop
canopy shades more and more of the ground area. When the crop is small, water
is predominately lost by soil evaporation, but once the crop is well developed and
completely covers the soil, transpiration becomes the main process. In Figure 1.2,

1.2 UNITS
The evapotranspiration rate is normally expressed in millimetres (mm) per unit time. The rate expresses the amount of water lost from a cropped surface in units of water
depth. The time unit can be an hour or fraction, a day, decade, month or even an entire
growing period or year. As one hectare has a surface of 10 000 m2 and 1 mm is equal to 0.001 m, a loss of 1 mm
of water corresponds to a loss of 10 m3 of water per hectare. In other words, 1 mm day-1
is equivalent to 10 m3 ha-1 day-1 (or 1 litre per square meter). Water depths can also be expressed in terms of energy received per unit area, i.e. the
energy or heat required to vaporize free water. This energy, known as the latent heat
of vaporization (λ), is a function of the water temperature. For example, at 20 °C, λ
is about 2.45 MJ kg-1. In other words, 2.45 MJ is needed to vaporize 1 kg or 0.001 m3
of water. Hence, an energy input of 2.45 MJ per m2 is able to vaporize 0.001 m or 1
mm of water; therefore, 1 mm of water is equivalent to 2.45 MJ m-2 (Example 1.1). The evapotranspiration rate when expressed in units of MJ m-2 day-1 is represented
by λET, the latent heat flux. Table 1.1. summarizes the units used to express the evapotranspiration rate and the

1.3 FACTORS AFFECTING EVAPOTRANSPIRATION
Weather parameters, crop characteristics, management and environmental aspects are
factors affecting evaporation and transpiration. The related ET concepts presented in
Figure 1.3 are discussed in the section on evapotranspiration concepts. 1.3.1 Weather parameters
The principal weather parameters affecting evapotranspiration are radiation, air
temperature, humidity and wind speed. Several procedures have been developed to
assess the evaporation rate from these parameters. The evaporation power of the
atmosphere is expressed by the reference crop evapotranspiration (ETo). The reference
crop evapotranspiration represents the evapotranspiration from a standardized vegetated
surface. The ETo is described in detail later in this Chapter and in Chapters 2 and 4. 1.3.2 Influencing crop factors
The crop type, variety and development stage should be considered when assessing
the evapotranspiration from crops grown in large, well-managed fields. Differences
in resistance to transpiration, crop height, crop roughness, reflection, ground cover
and crop rooting characteristics result in different ET levels in different types of crops
under identical environmental conditions. Crop evapotranspiration under standard
conditions (ETc) refers to the evaporating demand from crops that are grown in
large fields under optimum soil water, excellent management and environmental
conditions, and achieve full production under the given climatic conditions. The ETc
is detailed in Chapters 6 and 7. [TABLE 1]

1.3.3 Management and environmental conditions
Factors such as soil salinity, poor land fertility, limited application of fertilizers, the
presence of hard or impenetrable soil horizons, the absence of control of diseases
and pests and poor soil management may limit crop development and reduce
evapotranspiration. Other factors to be considered when assessing ET are ground
cover, plant density and the soil water content. The effect of soil water content on ET
is conditioned primarily by the magnitude of the water deficit and the type of soil. On
the other hand, too much water will result in waterlogging which might damage the
root and limit root water uptake by inhibiting respiration. When assessing the ET rate, additional consideration should be given to the range of
management practices that act on the climatic and crop factors affecting the ET process. Cultivation practices and the type of irrigation methods can alter the microclimate, affect
the crop characteristics or affect the wetting of the soil and crop surface. A windbreak
reduces wind velocities and decreases the ET rate of the field directly downwind of
the barrier. The effect can be significant especially in windy, warm and dry conditions
although evapotranspiration from the trees themselves may offset any reduction in
the field. Soil evaporation in a young orchard, where trees are widely spaced, can be
reduced by using a well-designed drip or trickle irrigation system. The drippers apply
water directly to the soil near trees, thereby leaving the major part of the soil surface
dry, and limiting the evaporation losses. The use of mulches, especially when the crop is
small, is another way of substantially reducing soil evaporation. Anti-transpirants, such
as stomata-closing, film-forming or reflecting material, reduce the water losses from the
crop and hence the transpiration rate. ETc act is discussed in Chapters 8, 9 and 10. Where field conditions differ from the standard conditions, correction factors are required
to adjust ETc to actual conditions, i.e. ETc act. The adjustment reflects the effect on crop
evapotranspiration by the environmental and management conditions of the field.

1.4 EVAPOTRANSPIRATION CONCEPTS
Distinctions are made (Figure 1.4) between reference crop evapotranspiration (ETo),
crop evapotranspiration under standard conditions (ETc) and crop evapotranspiration
under non-standard conditions, i.e. actual conditions (ETc act). ETo is a climatic
parameter expressing the evaporation power of the atmosphere. ETc refers to the
evapotranspiration from excellently managed and disease-free, large, well-watered
fields that achieve full production under the given climatic conditions. Due to suboptimal crop management and environmental constraints that affect crop growth
and yield and any presence of water stress, evapotranspiration may be limited, and
therefore the actual ETc under non-standard conditions, ETc act, requires a correction. 1.4.1 Reference crop evapotranspiration (ETo)
The evapotranspiration rate from a crop reference surface, not short of water, is called
the reference crop evapotranspiration or reference evapotranspiration and is denoted
as ETo. The reference surface is a hypothetical grass reference crop with specific
characteristics. The use of other denominations and terms such as potential ET is
strongly discouraged due to ambiguities in their definitions. The concept of reference evapotranspiration was introduced to study the evaporative
demand of the atmosphere independent of crop type, crop development and management
practices. As water is abundantly available at the reference evapotranspiring surface,
soil factors do not affect ETo. Relating ETo to a specific surface provides a reference to
which ET from other surfaces can be related. It obviates the need to define a separate
ET equation or level for each crop and stage of growth. ETo values measured or
calculated at different locations or in different seasons are comparable as they refer to
the ET from the same reference surface. The only factors affecting ETo are climatic parameters. Consequently, ETo is a climatic
parameter and must be computed from weather data. ETo expresses the evaporating
power of the atmosphere at a specific location and time of the year and does not
consider crop characteristics and soil factors. Given the specific characteristics of the
standardized hypothetical grass reference crop, that are not possible to consistently and
accurately reproduce in a lysimeter, ETo, in general, cannot be easily estimated in an
operational manner from lysimetric observations. Thus, the FAO Penman-Monteith
method (FAO-PM ETo) is recommended as the sole method for determining ETo. The
method has been selected because it closely approximates grass ETo at the locations
evaluated, is physically based, and explicitly incorporates both physiological and
aerodynamic parameters. Moreover, procedures have been developed for estimating
missing climatic parameters. Typical ranges for ETo values for different agroclimatic regions are given in Table
1.2. These values are intended to familiarize users with typical ranges that may be
compared with locally computed values and are not intended for direct application. The calculation of the reference crop evapotranspiration is discussed in Part A of these
guidelines (Box 1.1).

BOX 1.1
Chapters concerning the calculation of the reference crop evapotranspiration (ETo)
PART A
Chapter 2 - FAO Penman-Monteith ETo equation:
The Chapter introduces the user to the need to standardize one method to compute
ETo from meteorological data. The FAO-PM method is recommended as the method
for determining reference ETo. The method, its derivation, the required meteorological
data; the corresponding definition of the reference surface are described in this
chapter. Also included is the correction of data collected over non-reference weather
sites and application of QAQC to measured meteorological data. Chapter 3 - Meteorological variables and parameters:
The FAO-PM ETo method requires radiation, air temperature, air humidity, and
wind speed data. Calculation procedures to derive climatic parameters from the
meteorological data are presented. Procedures to estimate missing meteorological
variables required for calculating ETo are outlined. This Chapter discussed the source,
measurement and computation of all data required for the calculation of the reference
evapotranspiration (ETo) by means of the FAO-PM method under circumstances,
even in the case of missing climatic data or, for example, having only air temperature
data. Different examples illustrate the various calculation procedures. Chapter 4 - Determination of ETo:
The calculation of ETo by means of the FAO-PM ETo equation, with different time
steps, from the principal weather parameters and with missing data is described. The
determination of ETo from pan evaporation is also presented. 1.4.2 Crop evapotranspiration under standard conditions (ETc)
The crop evapotranspiration under standard conditions, denoted as ETc, is the
evapotranspiration from disease-free, well-fertilized crops, grown in large fields,
under optimum soil water conditions, and achieving full production under the given
climatic conditions. It must be noted that the target is achieving full production and
not necessarily attaining maximum evapotranspiration. In addition, any reductions to
be made to ETc to exercise limitations specified by water use policy must be applied
outside of the ETc calculation process. The amount of water required to satisfy the evapotranspiration from the cropped field is
defined as the crop water requirement. Although the values for crop evapotranspiration
and crop water requirement are identical, crop water requirement refers to the
amount of water that needs to be supplied naturally or through irrigation, while crop
evapotranspiration refers to the amount of water that is transferred to the atmosphere
through evapotranspiration. The irrigation water requirement basically represents
the difference between the crop water requirement and effective precipitation. The
irrigation water requirement also includes additional water for the leaching of salts and
to compensate for the non-uniformity of water application. Crop evapotranspiration can be calculated from climatic data and by integrating directly
the crop resistance, albedo and air resistance factors for the standardized reference
crop into the Penman-Monteith combination equation. As there is still a considerable
lack of information for different crops, the Penman-Monteith method is used for the
estimation of the standard reference crop to determine its evapotranspiration rate, i.e.

1. Introduction to evapotranspiration
ETo. Experimentally, determined ratios of ETc/ETo, called crop coefficients (Kc), are
used to relate ETc to ETo as ETc = Kc ETo. Differences in leaf anatomy, stomatal characteristics, aerodynamic properties and
even albedo cause the crop evapotranspiration to differ from the reference crop
evapotranspiration under the same climatic conditions. Due to variations in the crop
characteristics throughout its growing season, Kc for a given crop changes from sowing
to harvest. The calculation of crop evapotranspiration under standard conditions (ETc)
is discussed in Part B of this guidelines (Box 1.2). BOX 1.2
Chapters concerning the calculation of crop evapotranspiration under standard
conditions (ETc)
PART B
Chapter 5 - Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc) and its measurement:
This chapter introduces the user to the “Kc ETo” approach for calculating crop
evapotranspiration. The effects of characteristics that distinguish field crops from
the reference grass crop are integrated into the crop coefficient Kc. Differences in
evaporation and transpiration between field crops and the reference grass surface can
be integrated into a single crop coefficient (Kc) or separated into two coefficients: a
basal crop (Kcb) and a soil evaporation coefficient (Ke), i.e. Kc = Kcb + Ke. The approach
to follow should be selected as a function of the purpose of the calculation, the
accuracy required and the data available. A review of ETc measurement using ground
and remote observations and sensors is added. Chapter 6 - ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc):
This chapter deals with the calculation of crop evapotranspiration (ETc) under
standard, pristine, non-stressed cropping conditions. ETc is determined by the single
crop coefficient approach whereby the effects of the various weather conditions are
incorporated into ETo and the crop characteristics into the standard Kc coefficient. This chapter presents the tabulated Kc values of numerous annual and perennial
crops as well as the main types of natural vegetation. Guidelines for the use and
computation of Kc are presented. Chapter 7 - ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke):
This chapter presents the dual calculation method for crop evapotranspiration. Kc is split into two separate coefficients, one for crop transpiration (i.e. the basal
crop coefficient Kcb) and one for soil evaporation (Ke). Guidelines for the daily
computation are given and tabulated values for standard Kcb of annual and perennial
crops are provided. 1.4.3 Crop evapotranspiration under non-standard conditions (ETc act)
The crop evapotranspiration under non-standard conditions, i.e. actual crop conditions
(ETc act) is the evapotranspiration from crops grown under management and environmental
conditions that differ from the standard conditions. When cultivating crops in fields, the
real crop evapotranspiration may fall below ETc due to non-optimal conditions such as
the presence of pests and diseases, soil salinity and/or low soil fertility that impact plant
size or vigour, and by water shortage or waterlogging, as well as non-optimal planting
density and other crop management issues. This may result in scanty plant growth, low
canopy density and may reduce the evapotranspiration rate below ETc.

The crop evapotranspiration under non-standard conditions is calculated by using a
water stress coefficient Ks and/or by adjusting Kc for all kinds of other stresses and
environmental constraints on crop evapotranspiration. The adjustment of ETc for
water stress, management and environmental constraints is discussed in Part C of these
guidelines (Box 1.3). BOX 1.3

1.5.1 ET measurement and estimation
Evapotranspiration is not easy to measure. Specific devices and accurate measurements
of various physical parameters include the soil water balance in lysimeters or the field,
as well as the energy balance performed on the ground or through remote sensing, and
are required to determine evapotranspiration. The methods are commonly expensive,
demanding in terms of accuracy of measurements and can only be fully exploited by
well-trained research personnel. Although the methods are inappropriate for routine
measurements, they remain important for the evaluation of ET estimates obtained by
more indirect methods. This section describes the main methods for measuring actual ETc or indirectly deriving
ETc estimates, and emphasizes the need for accuracy in measurements, describing some
essential aspects that affect measurement accuracy.

1. Introduction to evapotranspiration
When used correctly, the accuracy of the described measurement systems can be
very high. However, in many instances, understanding the underlying physics of
turbulence and heat, water and energy transfer that govern the measurement is crucial
to avoid subtle biases and mistakes that will compromise the accuracy of the data. For the purpose of producing representative and reliable data, the deployment of
equilibrium air-boundary layer systems, such as eddy covariance, the Bowen ratio, and
scintillometers, must abide by fetch requirements and minimum equipment heights. Energy balance methods like the Bowen ratio and scintillometers must incorporate
representative measurements of net radiation and soil heat flux density, which typically
require multiple locations for sensors, especially when used in spatially non-uniform
systems such as riparian and other non-agricultural systems. Measurements of eddy
covariance and scintillometry require physically based “corrections”, for example, to
obtain the so-called energy balance closure where the sum of λET, sensible heat flux
and ground heat flux equals the net radiation as introduced in the next section. Many
practitioners may lack the necessary training or experience to use ETc measurement
methods, which can lead to significant measurement biases. Lysimeters and soil water balance methods are older techniques that can potentially
provide reliable measurements, but only if certain fundamental criteria for the
representativeness of vegetation and environmental conditions are met. Sap flow
sensors rely on empirical correction factors derived from the physiology and anatomy
of species under consideration, and on the accuracy of the scaling techniques used to
go from a branch or tree to a group of plants and larger area estimates of ET, including
evaporation from soil. In order to achieve high integrity data, the following sections provide a brief overview
of ET measurement and estimation systems, as well as different problems and
requirements related to each one of these. 1.5.2 Energy balance and micro-climatological methods
Evaporation of water requires relatively large amounts of energy, either in the form of
sensible heat or radiant energy. Therefore, the evapotranspiration process is governed
by energy exchange at the vegetation surface and is limited by the amount of energy
available. Because of this limitation, it is possible to estimate the evapotranspiration
rate by applying the principle of energy conservation. The energy arriving at the
surface must equal the energy leaving the surface for the same period. The energy
leaving the surface includes the energy consumed by the λET process. The λ variable
represents the latent heat of vaporization, described earlier, that is required per unit of
ET. The use of the word “latent” means that this energy is “hidden” in the vapour that
is produced by the ET. All primary fluxes of energy should be considered when deriving an energy balance
equation. The equation for an evaporating surface can be written as:
Rn - G - λET - H = 0
(1.1)
where Rn is the net radiation, H is the sensible heat flux, G is the soil heat flux and λET
is the latent heat flux. The various terms can be either positive or negative. Positive
Rn supplies energy to the surface and positive G, λET and H remove energy from the
surface (Figure 1.5).

In Equation 1.1. only vertical fluxes are considered and any energy that is being
transferred horizontally, by local advection of dry air or heat near the edge of a field
that is surrounded by dryness, is ignored. Therefore, the equation is to be applied for
large, extensive surfaces of homogeneous vegetation only. In addition, the methodology,
especially the estimation of ETo, does not apply to greenhouses and other protected
cultivation facilities where aerodynamic conditions and energy exchange can be much
different than those experienced for open agricultural fields. The equation is restricted
to the four components: Rn, λET, H and G. Other energy terms, such as heat stored or
released in the plant, or the energy used in metabolic activities and photosynthesis, are
not considered. These terms account for only a small fraction of the daily net radiation
and can be considered negligible when compared with the other four components. The latent heat flux (λET) representing the evapotranspiration fraction can be
derived from the energy balance equation if all other components are known. Net radiation (Rn) and soil heat fluxes (G) can be measured or estimated from
climatic parameters. Measurements of the sensible heat (H) are however complex
and cannot be easily obtained. H requires accurate measurement of temperature
gradients above the surface. Another method for estimating evapotranspiration is using a mass transfer method. This
approach considers the vertical movement of small parcels of air (eddies) above a large
homogeneous surface. The eddies transport material (water vapour) and energy (heat
and momentum) from and towards the evaporating surface. By assuming steady state
conditions and that the eddy transfer coefficients for water vapour are proportional to
those for heat and momentum, the evapotranspiration rate can be computed from the
vertical gradients of air temperature and water vapour above the surface via the Bowen
Ratio Energy Balance (BREB). The Bowen ratio BR is defined as the ratio of H to
λET (BR = H/λET) and λET is determined as λET = (Rn−G)/(1+BR).

1. Introduction to evapotranspiration
Other direct estimation methods use gradients of wind speed and water vapour
to directly estimate the vapour flux. These methods and other methods, such as
Eddy Covariance (EC), require accurate measurement of vapour pressure, and air
temperature or wind speed at different levels above the surface. Therefore, their
application is restricted to primarily research situations. The BREB technique performs best when ET is not constrained by soil water so that
λET tends to be larger than H and relative error is reduced. The Bowen ratio rises and
the relative error in ET increases as water becomes less readily available. Requirements of the BREB system include:
•  sufficient distance of fetch to establish an equilibrium boundary layer (EBL)
deeper than the instrument height (this requirement is frequently violated);
•  sufficient elevation of the instrument above the canopy to avoid the roughness
sublayer where gradients of temperature and vapour pressure are difficult to
establish and may not be in proportion to the true BR;
•  representative and accurate measurement of Rn and G; and
•  multiple net radiometers and soil heat flux plates, required when measurements
are performed over heterogeneous or sparse areas. Eddy covariance (EC) systems are often used for crop ET monitoring due to their relative
simplicity of setup, moderate sensor prices and, depending on the equipment settings, the
ability to simultaneously measure H, λET and CO2 fluxes. The concept of eddy covariance
(also known as eddy correlation) refers to the statistical covariance between vertical
fluxes of vapour or sensible heat within the upward and downward legs of turbulent
eddies. Quick response sensors must be used to make high speed measurements of air
temperature (T), vertical wind velocity (w), and mean vapour pressure (e) or mean specific
humidity (q), normally at frequencies of 5-20 Hz (5-20 times per second), typically at
10 Hz. Additionally, ET can be calculated as a residual from the energy balance equation
as λET = Rn – G – H, which has the advantage of eliminating the need to measure q,
although it does require accurate measurements of Rn and G. A large number of corrections are required with the EC procedure, and there is a
variety of software available for EC flux processing. Many studies have reported a
lack of energy balance closure for EC data since the sum of the measured turbulent
fluxes (H + λET) usually underestimates the measured available energy (Rn − G). This
underestimation can often be as large as 30 percent. Potential causes for the lack of
closure may be horizontal advection, storage of heat in the canopies, energy used by
photosynthesis, change in storage of heat in the developing boundary layer below the
instrumentation (causing flux divergence), errors in the measurements of turbulent
fluxes, error in measurement of the vertical wind velocity by the sonic anemometer,
and inadequate or too much separation between the anemometer and humidity sensor. Additionally, an error can occur in Rn or G measurements due to miscalibration and
improper installation or nonrepresentative placement of sensors over nonuniform
vegetation such as with rows of trees. The literature is not conclusive about the method to be followed for resolving the
energy imbalance, although the most important issue is that the EC measurements
are consistent with the conservation of energy. Generally, users force the energy
balance closure using the residual technique by scaling H and λET in the same
proportion until the sum equals Rn – G, or by assuming correct H measurement and

underestimation of λET. Days associated with vertical regional advection of warm,
dry air may show a poor energy balance closure as compared to the rest of the days. Therefore, energy balance closure cannot be considered as a data quality assessment,
since closure error can still be present even if data acquired by the EC system are of
good quality and vice versa. The EC system requirements are as follows:
•  a uniform fetch with sufficient distance to create an equilibrium boundary layer
(EBL) deeper than the instrument height (this is frequently violated);
•  sufficient elevation of instruments above the canopy to reduce roughness sublayer
impacts and to increase mean eddy size to match the sensor path lengths;
•  accomplishing the necessary data “corrections”;
•  accurate, high frequency instrumentation and a good knowledge and understanding
of the physics of turbulence; and
•  utilization of net radiation and soil heat flux measurements if energy balance
closure error is to be identified and corrected. A scintillometer is an optical device that measures small fluctuations in the refractive
index of air caused by temperature, humidity, and pressure induced variations in
density. The most common scintillometers measure sensible heat flux, H, by relating
the structure parameter to a temperature parameter and the Monin-Obukhov stability
parameters. A scintillometer system for measuring sensible heat flux consists of an
optical transmitter and a receiver at the ends of an atmospheric propagation path. The
receiver detects and evaluates the intensity of fluctuations of the transmitted signal,
called scintillations. λET is estimated as a residual of the surface energy balance. To
obtain λET, measurements of Rn and G are needed, which can be problematic and
biased in heterogeneous and sparse vegetation systems. Scintillometers are relatively simple to operate and maintain. Their cost can equal
or exceed those of BREB and EC systems. A distinct advantage of scintillometry
is the ability to derive sensible heat flux that is integrated over a long transect, up
to several km in length. This integration is especially useful for measuring H over
complex natural vegetation where spatial variation can have scales of hundreds of
meters. However, insufficient representativeness of Rn and G measurement over a
transect can greatly reduce the accuracy of ET determined from the scintillometerbased integration of H. Rn measurements may need augmentation by satellite-based
images of albedo and surface temperature. Soil heat flux densities can vary in the
same manner along a mixed transect. 1.5.3 Soil water balance
Evapotranspiration can also be determined by measuring the various components
of the soil water (SW) balance. The method consists of assessing the incoming and
outgoing water flux into the crop root zone over some time period (Figure 1.6). Irrigation (I) and rainfall (P) add water to the root zone. Part of I and P might
be lost by surface runoff (RO) and by deep percolation (DP) that will eventually
recharge the water table. Water might also be transported upward by capillary
rise (CR) from a shallow water table towards the root zone or even be transferred
horizontally by subsurface flow in (SFin) or out (SFout) of the root zone. In many
situations, however, except under conditions with large slopes, SFin and SFout are
minor and can be ignored. Soil evaporation and crop transpiration deplete water

1. Introduction to evapotranspiration
from the root zone. If all fluxes other than evapotranspiration (ET) can be assessed,
the evapotranspiration can be deduced from the change in soil water content (ΔSW)
over the selected time period:
ET = I + P - RO - DP + CR - ΔSF - ΔSW
(1.2)
A positive ΔSW indicates an increase in total soil water content. Some fluxes
such as subsurface flow, deep percolation and capillary rise from a water table
are difficult to assess when very short time periods are considered. The soil water
balance method can generally give ET estimates over long time periods on the order
of week-long or ten-day periods but can only provide accurate daily ET estimates
when appropriate and highly accurate soil water content sensors are adopted and
appropriate modelling software is used. It may be difficult to capture the increase
in evaporation following a large irrigation event when soils are such that one day
or more is required for water within the root zone to drain. FIGURE 1.6

Evapotranspiration from mass balance over large areas, also referred to as the inflowoutflow or mass balance method, is a water balance technique that can be applied over
large, integrated areas of land and water to develop watershed scale estimates of ET. These estimates may be useful for calibration of or comparison to watershed and
remote-sensing based models. Examples of ET by water balance are applications to
large areas such as valleys where the inflow and outflow are determined from stream
flow and precipitation measurements, and where the basin is confined to eliminate
other significant sources of inflow or outflow such as groundwater underflow. Such
applications generally provide only gross seasonal estimates of the average ET from

agricultural and non-agricultural areas within the watershed. The results represent ET
from a combination of vegetation types and are generally applicable only to climatic,
vegetation and water availability conditions similar to those existing in the study area. Mass balances require precipitation as the primary input and consequently, the ET
estimate can only be as accurate as the precipitation estimate. Fine resolution grids of
precipitation on the scale of a km or less may be required in areas having substantial
precipitation from convective storms and areas having substantial relief with orographic
influence on precipitation amounts. As with soil water balance applications, precipitation
data from standard gauges may need to be corrected for under-catch. Accurate
measurement of basin or irrigation project outflow is necessary as is locating the
measurement area boundaries to minimize groundwater inflows and outflows. 1.5.4 Lysimeters
By isolating the crop root zone from its environment and controlling the processes
that are difficult to measure, the different terms in the soil water balance equation can
be determined with greater accuracy. This is done in lysimeters where the crop grows
in isolated tanks filled with either disturbed or undisturbed soil. In precision weighing
lysimeters, where the water loss is directly measured by measuring the change of mass
of the complete system, evapotranspiration can be obtained with an accuracy of a few
hundredths of a millimetre, and small time periods such as an hour or even less can be
considered. In non-weighing drainage lysimeters, the evapotranspiration for a given
time period is determined by deducting the drainage water, collected at the bottom
of the lysimeters, from the total water input. Non-weighing drainage lysimeters
can generally only provide ET information at a weekly or longer time scale. On the
contrary, static water table lysimeters can be very accurate and provide for daily time
step or longer measurements since ET corresponds to the amount of water transferred
during the considered time period from the groundwater. These lysimeters are of
particular interest for studies referring to the contribution of the groundwater to the
crop under study. They are commonly used to define the target depth of the water
table, or when the groundwater is saline. Many studies have used lysimeter ET measurements for evaluation, calibration and
validation of different ET approaches. However, lysimeter measurements are very
sensitive to environmental aspects, which are often not well interpreted or even taken
into account. Moreover, there tends to be a lack of necessary information reported
for associated meteorological and environmental conditions, and processing of
lysimeter data in published scientific papers, which calls into question the validity and
representativeness of certain reported data sets. A requirement of lysimeters is that the vegetation both inside and immediately outside
of the lysimeter be perfectly matched (same height and leaf area index) to that of the
surrounding field. This requirement has historically not been closely adhered to in a
majority of lysimeter studies and has resulted in severely erroneous and unrepresentative
ETc and Kc data sets. Typical positive measurement biases include a clothesline effect
where lysimeter vegetation is taller than that outside and situations where vegetation
from inside the lysimeter creeps outside the lysimeter due to lower vegetation density
outside the lysimeter. Lower vegetation density immediately outside a lysimeter can
occur due to foot traffic or soil compaction or a thick lysimeter boundary. The outward
extension of vegetation from the lysimeter can thereby increase the amount of solar
radiation captured by lysimeter vegetation and converted to ET. This causes an overmeasurement and overstatement of true field-wide ET.

1. Introduction to evapotranspiration
In a similar manner, one serious problem in lysimeter data is produced by a so-called
“bloom effect” on small lysimeters, which means that the area of exposure of plant
canopy to solar radiation is higher than the considered effective area of the lysimeter. Finally, radiation emission from warmed sides of a lysimeter into the inner vegetation
can increase lysimeter ET to rates higher than the surrounding field. Recent studies have established guidelines for the requirements of lysimeter-based ET
measurements, including a minimum fetch of 50 m around the lysimeter, while plant
population, crop height, leaf area, ground coverage, irrigation water management and
soil conditions inside the lysimeter must be identical to those in the rest of the field. In
conclusion, because a lysimeter represents a small sample of ET for an entire field condition,
it is essential that the lysimeter represents an exact reproduction of the field condition. As
lysimeters are difficult and expensive to construct and as their operation and maintenance
require special care, their use is limited to specific and careful research purposes. 1.5.5 Sap flow systems
Sap flow methods have been used to estimate transpiration from individual plants. The
systems introduce a small source of heat into the trunk or branch of a plant and estimate
the flow of water in the xylem by either measuring the velocity of a heat pulse carried
away from the heat source in the transpiration stream or by the dissipation of heat
energy in the stem due to convection in the transpiration stream. These methods do
not measure the direct evaporation component of ET, but only the plant transpiration
component. This can be an advantage if the goal is to measure plant water use, but is a
disadvantage if the goal is to estimate total ET over an extended heterogeneous surface. Three main methods can be employed. Literature suggests that no one set of theory
and instrumentation is applicable to all sizes or species of trees. Heat pulse velocity measurements can determine transpiration in forests and orchards,
where the sensors can be applied to any woody stem larger than about 40 mm in
diameter. The system is inexpensive, easy to install, and suited to automated data
collection. The most commonly used correction method is the compensation heat pulse
method. The method may require a knowledge of the wood anatomy of the species
being measured to determine sapwood area. The Granier heat dissipation method is suited to transpiration measurements in trees,
and it involves inserting a heating needle into the sapwood layer of a large trunk or
branch. Heat is applied at a constant rate rather than as a pulse. Different calibration
coefficients may be needed for each tree species and the method assumes that sap flow
is radially uniform around the trunk. The tissue heat balance method is the most direct sap flux method with the fewest
assumptions. It involves wrapping a heating wire around an entire branch segment
and measuring conductive heat losses upstream, downstream and radially away from
the heat source by thermocouples referenced to the temperature at the heating wire. The energy balance is conducted on the entire stem segment so that no knowledge of
the xylem anatomy or area of conducting sapwood is needed. Unfortunately, this is
the most difficult method to implement and can only be applied to branches under
50 mm in diameter, because the heat source must be able to uniformly heat the entire
segment of the branch around which it is wrapped. Whereas heat pulse and heat
dissipation sensors placed in a tree trunk can measure transpiration through the entire
tree, numerous tissue heat balance sensors, placed on individual branches would be
needed to sample sap flux on a single tree, and a scaling method would then be needed
to extrapolate from the branches to the whole tree.

The heat pulse and thermal dissipation methods must be calibrated for each new
application, ideally through the use of weighing lysimeters or by pulling water through
stem sections of the plants of interest while measuring velocity and heat dissipation
parameters with sap flux. Scaling ET from individual limbs to full plants and from
full plants to large areas is uncertain due to differences among tree structure, radiation
interception per tree, and water availability. Shaded limbs tend to have lower rates
of transpiration than sunlit limbs, and limbs lower in a canopy tend to have less
aerodynamic exchange of energy and vapor. Besides scaling of transpiration from
specific species of trees, additional uncertainty in areal ET is caused by stands of
multiple species, the presence of understory vegetation, and evaporation from bare soil. 1.5.6 Remote Sensing
Remote sensing from vegetation indices. The estimation of ET using a vegetation index
(VI) is possible due to the generally close correspondence between vegetation amount
and transpiration, where, as vegetation cover increases, leaf area increases, and the
relative rate of transpiration increases. Generally, the estimation of ET is made using
the Kc act ETo approach where the value for Kc act is estimated from the VI. The VI is
usually updated over time using satellite or drone imagery. Because the Kc act from VI
represents the transpiration component, challenges with VI-based methods include
estimating evaporation from bare soil associated with precipitation and irrigation
events. Also challenging is the estimation of reduced ET associated with soil-water
shortage, because these processes are not generally shown by the VI. Under conditions
of long periods of water stress, vegetation growth is expected to be less and therefore
the VI may be less. However, during conditions of short periods of water stress, the VI
may appear to be at unstressed levels even though the ET may decline due to partial or
full closure of stomates. Therefore, VI-based methods are often best used to estimate
ET under adequate water supplies. More discussion on estimating Kc from VI is given
in Chapter 5 and Chapter 9. Remote sensing from energy balance. Remote sensing surface energy balance (RSSEB)
methods take advantage of the physical fact that conversion of liquid water to the vapour
form requires very substantial amounts of energy. This conversion of liquid to vapour
during the evaporation process involves the same physical requirements whether the
process is the transpiration of water from inside a plant leaf or the evaporation of water
from a wet soil surface. Approximately 2.4 million Joules (2.4 megajoules) of energy are
required to evaporate one kilogram of water at room temperature. The energy source
can be in the form of heat energy from the surrounding air (this is termed “sensible
heat” since it can be sensed with a thermometer), and the energy source also includes
the radiant energy from the sun and atmosphere in the form of photons contacting the
evaporating surface. Energy from photons is converted into freeing water molecules
from a liquid to vapour state. The surface energy balance determination of ETc act is usually conducted using Equation
1.1. RSSEB is useful in that it produces the combined ET including both transpiration
from vegetation and evaporation of water from wet soil surfaces. Thermal sensorbased RSSEB models are capable of estimating actual crop ET, ETc act. RSSEB-based
estimation of ETc act is useful in situations where ETc act is lower than the potential crop
ET, ETc, during times of water shortage or due to poor water management. The more
dependable and universal satellite-based models employ a complete surface energy
balance (SEB), introduced in Equation 1.1, where ET is computed as a residual of
surface energy. This determination requires a thermal imager onboard the satellite. The
focus of RSSEB is often on the production of field-scale resolution maps of actual ET,
meaning those produced from moderately high resolution thermal sensor-equipped

1. Introduction to evapotranspiration
satellites such as Landsat that have 30-m pixel size, a thermal sensor, and a relatively
frequent revisit time (8 days for Landsat). RSSEB can help evaluate variation in ETc act
across large populations of fields having the same crop type but differing cropping
dates, crop varieties or water management. RSSEB provides a valuable complement to the Kc ETo approach. RSSEB can be used
to confirm or calibrate crop coefficients for new crops or in new areas. In turn, the
Kc ETo approach is useful in checking or confirming ETc act estimates made by RSSEB
models. Some RSSEB models, for example, the METRIC model, utilize reference ET
to establish upper limits on the estimated ETc act. 1.5.7 ET computed from meteorological data
Owing to the difficulty of obtaining accurate field measurements, ET is commonly
computed from weather data. A large number of empirical or semi-empirical equations
have been developed for assessing crop or reference crop evapotranspiration from
meteorological data. Some of the methods are only valid under specific climatic and
agronomic conditions and cannot be applied under conditions different from those
under which they were originally developed. Numerous researchers have analyzed the performance of the various calculation
methods for different locations. As a result of an Expert Consultation held in May
1990, the FAO Penman-Monteith ETo method is recommended as the standard
method for the definition and computation of the grass reference evapotranspiration
(ETo). The ET from crop surfaces under standard conditions is determined by crop
coefficients (Kc) that relate ETc to ETo. The ET from crop surfaces under non-standard
conditions is adjusted by a water stress coefficient (Ks) and/or by modifying the crop
coefficient (ETc act = Ks Kc ETo = Kc act ETo). 1.5.8 ET estimated from pan evaporation
Evaporation from an open water surface provides an index of the integrated effects
of radiation, air temperature, air humidity and wind on evapotranspiration. However,
differences in the water and cropped surface produce significant differences in the water
evaporation from an open water surface and the crop canopy. The pan has proved its
practical value and has been used successfully to estimate reference evapotranspiration
by observing the evaporation loss from a water surface and applying empirical
coefficients to relate pan evaporation to ETo. The procedure is outlined in Chapter 4.

2. FAO Penman-Monteith ETo equation
FAO Penman-Monteith ETo equation
This chapter introduces the user to the need to standardize one method to compute
reference evapotranspiration (ETo) from meteorological data. The FAO Penman-
Monteith method is recommended as the sole standard ETo method for determining
reference evapotranspiration. The method, its derivation, the required meteorological
data and reference weather site conditions, and the corresponding definition of the
reference surface are described in this chapter. Also included is the correction of data
collected over non-reference weather sites and the application of Quality Assurance
and Quality Control (QAQC) to measured meteorological data. 2.1 NEED FOR A STANDARD ETO METHOD
A large number of more or less empirical methods have been developed over the last 80
years by numerous scientists and specialists worldwide to estimate evapotranspiration
using different climatic variables. Relationships were often subject to rigorous local
calibrations and have proved to have limited global validity. Testing the accuracy of
ET methods under a new set of conditions is laborious, time-consuming and costly,
and yet evapotranspiration data are frequently needed at short notice for project
planning or irrigation scheduling design. To meet this need, guidelines were developed
and published in the FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 24 “Crop water
requirements”. To accommodate users with different data availability, four methods
were presented to calculate the reference crop evapotranspiration (ETo): the Blaney-
Criddle, radiation, modified Penman and pan evaporation methods. The modified
Penman method was considered to offer the best results with a minimum possible error
in relation to a living grass reference crop. It was expected that the pan method would
give acceptable estimates, depending on the location of the pan. The radiation method
was suggested in FAO Paper No. 24 for areas where available climatic data include
measured air temperature and sunshine, cloudiness or radiation, but not measured
wind speed and air humidity. Finally, the publication proposed the use of the Blaney-
Criddle method for areas where available climatic data cover air temperature data only. These climatic methods to calculate ETo were all calibrated for ten-day or monthly
calculations, not for daily or hourly calculations. The Blaney-Criddle method was
recommended for periods of one month or longer. For the pan method, it was suggested
that calculations should be done for periods of ten days or longer. Users have not always
respected these conditions and calculations have often been done on daily time steps. Advances in research and the more accurate assessment of crop water use have revealed
weaknesses in the methodologies. Numerous researchers have analyzed the performance
of the four methods for different locations. Although the results of such analyses could
have been influenced by site or measurement conditions, or by bias in weather data
collection, it became evident that the proposed methods do not behave the same way in
different locations around the world. Deviations from computed to observed values were
often found to exceed ranges indicated by FAO. The modified Penman was frequently
found to overestimate ETo, even by up to 20 percent for low evaporative conditions. The
other FAO recommended equations showed variable adherence to the reference crop
evapotranspiration standard of clipped, cool-season grass. Chapter 2

To evaluate the performance of these and other estimation procedures under different
climatological conditions, a major study was undertaken under the auspices of the
Committee on Irrigation Water Requirements of the American Society of Civil
Engineers (ASCE). The ASCE study analyzed the performance of 20 different
methods, using detailed procedures to assess the validity of the methods compared to
a set of carefully screened lysimeter data from 11 international locations with a broad
range of climatic conditions. The study proved very revealing and showed the widely
varying performance of the methods under different climatic conditions. In a parallel
study commissioned by the European Community, a consortium of European research
institutes evaluated the performance of various evapotranspiration methods using data
from different lysimeter studies in Europe. The studies confirmed the overestimation of the modified Penman introduced in FAO
Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 24, and the variable performance of the different
methods depending on their adaptation to local conditions. The comparative studies
may be summarized as follows:
•  The semi-empirical Penman methods may require local calibration of the wind
function to achieve satisfactory results.
•  The radiation methods show good results in humid climates where the aerodynamic
term is relatively small, but performance in arid conditions is erratic and tends to
underestimate evapotranspiration.
•  Temperature methods remain empirical and require local calibration in order to
achieve satisfactory results. A possible exception is the 1985 Hargreaves-Samani
method, which has shown reasonable ETo results with a global validity. However,
it requires validated parameterization.
•  Pan evapotranspiration methods clearly reflect the shortcomings of predicting
crop evapotranspiration from open water evaporation collected from a shallow
pan. The methods are susceptible to the microclimatic conditions under which
the pans are operating and the rigour of station maintenance. Their performance
proves erratic.
•  The relatively accurate and consistent performance of the FAO Penman-Monteith
approach (FAO-PM ETo) in both arid and humid climates has been indicated in
both the ASCE and European studies. The analysis of the performance of the various calculation methods reveals the need
for formulating a standard method for the computation of ETo. The FAO-PM method
is recommended as the sole standard method. It is a method with a strong likelihood
of correctly predicting ETo in a wide range of locations and climates and has provision
for application in data-short situations. The use of older FAO or other reference ET
methods is no longer encouraged. As a result, the FAO-PM method was utilized in
the 1998 edition of FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 56 as the sole standard
ETo method. Its adoption has been widely accepted by the international community as
attested by citations in more than 47 000 publications and a large number of tests on
overall accuracy. The FAO-PM ETo method continues to be the ETo method utilized
in this 2025 edition of FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 56.

2. FAO Penman-Monteith ETo equation
2.2 FORMULATION OF THE PENMAN-MONTEITH EQUATION
2.2.1 Penman-Monteith combination equation
In 1948, Penman combined the energy balance with the mass transfer method and
derived an equation to compute the evaporation from an open water surface from
standard climatological records of sunshine, temperature, air humidity and wind
speed. This so-called combination method was further developed by many researchers,
including Monteith in 1965, and was extended to cropped surfaces by introducing
resistance factors. The resistance nomenclature distinguishes between aerodynamic resistance and
surface resistance factors (Figure 2.1). The surface resistance parameters are often
combined into one parameter, the “bulk” surface resistance parameter, which operates
in series with the aerodynamic resistance. The surface resistance, rs, describes the
resistance of vapour flow through stomata openings, total leaf area and soil surface. The aerodynamic resistance, ra, describes the resistance to vapour and heat flow from
the vegetation upward and involves friction from air flowing over vegetative surfaces
(Figure 2.1). Although the exchange process in a vegetation layer is too complex to
be fully described by the two resistance factors, good correlations can be obtained
between measured and calculated evapotranspiration rates, especially for a uniform
grass reference surface. FIGURE 2.1

To obviate the need to define unique evaporation parameters for each crop and stage of
growth, the concept of a reference surface was introduced. Evapotranspiration rates of
the various crops are related to the evapotranspiration rate from the reference surface
(ETo) by means of crop coefficients. In the past, an open water surface has been proposed as a reference surface. However,
the differences in aerodynamic, vegetation control and radiation characteristics present
a strong challenge in relating ET to measurements of free water evaporation. Relating
ETo to a specific crop has the advantage of incorporating the biological and physical
processes involved in ET from cropped surfaces. Grass, together with alfalfa, is a well-studied crop regarding its aerodynamic and
surface characteristics and is accepted worldwide as a reference surface. Because the
resistance to diffusion of vapour strongly depends on crop height, ground cover, LAI
and soil moisture conditions, the characteristics of the reference crop should be well

defined and fixed. Changes in crop height result in variations in the roughness and
LAI. Consequently, the associated canopy and aerodynamic resistances will vary
appreciably with time. Moreover, water stress and the degree of ground cover have an
effect on the resistances and also on the albedo. To avoid problems of local calibration which would require demanding and expensive
studies, a hypothetical grass reference has been selected with well-defined properties. Difficulties with a living grass reference result from the fact that the grass variety and
morphology can significantly affect the evapotranspiration rate, especially during peak
water use. Large differences may exist between warm-season and cool-season grass
types. Cool-season grasses have a lower degree of stomatal control and hence higher
rates of evapotranspiration. However, it may be difficult to grow cool-season grasses
in some arid, tropical climates. The 1990 FAO Expert Consultation on Revision of FAO Methodologies for Crop
Water Requirements accepted the following unambiguous definition for the reference
surface when applied using 24-hour calculation timesteps (Figure 2.3):
