4.1.1 Calculation procedure
Calculation sheet
ETo can be estimated for daily (24-hour) calculation time steps by means of the
calculation sheet presented in Box 4.1. The calculation sheet refers to tables in Annex
2 for the determination of some of the climatic parameters. The calculation procedure
consists of the following steps:
1. Derivation of some climatic parameters from the daily maximum (Tmax) and
minimum (Tmin) air temperature, altitude (z) and mean wind speed (u2). 2. Calculation of the vapour pressure deficit (es − ea). The saturation vapour pressure
(es) is derived from Tmax and Tmin, while the actual vapour pressure (ea) can be
derived from the dewpoint temperature (Tdew), from maximum (RHmax) and
minimum (RHmin) relative humidity, or from the maximum (RHmax), or from mean
relative humidity (RHmean). 3. Determination of the net radiation (Rn) as the difference between the net shortwave
radiation (Rns) and the net longwave radiation (Rnl). In the calculation sheet, the
effect of soil heat flux (G) is ignored for daily calculations as the magnitude of the
flux in this case is relatively small. The net radiation, expressed in MJ m-2 day-1, is
converted to mm day-1 (equivalent evaporation) in the FAO-PM ETo equation by
using 0.408 as the conversion factor within the equation. 4. ETo is obtained by combining the results of the previous steps. Examples 4.1, 4.2, and 4.3 present typical cases using the calculation sheet for monthly,
daily, and hourly calculation timesteps. It is highly recommended that computerized
software be verified by comparing, step-by-step, with component calculations in these
examples. Computerized calculations
Calculations of the reference crop evapotranspiration (ETo) are nearly always
computerized. The calculation procedures of all data required for the calculation
of ETo by means of the FAO-PM ETo equation are presented in Chapter 3. Typical
sequences in which the calculations can be executed are given in the calculation sheets. The procedures presented in Boxes 3.1 (vapour pressure deficit), 3.3 (extraterrestrial
radiation and daylight hours), 3.4 (net radiation) and 4.1 (ETo) can be used when
developing a spreadsheet or computer program to calculate ETo. Examples 4.1, 4.2 and
4.3 can be used to confirm computerized calculations for monthly, daily, and hourly
timesteps, respectively. Many software packages already use the FAO-PM ETo equation to assess the reference
evapotranspiration. As an example, the output of CROPWAT, the FAO software for
irrigation scheduling, is presented in Figure 4.1
4.1.2 ETo calculated with different time steps
The selection of the time step with which ETo is calculated depends on the purpose of
the calculation, the accuracy required and the time step of the climatic data available.

4. Determination of ETo
Ten-day or monthly time step
Notwithstanding the non-linearity in the FAO-PM ETo equation and some weather
parameter methods, mean ten-day or monthly weather data can be used to compute
the mean ten-day or monthly values for the reference evapotranspiration. The value
of the reference evapotranspiration calculated with mean monthly weather data is
indeed very similar to the average of the daily ETo values calculated with daily average
weather data for that month. The meteorological data consist of:
•  Air temperature: ten-day or monthly average daily maximum (Tmax) and average
daily minimum temperature (Tmin).
•  Air humidity: ten-day or monthly average of the daily actual vapour pressure (ea)
derived from psychrometric, dewpoint or relative humidity data.
•  Wind speed: ten-day or monthly average of daily wind speed data transformed to
a 2 m height (u2).
•  Radiation: ten-day or monthly average of daily net radiation (Rn) computed
from the mean ten-day or monthly measured shortwave radiation or from actual
duration of daily sunshine hours (n). The extraterrestrial radiation (Ra) and daylight
hours (N) for a specific day of the month can be computed using Equations 3.18
and 3.31 in Chapter 3, or can be selected from Tables A2.5 and A2.6 in Annex 2. When the soil is warming (spring) or cooling (autumn), the soil heat flux (G) for
monthly periods may become significant relative to the mean monthly Rn. In these
cases G cannot be ignored and its value should be determined from the mean monthly
air temperatures of the previous and next month. Chapter 3 outlines the calculation

4. Determination of ETo
Daily time step
Calculation of ETo with the FAO-PM ETo equation on 24-hour time scales will
generally provide accurate results. The required meteorological data consists of:
•  Air temperature: maximum (Tmax) and minimum (Tmin) daily air temperatures.
•  Air humidity: mean daily actual vapour pressure (ea) derived from psychrometric,
dewpoint temperature or relative humidity data.
•  Wind speed: daily average for 24 hours of wind speed transformed to the 2 m
height (u2).
•  Radiation: net radiation (Rn) measured or computed from solar and longwave
radiation or from the actual duration of sunshine (n). The extraterrestrial
radiation (Ra) and daylight hours (N) for a specific day of the month should be
computed using Equations 3.18 and 3.31. As the magnitude of daily soil heat
flux (G) beneath the reference grass surface is relatively small, it may be ignored
for 24-hour time steps. EXAMPLE 4.2

4. Determination of ETo
Hourly time step
In areas where substantial changes in wind speed, dewpoint or cloudiness occur during
the day, calculation of the ETo equation using hourly time steps is generally better than
using 24-hour calculation time steps. Such weather changes can cause 24-hour means
to misrepresent the evaporative power of the environment during parts of the day
and may introduce errors in the calculations. However, under most conditions, the
application of the FAO-PM ETo equation with 24-hour data produces accurate results. With the advent of electronic, automated weather stations, weather data are increasingly
reported for hourly or shorter periods. Therefore, in situations where calculations are
computerized, the FAO-PM ETo equation can be applied on an hourly basis with good
results. When applying the FAO-PM ETo equation on an hourly or shorter time scale,
the equation and some of the procedures for calculating meteorological data should be
adjusted for the smaller time step. The FAO-PM ETo equation for:

Since the ratio Rs/Rso is used to represent cloud cover, when calculating Rnl for hourly
periods during the nighttime, Rso becomes zero, so that the ratio Rs/Rso does not apply. That ratio in Equation 3.42 can be set equal to the Rs/Rso calculated for a time period
occurring 2-3 hours before sunset, before the sun angle becomes small. This will generally
serve as a good approximation of cloudiness occurring during the subsequent nighttime. The hourly period that is 2 to 3 hours before sunset can be identified during the
computation of Ra as the period where ω, calculated from Equation 3.28, is within the
range (ωs − 0.79) ≤ ω ≤ (ωs − 0.52), where ωs is calculated using Equation 3.22. As a more
approximate alternative, one can assume Rs/Rso = 0.4 to 0.6 during nighttime periods
in humid and subhumid climates and Rs/Rso = 0.7 to 0.8 in arid and semiarid climates. A value of Rs/Rso = 0.3 presumes total cloud cover. Soil heat flux is important for hourly calculations. Equations 3.48 and 3.49 can be used
to derive G for the hourly periods. The required meteorological data consists of:
•  Air temperature: mean hourly temperature (Thr).
•  Air humidity: average hourly relative humidity (RHhr) or hourly dewpoint
temperature.
•  Wind speed: average hourly wind speed data measured at or transformed to 2 m
height (u2).
•  Radiation: total hourly solar (Rs) or net radiation (Rn). Because of the need for standardization, the constants in Equations 2.5 are based on a
constant surface resistance (rs) of 50 s m-1 during daytime periods, i.e., when Rn > 0. The
rs = 50 s m-1 is represented by the 0.24 coefficient in the denominator of Equation 2.5a. This constant resistance best represents the behaviour of the clipped grass reference
during daytime hours. The constant resistance is increased to 200 s m-1 for night-time
periods, when Rn < 0, and is represented by using a constant 0.96 in the denominator
of Equation 2.5b instead of the constant 0.24. When the calculations of hourly ETo from Equation 2.5a and 2.5b are summed over
24-hour periods to produce 24-hour ETo, the hourly sums are generally equivalent to
calculations of ETo made on a 24-hour time step. Precise estimates of ETo for specific hourly periods may require the use of aerodynamic
stability functions and functions for modifying the value for rs based on levels of
radiation, humidity and temperature. Application of these complex functions is not

4.2.1 Calculation alternatives
The meteorological data, required to estimate ETo by means of the FAO-PM ETo
equation, consists of air temperature, air humidity, wind speed and radiation. Where
some of these data are missing or cannot be calculated, it is strongly recommended that
the user estimate the missing climatic data with one of the procedures presented in
Chapters 2 and 3 and that the FAO-PM method be used for the calculation of ETo. The
use of an alternative ETo calculation procedure, requiring only limited meteorological
parameters, is less recommended. Example 4.4 illustrates the estimation of monthly ETo with the FAO-PM for a data
set containing only maximum and minimum air temperature. The procedures given in
Chapters 2 and 3 to estimate missing humidity, radiation and wind speed data should
be validated by comparing ETo calculated with full and with limited data sets for

4. Determination of ETo
The performance of AI models relies heavily on the quality and availability of data. AI can not readily correct for faulty data that may be ingested into the AI process,
but are not recognized as faulty. Nor does AI provide a replacement for physics-based
relationships. These guidelines wish to be quite clear that the FAO-PM equation does
NOT need to be replaced by an AI-generated simpler equation, even when some
weather data are missing. The FAO-PM equation is a physics-based equation that
contains the internal, physical responses and sensitivities to impacts of the four primary
weather parameters that drive the ET process. These parameters are solar radiation
(and therefore net radiation), air temperature, air humidity and wind speed. These
parameters have strong interactions within the ET process that utilizes knowledge of
available environmental energy and aerodynamic transfer processes to estimate the
total transfer and transformation of energy into the vapourization of liquid water. Many practitioners are learning to use AI, but they may not be learning or adhering
to the physics that govern ET processes. In addition, users of AI may not first gain or
exercise an ability to recognize or to question faulty data prior to ingestion into an AI
procedure. As a result, they may create abstract and incorrect relationships between
ETo and weather data or between ETo and ground-measurements of reference ET that
may not have the appropriate structures, accuracies and sensitivities. Good quality
assessment and quality control (QAQC) is fundamental to the process. The QAQC
step requires overview, correction and concurrence by a knowledgeable human. These guidelines make it clear that it is best to remain with the use of a physics-based
reference equation, the FAO-Penman-Monteith equation, and make best estimates for
missing weather data, rather than to employ an AI engine that may not adhere to all
physical laws that govern ET. The result of the latter process can be the production
of tangential errors that violate physical principles. Precaution, coupled with human
oversight and review, is critical. A well-designed and trained AI process may be useful for recognizing deviation of
weather data from that occurring under reference (well-watered) conditions due to aridity
in or surrounding a weather station. The process can then make necessary adjustments to
the data using procedures similar to those addressed previously in Chapter 2. 4.3 PAN EVAPORATION METHOD
4.3.1 Pan evaporation
The evaporation rate from pans filled with water is easily obtained. In the absence of
rain, the amount of water evaporated during a period (mm day-1) corresponds with the
decrease in water depth in that period. Pans provide a measurement of the integrated
effect of radiation, wind, temperature and humidity on the evaporation from an open
water surface. Although the pan responds in a similar fashion to the same climatic
factors affecting crop transpiration, several factors produce significant differences in
loss of water from a water surface and from a cropped surface. The reflection of solar
radiation from water in the shallow pan might be different from the assumed 23 percent
for the grass reference surface. Storage of heat within the pan can be appreciable and
may cause significant evaporation during the night while most crops transpire only
during the daytime. There are also differences in turbulence, temperature and humidity
of the air immediately above the respective surfaces. Heat transfer through the sides of
the pan occurs and affects the energy balance.

Notwithstanding the difference between pan-evaporation and the evapotranspiration
of cropped surfaces, the use of pans to predict ETo for periods of 10 days or longer may
be warranted. The pan evaporation is related to the reference evapotranspiration by an
empirically derived pan coefficient:

Pan types and environment
Different types of pans exist. Descriptions of Class A and Colorado sunken pans are
given in Boxes 4.2 and 4.3. As the colour, size, and field position of the pan have a
significant influence on the measured results, the pan coefficients are pan specific. In selecting the appropriate pan coefficient, not only the pan type, but also the
ground cover in the station, its surroundings as well as the general wind and humidity
conditions, should be checked. The siting of the pan and the pan environment also
influence the results. This is particularly so where the pan is placed in fallow rather
than cropped fields. Two cases are commonly considered: Case A where the pan is sited
on a short green (grass) cover and surrounded by fallow soil; and Case B where the pan
is sited on fallow soil and surrounded by a green crop (Figure 4.2). FIGURE 4.2

BOX 4.2
Description of Class A pan
The Class A Evaporation pan is circular, 120.7 cm in diameter and 25 cm deep. It is
made of galvanized iron (22 gauge) or Monel metal (0.8 mm). The pan is mounted on
a wooden open frame platform which is 15 cm above ground level. The soil is built up
to within 5 cm of the bottom of the pan. The pan must be level. It is filled with water
to 5 cm below the rim, and the water level should not be allowed to drop to more
than 7.5 cm below the rim. The water should be regularly renewed, at least weekly, to
eliminate extreme turbidity. The pan, if galvanized, is painted annually with aluminum
paint. Screens over the pan are not a standard requirement and should preferably not
be used. Pans should be protected by fences to keep animals from drinking. The site should preferably be under grass, 20 by 20 m (at least 15 by 15), open on all
sides to permit free circulation of the air. It is preferable that stations be located in the
centre or on the leeward side of large cropped fields. Pan readings are taken daily in the early morning at the same time that precipitation
is measured. Measurements are made in a stilling well that is situated in the pan near
one edge. The stilling well is a metal cylinder of about 10 cm in diameter and some 20
cm deep with a small hole at the bottom.

BOX 4.3
Description of Colorado sunken pan
The Colorado sunken pan is 92 cm (3 ft) square and 46 cm (18 in) deep, made of 3
mm thick iron, placed in the ground with the rim 5 cm (2 in) above the soil level. Also, the dimensions 1 m square and 0.5 m deep are frequently used. The pan is
painted with black tar paint. The water level is maintained at or slightly below
ground level, i.e. 5-7.5 cm below the rim. Measurements are taken similarly to those for the Class A pan. Siting and environment
requirements are also similar to those for the Class A pan. Sunken Colorado pans are
sometimes preferred in crop water requirements studies, as these pans give a better
direct estimation of the reference evapotranspiration than does the Class A pan. The
disadvantage is that maintenance is more difficult and leaks are not visible. Pan coefficients
Depending on the type of pan and the size and state of the upwind buffer zone (fetch),
pan coefficients will differ. The larger the upwind buffer zone, the more the air moving
over the pan will be in equilibrium with the buffer zone. At equilibrium with a large
fetch, the air contains more water vapour and less heat in Case A than in Case B
(Figure 4.2). Pan coefficients for the Class A pan and for the Colorado sunken pan for
different ground cover, fetch and climatic conditions are presented in Tables 4.1 and
4.2. For extensive areas of bare-fallow soils and no agricultural development, reduce
Kp by 20 percent under hot, windy conditions; by 5-10 percent for moderate wind,
temperature and humidity conditions. Regression equations derived from the tables are presented in Table 4.3. Where measured
data from other types of sunken pans are available, such data should first be related to
Colorado sunken pan data or to the FAO Penman-Monteith equation to develop Kp. Ratios between evaporation from sunken pans and from the Colorado sunken pan for
different climatic conditions and pan environment are given in Table 4.4.

4. Determination of ETo
Adjustments
Under some conditions not accounted for in the tables, the presented Kp coefficients
may need some adjustment. This is the case in areas with no agricultural development,
or where the pans are enclosed by tall crops. Not maintaining the standard colour
of the pan or installing screens can affect the pan readings and will require some
adjustment of the pan coefficient. In areas with no agricultural development and extensive areas of bare soils (large fetch, Case
B), as found under desert or semi-desert conditions, the listed values for Kp given for arid,
windy areas may need to be reduced by up to 20 percent; for areas with moderate levels of
wind, temperature and relative humidity, the listed values may need to be reduced by 5-10
percent; no or little reduction in Kp is needed in humid, cool conditions. Where pans are placed in a small enclosure but surrounded by tall crops, for example
2.5 m high maize, the listed pan coefficients will need to be increased by up to 30
percent for dry windy climates, whereas only a 5-10 percent increase is required for
calm, humid conditions. Painting the pans may affect the pan evaporation. The pan coefficients presented
apply to galvanized pans annually painted with aluminium and to stainless steel pans. Little difference in Epan will occur where the inside and outside surfaces of the pan
are painted white. An increase in Epan of up to 10 percent may occur when they are
painted black. The material from which the pan is made may account for variations
of only a few percent. The level at which the water is maintained in the pan is important; resulting errors may
be up to 15 percent when water levels in the Class A pan fall 10 cm below the accepted
standard of between 5 and 7.5 cm below the rim. Screens mounted over pans will reduce
Epan by up to 10 percent. In an attempt to avoid pans being used by birds for drinking,
pans filled to the rim with water can be placed near the Class A pan; birds may prefer
to use the fully filled pan. The evaporation pan should be placed in a large, secure, wire
enclosure to prevent animals from entering and drinking. The turbidity of the water
in the pan usually does not affect Epan by more than 5 percent. The overall variation in
Epan is not constant with time because of aging, deterioration and repainting. Recommendations
The above considerations and adjustments indicate that the use of tables or the
corresponding equations may not be sufficient to consider all local environmental factors
influencing Kp and that local adjustment may be required. To do so, an appropriate
calibration of Epan against ETo computed with the Penman-Monteith method is
recommended. It is recommended that the pan should be installed inside a short green cropped area with
a size of a square of at least 15 by 15 m. The pan should not be installed in the centre but
at a distance of at least 10 m from the green crop edge in the general upwind direction. Where observations of wind speed and relative humidity, required for the computation
of Kp, are not available at the site, estimates of the weather variables from a nearby
station have to be utilized. It is then recommended that these variables be averaged for
the computation period and that Epan be averaged for the same period. Notice from the Example 4.5 that the for pan sittings produce the same pan evaporation
7.9 mm per day but necessarily selecting distinct pan coefficients leads to very different
results for the reference evapotranspiration, thus much care is required in selecting the
pan coefficient.

5. Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc ) and its measurement
Introduction to crop
evapotranspiration (ETc)
and its measurement
This chapter outlines the crop coefficient (Kc) approach for calculating the crop
evapotranspiration under standard conditions (ETc). The standard conditions refer
to crops grown in large fields under excellent agronomic and soil water conditions. The crop evapotranspiration differs distinctly from the reference evapotranspiration
(ETo) as the ground cover, canopy properties and aerodynamic resistance of the crop
are different from grass. The effects of characteristics that distinguish field crops from
grass are integrated into the crop coefficient. In the crop coefficient approach, crop
evapotranspiration is calculated by multiplying ETo by Kc. Differences in evaporation and transpiration between field crops and the reference
grass surface can be integrated into a single crop coefficient (Kc) or separated into
two coefficients: a basal crop (Kcb) and a soil evaporation coefficient (Ke), i.e. Kc =
Kcb + Ke. The approach to follow should be selected as a function of the purpose of
the calculation, the accuracy required and the data available. A brief review of ETc
measurement using ground and remote observations and sensors is added. 5.1 CALCULATION PROCEDURES
5.1.1 Direct calculation
The evapotranspiration rate from a cropped surface can be directly measured by the
mass transfer or the energy balance method. It can also be derived from studies of the
soil water balance determined from cropped fields or from lysimeters. Crop evapotranspiration can also be derived from meteorological and crop data by
means of the FAO-PM ETo equation (Equation 2.1). By adjusting the albedo and
the aerodynamic and canopy surface resistances to the growing characteristics of
the specific crop, the evapotranspiration rate can be directly estimated using the
Penman-Monteith combination equation (Equation 2.3). The albedo and resistances
are, however, difficult to estimate accurately as they may vary continually during
the growing season as climatic conditions change, as the crop develops, and with the
wetness of the soil surface. The canopy resistance will further be influenced by the soil
water availability, and it increases strongly if the crop is subjected to water stress. As there is still a considerable lack of consolidated information on the aerodynamic and
canopy resistances for the various cropped surfaces, the FAO-PM ETo equation is used
in these guidelines only for estimating ETo, the evapotranspiration from a well-watered
(hypothetical) grass surface having fixed crop height, albedo, and surface resistance. Chapter 5

5.1.2 Crop coefficient approach
In the crop coefficient approach the crop evapotranspiration, ETc, is calculated by
multiplying the reference crop evapotranspiration, ETo, by a crop coefficient, Kc:
ETc = Kc ETo
(5.1)
where ETc
crop evapotranspiration [mm d-1],
Kc
crop coefficient [dimensionless],
ETo
reference crop evapotranspiration [mm d-1]. Most of the effects of the various weather conditions are incorporated into the ETo estimate. Therefore, as ETo represents an index of climatic demand, Kc varies predominately with
the specific crop characteristics and only to a limited extent with climate. This enables
the transfer of standard values for Kc between locations and between climates. This has
been a primary reason for the global acceptance and usefulness of the crop coefficient
approach and the Kc standard values developed in past studies. The reference ETo is defined and calculated using the FAO-PM ETo equation (Chapters
2 and 4). The crop coefficient, Kc, is basically the ratio of the crop ETc to the reference
ETo, and it represents an integration of the effects of four primary characteristics that
distinguish the crop from the reference grass. These characteristics are:
•  Crop height: the crop height influences the aerodynamic resistance term, ra, of the
FAO-PM ETo equation and the turbulent transfer of vapour from the crop into
the atmosphere. The ra term appears twice in the full form of the FAO-PM ETo
equation.
•  Albedo (reflectance) of the crop-soil surface: the albedo is affected by the fraction
of ground covered by vegetation and by the soil surface wetness. The albedo of
the crop-soil surface influences the net radiation of the surface, Rn, which is the
primary source of the energy exchange for the evaporation process.
•  Canopy resistance: the resistance of the crop to vapour transfer is affected by
leaf area (number of stomata), leaf age and condition, and the degree of stomatal
control. The canopy resistance influences the surface resistance, rs.
•  Evaporation from soil, especially exposed soil. The soil surface wetness and the fraction of ground covered by vegetation influence
the surface resistance, rs. Following soil wetting, the vapour transfer rate from the soil
is high, especially for crops having incomplete ground cover. The combined surface
resistance of the canopy and the soil determines the (bulk) surface resistance, rs. The
surface resistance term in the Penman-Monteith combination Equation 2.3 represents
the resistance to vapour flow from within plant leaves and from beneath the soil surface. The Kc in Equation 5.1 predicts ETc under standard conditions. The standard condition
represents an upper envelope of crop evapotranspiration and represents conditions where
no limitations are placed on crop growth or evapotranspiration due to water shortage,
low crop density, or disease, weed, insect, or salinity pressures. The ETc estimated by Kc
is adjusted if necessary to non-standard conditions. The non-standard actual condition,
which is assumed to represent the actual ET condition, is termed ETc act. ETc act is
estimated and applied when any environmental condition or characteristic is known to
have a negative impact on, or sets a limit on ETc. Factors for correcting ETc to ETc act
are described in Chapter 8 (Part C).

5. Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc ) and its measurement
5.2 FACTORS DETERMINING THE CROP COEFFICIENT
The crop coefficient integrates the effect of characteristics that distinguish a typical field
crop from the grass reference, where the standardized grass reference has a constant
appearance and a complete ground cover. Consequently, different crops will have
different Kc coefficients. The changing characteristics of the crop over the growing
season affect the Kc coefficient. Finally, as evaporation is an integrated part of crop
evapotranspiration, conditions affecting soil evaporation will also have an effect on Kc. 5.2.1 Crop type
Due to differences in albedo, crop height, aerodynamic properties, and leaf and stomata
properties, the evapotranspiration from full-grown, well-watered crops differs from ETo. The close spacings of plants and taller canopy height and roughness of many fullgrown agricultural crops cause these crops to have Kc factors that are larger than 1. The Kc factor is often 5-10 percent higher than the reference (where Kc = 1.0), and even
15-20 percent greater for some tall crops such as maize, sorghum or sugar cane (Figure
5.1). Typical values for the crop coefficient for full-grown crops (Kc mid) are listed in
Tables 6.1 – 6.5 of Chapter 6. In most species, the stomata open as irradiance increases. In addition to the stomatal
response to the environment, the position and number of the stomata and the resistance
of the cuticula to vapour transfer determine the water loss from the crop. Species
with stomata on only the lower side of the leaf and/or large leaf resistances will have
relatively smaller Kc values. This is the case for citrus and most deciduous fruit trees. Transpiration control and spacing of the trees, providing only 70 percent ground cover
for mature trees, may cause the Kc of those trees, if cultivated without a ground cover
crop, to be smaller than 1.0 (Figure 5.1). 5.2.2 Climate
The Kc values of Tables 6.1 – 6.5 of Chapter 6 are typical values expected for average
Kc under a standard climatic condition, which is defined as a sub-humid climate with
average daytime minimum relative humidity (RHmin) ≈ 45% and having calm to
moderate wind speeds averaging u2 = 2 m s-1. Variations in wind speed alter the aerodynamic resistance of the crops and may alter
their crop coefficients, especially for those crops that are substantially taller than the
hypothetical grass reference. The effect of the difference in aerodynamic properties
between the grass reference surface and agricultural crops is not only crop-specific
but it also varies with the climatic conditions and crop height. Because aerodynamic
properties are greater for many agricultural crops as compared to the grass reference,
the ratio of ETc to ETo (i.e. Kc) for many crops increases as wind speed increases and as
relative humidity decreases. More arid climates and conditions of greater wind speed
will tend to have higher values for Kc. More humid climates and conditions of lower
wind speed will have lower values for Kc. The relative impact of the climate on Kc for full-grown crops is illustrated in Figure

in Kc as climate and weather conditions change are quite small for short crops but are
large for tall crops. Guidelines for the adjustment of Kc to the climatic conditions as a
function of crop height are given in Chapter 6.

5. Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc ) and its measurement
Under humid and calm wind conditions, Kc becomes less dependent on the differences
between the aerodynamic components of ETc and ETo and the Kc values for “fullcover” agricultural crops do not exceed 1.0 by more than about 0.05. This is because
full-cover agricultural crops and the reference crop of clipped grass both provide for
nearly maximum absorption of shortwave radiation, which is the primary energy source
for evaporation under humid and calm conditions. Generally, the albedos, α, are similar
over a wide range of full-cover agricultural crops, including the reference crop. Because
the vapour pressure deficit (es − ea) is small under humid conditions, differences in ET
caused by differences in aerodynamic resistance, ra, between the agricultural crop and
the reference crop are also small, especially with low to moderate wind speed. Under arid conditions, the effect of differences in ra between the agricultural crop and
the grass reference crop on ETc becomes more pronounced because the (es − ea) term
may be relatively large. The larger magnitudes of (es − ea) amplify differences in the
aerodynamic term in the numerator of the Penman-Monteith combination equation
(Equation 2.1) for both the crop and the reference crop. Hence, Kc will be larger under
arid conditions when the agricultural crop has a leaf area and roughness height that are
greater than that of the grass reference. Because the 1/ra term in the numerator of the FAO-PM ETo equation (Equation 2.4
and 2.5a, b) is multiplied by the vapour pressure deficit (es − ea), the ET from tall crops
increases proportionately more relative to ETo than does ET from short crops when
relative humidity is low. The Kc for tall crops, such as those 2-3 m in height, can be as
much as 30 percent higher in a windy, arid climate as compared with a calm, humid
climate. The increase in Kc is due to the influence of the larger aerodynamic roughness
of the tall crop relative to grass on the transport of water vapour from the surface. 5.2.3 Soil evaporation
Differences in soil evaporation and crop transpiration between field crops and the
reference surface are integrated within the crop coefficient. The Kc coefficient for fullcover crops primarily reflects differences in transpiration as the contribution of soil
evaporation is relatively small. After rainfall or irrigation, the effect of evaporation is
predominant when the crop is small and scarcely shades the ground. For such lowcover conditions, the Kc coefficient is determined largely by the frequency with which
the soil surface is wetted. Where the soil is wet for most of the time from irrigation or
rain, the evaporation from the soil surface will be considerable and Kc may exceed 1. On the other hand, where the soil surface is dry, evaporation is restricted, and Kc will
be small and might even drop to less than 0.20 (Figure 5.3). Differences in soil evaporation between the field crop and the reference surface can be
forecast more precisely by using a dual crop coefficient. 5.2.4 Crop growth stages
As the crop develops, the ground cover, crop height and leaf area change. Due to
differences in evapotranspiration during the various growth stages, the Kc for a given crop
will vary over the growing period. The growing period can be divided into four distinct
growth stages: initial, crop development, mid-season, and late season. Figure 5.4 illustrates
the general sequence and proportions of these stages for different types of crops.

Crop development stage
The crop development stage runs from 10 percent ground cover to effective full cover. Effective full cover for many crops occurs at the initiation of flowering. For row crops
where rows commonly interlock leaves such as beans, sugar beets, potatoes and maize,
effective cover can be defined as the time when some leaves of plants in adjacent rows
begin to intermingle so that soil shading becomes nearly complete, or when plants
reach nearly full size if no intermingling occurs. For some crops, especially those taller
than 0.5 m, the average fraction of the ground surface covered by vegetation (fc) at
the start of effective full cover is about 0.7-0.8. Fractions of sunlit and shaded soil and
leaves do not change significantly with further growth of the crop beyond fc ≈ 0.7 to
0.8. It is understood that the crop or plant can continue to grow in both height and leaf
area after the time of effective full cover. Because it is difficult to visually determine
when densely sown vegetation such as winter and spring cereals and some grasses reach
effective full cover, the more easily detectable stage of heading (flowering) is generally
used for these types of crops. For dense grasses, effective full cover may occur at about 0.10-0.15 m in height. For thin
stands of grass (dry rangeland), grass height may approach 0.3-0.5 m before effective full
cover is reached. Densely planted forages such as alfalfa and clover reach effective full
cover at about 0.3-0.4 m. Another way to estimate the occurrence of effective full cover
is when the leaf area index (LAI) reaches three in case of very dense low crops. LAI is
defined as the average total area of leaves (one side) per unit area of ground surface. In the case of evergreen woody perennials, it is difficult to distinguish when crop
development started and when it ends. Leaves are there and shade the ground through
the full crop season. Differences in Kc mostly result from the frequency of wettings
by rain and irrigation covering the full surface. Partial cover of irrigation produces
small impacts. In the case of deciduous woody perennials, full development of leaves is
attained quickly and rain and irrigation impacts are minor. As the crop develops and shades more and more of the ground, evaporation becomes
more restricted, and transpiration gradually becomes the major process. During the
crop development stage, the Kc value corresponds to the amounts of ground cover and
plant development. Typically, if the soil surface is dry, Kc = 0.5 corresponds to about
25-40 percent of the ground surface covered by vegetation due to the effects of shading
and due to microscale transport of sensible heat from the soil into the vegetation. A Kc
= 0.7 often corresponds to about 40-60 percent ground cover. These values will vary,
depending on the crop, frequency of wetting and whether the crop uses more water
than the reference crop at full ground cover (e.g. depending on its canopy architecture
and crop height relative to clipped grass). Mid-season stage
The mid-season stage runs from effective full cover to the start of maturity. The start
of maturity is often indicated by the beginning of the aging, yellowing or senescence
of leaves, initial leaf drop, or the browning of fruit to the degree that the crop
evapotranspiration is reduced relative to the reference ETo. The mid-season stage is
the longest stage for perennials and many annuals, but it may be relatively short for
vegetable crops that are harvested fresh for their green vegetation. At the mid-season stage the Kc reaches its maximum value. The value for Kc (Kc mid)
is relatively constant for most growing and cultural conditions, namely for both
evergreen and deciduous woody perennials. Deviation of the Kc mid of annuals from
the reference value “1.0” is primarily due to differences in crop height and resistance
between the grass reference surface and the agricultural crop, and weather conditions.

5. Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc ) and its measurement
Late season stage
The late season stage runs from the start of maturity to harvest or full senescence. The
calculation for Kc and ETc is presumed to end when the crop is harvested, dries out
naturally, reaches full senescence, or experiences leaf drop. For some perennial vegetation in frost-free climates, crops may grow year-round so
that the date of termination may be taken as the same as the date of planting or greenup. This is the case of evergreen woody perennials, which Kc value may not change;
however, for deciduous woody perennials Kc decreases until leaf dropping or is kept
relatively high if autumn irrigation is required to ensure physiological processes that
determine next year yield. The Kc value at the end of the late season stage (Kc end) reflects crop and water
management practices (Figure 5.5). The Kc end value is high if the crop is frequently
irrigated until harvested fresh. If the crop is allowed to senesce and to dry out in the
field before harvest, the Kc end value will be small. Senescence is usually associated with
less efficient stomatal conductance of leaf surfaces due to the effects of aging, thereby
causing a reduction in Kc. 5.3 CROP EVAPOTRANSPIRATION (ETc)
Crop evapotranspiration is calculated by multiplying ETo by Kc, a coefficient expressing
the difference in evapotranspiration between the cropped and the reference grass
surface. The difference can be combined into one single coefficient, or it can be split
into two factors describing separately the differences in evaporation and transpiration
between both surfaces. The selection of the approach depends on the purpose of the
calculation, the accuracy required, the climatic data available and the time step with
which the calculations are executed. Table 5.2 presents the general selection criteria. TABLE 5.2

5.3.1 Single and dual crop coefficient approaches
Single crop coefficient approach (Kc)
In the single crop coefficient approach, the effect of crop transpiration and soil
evaporation are combined into a single coefficient. The coefficient Kc integrates
differences in the soil evaporation and crop transpiration rate between the crop and the
grass reference surface. As soil evaporation may fluctuate daily as a result of rainfall or
irrigation, the single crop coefficient expresses only the time-averaged (multi-day) effects
of crop evapotranspiration. [TABLE 1]

As the single Kc coefficient averages soil evaporation and transpiration, the approach
is used to compute ETc for weekly or longer time periods, although calculations may
proceed on a daily time step. The single, time-averaged Kc is used for planning studies
and irrigation system design where the time-averaging effects of soil wetting are
acceptable and relevant. This is the case for surface irrigation and set sprinkler systems
where the time interval between successive irrigation is of several days, often ten days
or more. For typical irrigation management, the time-averaged single Kc is valid. Dual crop coefficient approach (Kcb + Ke)
In the dual crop coefficient approach, the effects of crop transpiration and soil evaporation
are determined separately. Two coefficients are used: the basal crop coefficient (Kcb) to
describe plant transpiration, and the soil water evaporation coefficient (Ke) to describe
evaporation from the soil surface. The single Kc coefficient is replaced by:
Kc = Kcb + Ke

soil water evaporation coefficient. The basal crop coefficient, Kcb, is defined as the ratio of ETc to ETo when the soil
surface layer is dry but where the average soil water content of the root zone is
adequate to sustain full plant transpiration. The Kcb represents the baseline standard
Kc in the absence of the additional effects of soil wetting by irrigation or precipitation. The basal crop coefficient, Kcb, can also be defined as the ratio of transpiration, Tc
to ETo. Therefore, it is also called the transpiration coefficient. The soil evaporation
coefficient, Ke, describes the evaporation component from the soil surface. If the soil
is wet, following rain or irrigation, Ke may be large. However, the sum of Kcb and
Ke can never exceed a maximum value, Kc max, determined by the energy available for
evapotranspiration at the soil surface. As the soil surface becomes drier, Ke becomes
smaller and falls to zero when no water is left for evaporation. The estimation of Ke
requires a daily water balance computation for the calculation of the soil water content
remaining in the upper topsoil. The dual coefficient approach requires more numerical calculations than the procedure
using the single time-averaged Kc coefficient. The dual procedure is best for real-time
irrigation scheduling, for soil water balance computations, and for research studies
where the effects of day-to-day variations in soil surface wetness and the resulting
impacts on daily ETc, the soil water profile, and deep percolation fluxes are important. This is the case for high-frequency irrigation with micro-irrigation systems, namely
drippers, or lateral move systems such as centre pivots and linear move systems. 5.3.2 Crop coefficient curve
After the selection of the calculation approach, the determination of the lengths for
the crop growth stages and the corresponding crop coefficients, a crop coefficient
curve can be constructed. The curve represents the changes in the crop coefficient over
the length of the growing season. The shape of the curve represents the changes in the
vegetation and ground cover during plant development and maturation that affect the
ratio of ETc to ETo. From the curve, the Kc coefficient and, hence, ETc can be derived
for any period within the growing season.

The single “time-averaged” Kc curve in Figure 5.6 incorporates averaged wetting effects
into the Kc factor. The value for Kc mid is relatively constant for most growing and

during the mid-season stage, soil evaporation beneath the canopy has less effect on
crop evapotranspiration and the value for Kcb in the mid-season stage will be nearly
the same as Kc. Depending on the ground cover, the basal crop coefficient during the
mid-season may be only 0.05-0.10 lower than the Kc value. Depending on the frequency
with which the crop is irrigated during the late season stage, Kcb will be similar to (if
infrequently irrigated) or less than the Kc value.

5.5 DETERMINATION OF CROP EVAPOTRANSPIRATION AND
CROP COEFFICIENTS
The main methods for measuring actual and standard ETc are described in the last section
of Chapter 1, namely the soil water balance in lysimeters or the field, and the surface
energy balance performed with ground and remote sensing approaches. That section is
intended to draw the readers' attention to the need for accuracy in the determination
of crop ET, thus discussing some critical aspects that affect measurement accuracy and
the main pitfalls to be avoided. Over the last 25 years, hundreds of scientific papers
have been published reporting crop ET measurements or estimates, and new (updated)
Kc and Kcb values for nearly all vegetable and field crops, as well as for fruit trees and
vines. As a follow-up, the current section presents several examples of procedures for
determining crop coefficients using ground and remote sensing techniques. 5.5.1 Kc and Kcb curves from ground measurements
Figure 5.9 shows daily canola (Brassica napus L. cv. “Kabel”) ETc data measured by
a large weighing lysimeter, 2.7 × 2.3 × 1.7 m in size, near Albacete (SE Spain) under
pristine, well-watered conditions during two growing seasons. All agronomic practices
- fertilization, weeds, pest and disease control - were performed aiming at optimizing
crop growth conditions. ETc values increased quickly as the crop development period
progressed due to the fast increase of the canopy cover facilitated by favourable spring
temperatures. Peak ETc was reached during the mid-season period coinciding with a
maximum fraction of ground covered by vegetation. The peak ET periods had measured ETc approaching or even exceeding the values for
ETo. ETc declined during the late season stage as green canopy cover decreased. Seasonal
lysimeter-based canola ETc was 472 and 602 mm in 2008 and 2012, respectively. The
28 percent higher ETc value in 2012 was due to higher evaporative demand during the
growing season, mainly during the period of maximum canola water requirements. The midseason period was also 5 days longer in 2012. The total ETo was 74 percent
higher in 2012 than in 2008, because the midseason period occurred about 15 days later
in 2012 than in 2008, when ETo was higher, coinciding with the high temperatures of
late spring and early summer. The higher irrigation requirements by 2012 were due to
lower precipitation in that year relative to 2008. The larger number of irrigation events
in 2012 increased the total ETc through increased evaporation from the soil. Kc values, shown in Figure 5.10, were calculated as the ratio of the lysimetermeasured ETc to ETo, that was computed with the FAO-PM ETo equation. The Kc
values were adjusted to the FAO56 segmented crop coefficient curve relative to the
four canola growth stages. Kc values during crop development and late season stages
were linearly interpolated between Kc ini and Kc mid. Lengths of the growth stages were
determined so that the five-day Kc averages followed the linear segments as closely
as possible, with similar numbers of values above and below the curve segments. The
maximum average Kc values of 1.15 in 2008 and 1.24 in 2012 defined the Kc mid for the
mid-season stage. After adjusting to the standardized subhumid climate by solving
Equation 6.16 for Kc (tab), the estimated Kc mid values were 1.13 and 1.17. The Kc mid
value was higher in 2012 than in 2008, primarily due to the drier weather conditions
in 2012 (lower minimum relative humidity).

Actual Kcb and Kc values can be estimated using remote sensing based on field, aerial
or satellite platforms, using empirical approaches based on spectral reflectance. Remote
observations of Kcb and Kc are valuable when field information, such as planting dates
or rates of vegetation development, are not well known. The estimation of Kcb from
reflectance-based vegetation indices (VI) is possible because of the generally close
correspondence between vegetation amount and transpiration, where, as vegetation
cover increases, leaf area increases and transpiration and Kcb increase. The crop
coefficients obtained from reflectance represent the actual ET conditions of the field
(ideal or nonideal) and are termed Kcb act RS and Kc act RS. [TABLE 1]

5.5.3 Determination of Kc using energy balance from remote sensing
The remote sensing surface energy balance (RS-SEB) method was introduced and
described in Chapter 1. Over the last 25 years, various remote sensing approaches based
on surface energy balance have been developed and widely used. RS-SEB methods
take advantage of the physical fact that conversion of liquid water to vapour requires
very substantial amounts of energy. This conversion of liquid to vapour during the
evaporation process involves the same physical requirements whether the process is the
transpiration of water from inside a plant leaf or the evaporation of water from a wet
soil surface. The energy consumption by the conversion of liquid to vapour cools the
evaporating surface, thus variations in surface temperature can be used to estimate the
net radiation and sensible heat exchange at the surface. These estimates can then be used
with the energy balance equation (Equation 1.1) to estimate the crop evapotranspiration. As an example of a local application of RS-SEB, Figure 5.13 shows data from a field
experiment conducted near Albacete (SE Spain), where lysimeter observations and ETc
estimates using a Simplified Two-Source Energy Balance (STSEB) model are compared
for a sprinkler-irrigated wheat field cropped under near-pristine conditions. A quantitative analysis comparing modelled (STSEB) and observed (lysimeter) daily
ETc shows an average underestimation of ETc by the RS-SEB model of 0.18 mm day-1,
with a determination coefficient (r2) of 0.903. The combination of the two-source energy
balance with local radiometric temperatures has shown to effectively estimate actual

ETc values for a variety of crops and environmental conditions, which can be useful in
developing actual Kc act values, especially for conditions of water and salt stresses. The
main limitation to its operational application is the retrieval of land surface temperature
from satellite data with sufficient spatial and temporal resolution. The spatial resolution
of thermal data can be especially limiting in agricultural areas composed of cropped
fields smaller than 1 ha. FIGURE 5.13

5.5.4 Strengths and limitations of remote sensing for evapotranspiration
The VI-based and SEB-based approaches can be considered a complement to the
FAO 56 Kc approach because they can capture within-season sudden climatic,
environmental and management stresses, thus assisting in identifying potential
problems and developing corrective actions. Advantages of RS-based crop coefficients estimation include: Quick analyses can be
performed by mid-level technicians; large areas can be covered; relationships VI-Kcb
can be calibrated; the spatial resolution can be high, and costs can be relatively low. Disadvantages refer mainly to: latter relationships may vary with the stomatal control
that impacts the ET vs. greenness indices and Kcb vs. VI relationships, thus requiring
that crop type be known; when short of water, trees can exhibit more stomatal control
than annual crops and, therefore, cause a shift in the Kcb vs VI relationship; VI-based
relationships tend to overestimate ET during conditions of acute water shortage
because there is a VI time lag in any reduction in vegetation amount during periods
of water shortage, whereas vegetation can quickly reduce stomatal conductance
and therefore transpiration. The estimation of the soil evaporation component is
less accurate because there is not a direct relationship with the vegetation amount,
and VI’s may not identify or quantify multi-storeyed canopies, especially for dense
vegetation. Advantages and disadvantages of RS are given in Tables 5.4 and 5.5. A robust procedure is required to interpolate Kc act information from satellite or aerial

Surface Energy Balance for determination of Kc act
As previously described, VI-based methods perform best for estimating Kcb act due
to the close ties between transpiration, as represented by the Kcb, and the amount
of vegetation cover as represented by the VI. In contrast, RS-SEB models produce
estimates for total Kc act by viewing the combined processes of transpiration and
evaporation. As a result, RS-SEB models can be used to develop relationships between
Kc act and VI that can then be employed using the more frequently available VI-based
imagery. Another use of paired RS-SEB and VI-based estimates is to estimate whether
water shortage or drought is impacting crop production. This is done by noting periods
when RS-SEB-based ETc act is lower than the VI-based ETc estimate. Determinations
of reduced ET from water stress can be made difficult, however, by uncertainties,
inaccuracies and biases in both modeling approaches. 5.5.6 Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for developing Kc data and
precautions
Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms can ingest data from remote sensing, weather
stations, and ground measurements to learn complex relationships observed among
different factors and ET rates. AI models can help reduce uncertainty in ET estimations
by learning from various data sources and accounting for land cover dynamics. This can
lead to better water management practices and a more comprehensive understanding of
the water cycle. However, AI can not directly recognize nor correct for faulty data that
is ingested into the process. This is most true with Kc data, where substantial errors and
biases in both ground-based and remote-sensing-based measurements can frequently
occur. The application of powerful cognition and ingestion of large amounts of data
does not offset nor cure the impacts of faulty, biased data. In fact, AI may magnify
the influences of biased or faulty ET data on derived relationships. The result can be
a worse estimation of ET as compared to using direct Kc curves or remotely-sensed ET
procedures alone. Therefore, strong precautions should be taken, along with a required
precursor involving a study of the physics of the evapotranspiration processes, impacts
of agronomic practices and plant physiology. Some advantages of employing AI can include the classification of crop type in near real
time. Near-real-time classification, for example using satellite imagery, can facilitate the
forecasting of near- and mid-term, field-specific ET for irrigation management.

In addition, reported Kc curves often do not follow the defined procedure for the FAO
segmented curves, or Kc results are presented as time-dependent polynomial equations,
or are only referenced to weekly, 10-day or, more often, monthly periods. Crop growth
stages are sometimes defined contradictorily relative to definitions adopted in FAO 56
and previously in FAO 24. Information provided in those papers may be sufficient relative to the objectives of
the studies reported but is insufficient to provide for the transferability of reported
Kc into different environments. These limitations oblige the user to conduct a careful
review of published material to determine when derived Kc are only of local interest and
application and/or represent non-standard experimental conditions. This is in contrast
to when the reported Kc represents a standard Kc that adheres to recognizable potential
evaporative crop conditions that are expected to result from optimal, pristine cropping
practices, and are consequently transferable to other environments when adequately
adjusted to the standardized climate. The above concerns and observations were taken into account when compiling the
Kc information contained in the Tables of Chapters 6 and 7. Intending to provide
accurate standard and updated Kc values, the compilation procedure required that
the ET data reported in the literature were exempt from difficult-to-determine biases
and mistakes that could compromise the accuracy and representativeness of the data. Chapter 1 describes the primary methods for measuring actual ETc or indirectly
deriving ETc estimates, emphasizing the accuracy requirements in measurements and
the main pitfalls to avoid. These requirements were considered when assessing Kc and
ETc data from the literature.

6. ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc)
ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc)
This chapter deals with the calculation of crop evapotranspiration (ETc) under
standard, pristine, non-stressed cropping conditions. No limitations are placed on
crop growth and evapotranspiration from soil water and salinity stress, reduced crop
density, pests and diseases, weed infestation, or low fertility and nutrients (see Figure
1.4 bis). ETc is determined by the crop coefficient approach whereby the effect of the
various weather conditions are incorporated into ETo and the crop characteristics into
the standard Kc coefficient:
ETc = Kc ETo
(6.1)
The single Kc coefficient incorporates crop characteristics and averaged effects of
evaporation from the soil. For normal irrigation planning and management purposes,
for the development of basic irrigation schedules, and for most hydrologic water balance
studies, average crop coefficients are relevant and may be more convenient than the
Kc computed on a daily time step using the dual Kc approach where a separate crop
transpiration and soil evaporation coefficient are determined (Chapter 7). Only when
values for Kc are needed on a daily basis for specific fields of crops and/or for specific
years, or where wetting frequencies from precipitation or irrigation are frequent or
varied, must a separate transpiration and evaporation coefficient (Kcb + Ke) be considered. The calculation procedure for crop evapotranspiration, ETc, consists of:
1. identifying the crop growth stages, selecting the corresponding Kc coefficients
and determining their stage lengths;
2. adjusting the selected Kc coefficients for frequency of wetting or climatic
conditions during each stage;
3. constructing the crop coefficient curve, i.e. providing to determine Kc values
for any period during the growing season; and
4. calculating ETc as the product of ETo and Kc. 6.1 CROP COEFFICIENTS. TABULATED VALUES
Changes in vegetation and ground cover imply that the crop coefficient Kc varies
during the growing season. The trends in Kc during the growing season are represented
in the crop coefficient segmented curve. Only three values for Kc are required to
describe and construct the crop coefficient curve: those during the initial stage (Kc ini),
the mid-season stage (Kc mid) and at the end of the late season stage (Kc end). The standard values for Kc ini, Kc mid, and Kc end, presented as single-valued Kc for
agricultural crops and natural vegetation, are listed in Table 6.1 for vegetable crops,
Table 6.2 for field crops, Table 6.3 for fruit trees and vines, Table 6.4 for grasslands
and grasses, and in Table 6.5 for riparian and non-riparian wetland ecosystems. The
crop coefficients are organized by group type and alphabetic order inside the groups
to assist readers in locating the crop in the tables. In addition to Kc values, maximum
crop heights (h, m) and ranges of maximum root depths (Zr, m) are listed in the Tables. Chapter 6

(and irrigation) and, therefore, refinements to the value used for Kc ini should always be
made with consideration of the impacts of rainfall and/or irrigation on soil evaporation,
especially when the presence of bare soil can dominate. For frequent wettings such as
with high frequency sprinkler and drip irrigation, or rainfall, the values for Kc ini may
increase substantially. The tabulated Kc, particularly the Kc ini, may be substantially
reduced when the soil is mulched using plastic or organic mulches, which control and
decrease evaporation from the soil. These effects vary with the wetting frequency by
rainfall and irrigation, soil characteristics, soil-water conservation practices, and the
fraction of soil covered by the vegetation. Thus, the tabulated standard Kc does not
include the effects of soil mulching, which shall be considered specifically according to
the type and amount of mulches used as dealt with in Chapter 10.

The tabulated standard Kc values result from an in-depth review of crop coefficients
published in scientific and technical papers. This review led to the selection of only
those publications that have reported consistent field research approaches to derive
the Kc values, as well as adequate scientific computational and writing skills. The
first sources of information and data were the previous FAO Irrigation and Drainage
Papers Number 24 and 33 and the original version of the current Irrigation and
Drainage Paper Number 56. The updated reviews were published in various books or
reports and, mainly, in peer reviewed journal articles. Information from reviews was
assembled and tabulated in purposeful journal papers listed in the bibliography of the
current guidelines. These papers provide detailed information not included herein, and
that could be accessed in the original articles, which are of great interest to readers. The standard values for Kc mid and Kc end in Tables 6.1 and 6.2 represent those for a
standardized sub-humid climate having an average daytime minimum relative humidity
(RHmin) of about 45 percent and with calm to moderate wind speeds averaging
u2 = 2 m s-1. For more humid or arid conditions, or for more or less windy conditions,
the Kc values for the mid-season and end-season stages should be corrected for climate
as described hereafter in this chapter. The values for standard Kc in Tables 6.1, 6.2 and
6.3 represent values for non-stressed crops cultivated under excellent agronomic and
water management conditions and achieving maximum crop yield (standard conditions). Mild and controlled water stress that may favour yield quality, called eustress, also leads
to small water savings. It may be particularly interesting for tree and vine fruit crops,
which are often subjected to controlled and regulated mild water stress. The tabulated values of Kc for grasslands and grasses (Table 6.4.) include those for both
semi-natural vegetation and planted grasses, mostly pasturelands for grazing, often with
cuts for hay as is the case of mountain meadows, irrigated or not. They should be used as
standard crop coefficients. Planted grasslands may include forages for grazing and, less
frequently, for hay and silage. Typical but wide groups of such grasslands are therefore
identified, and Kc values are also assigned to them. Other numerous semi-natural
grasses used for grazing are those characterizing given biomes or ecosystems, including
in regions marked by aridity; Kc values are assigned to those typical groups. Finally,
there is a large number of cultivated grasses having specialized uses such as hay, grazing
or landscape, the latter referred to as turf grasses. Kc values are assigned to groups of
somewhat similar grass crops, but alfalfa is individually considered. Grasslands are kept
low if used for grazing and landscape, or with a variable height during every cutting
cycle. Their Kc values were not adjusted to climate. Users should compare the local climate with the standardized climate (RHmin of
about 45 percent and with calm to moderate wind speeds averaging u2 = 2 m s-1) and
adjust Kc values when required. Moreover, the Kc values should be reduced by 10 to
30 percent when vegetation conditions or cultivation practices are not optimal and
depart from the standard. [TABLE 1]

6.2 CROP COEFFICIENT FOR THE INITIAL STAGE (Kc ini)
6.2.1 Calculation procedure
The values for Kc ini in Tables 6.1 – 6.5 are only approximations and, for irrigation of crops,
should only be used for estimating ETc during preliminary or planning studies. For all
crops and vegetation, the value for Kc ini that is listed is considered representative of the
crop under typical irrigation water management, or under typical water supply conditions
in cases of semi-natural non-planted grasslands (Table 6.4) and wetlands and riparian
vegetation (Table 6.5). More accurate estimates of Kc ini can be obtained by considering:
a. The time interval between wetting events
Evapotranspiration during the initial stage for annual crops is predominately
in the form of evaporation from exposed soil due to low levels of vegetation. Therefore, accurate estimates for Kc ini should consider the frequency with which
the soil surface is wetted during the initial period. Where the soil is frequently
or continuously wet from irrigation, rain, or a natural surface or groundwater
source, the evaporation from the soil surface can be considerable and Kc ini will
be large, e.g. flooded rice and wetlands vegetation. On the other hand, where the
soil surface is dry, evaporation is restricted and the Kc ini will be small (Table 5.1).
b. Evaporation power of the atmosphere
The value for Kc ini is affected by the evaporating power of the atmosphere, i.e.
which is indicated by ETo. The higher the evaporation power of the atmosphere,
the quicker the soil will dry between water applications and the smaller the timeaveraged Kc ini will be for any particular period. In contrast, Kc ini will generally be
high for inundated vegetation.
c. Magnitude of the wetting events
The amount of water available in the topsoil for evaporation and hence the time
for the soil surface to dry is a function of the magnitude of the wetting event. Therefore, Kc ini will be smaller for light wetting events than for large wettings. Depending on the time interval between wetting events, the magnitude of the
wetting event and the evaporation power of the atmosphere, Kc ini can vary
between 0.10 and 1.15. In general, Kc ini for flooded vegetation is not affected by
precipitation events. [TABLE 1]

6.2.2 Time interval between wetting events under irrigation
For estimating Kc ini, a mean time interval between wetting events is estimated by
counting all rainfall and irrigation events occurring during the initial period that are
greater than a few millimetres. Wetting events occurring on adjacent days can be
counted as one event. The mean wetting interval is estimated by dividing the time length
(days) of the initial period by the number of events (Example 6.1). EXAMPLE 6.1

6.2.7 Background and computations for Kc for the initial stage of
annual crops
Evaporation from bare soil (Es) can be characterized as occurring in two distinct stages. Stage 1 is termed the "energy-limited" stage. During this stage, moisture is transported
to the soil surface at a rate sufficient to supply the potential rate of evaporation (Eso),
which, in turn, is governed by energy availability at the soil surface. In this procedure,
Eso is estimated from
Eso = 1.15 ETo
(6.5)
where Eso is the potential rate of evaporation [mm d-1] and ETo is the mean ETo during
the initial period [mm d-1]. The value 1.15 represents increased evaporation potential
due to the low albedo of wet soil and the possibility of heat stored in the surface layer
during previous dry periods. Stage 2 is termed the "soil water limited" stage, where hydraulic transport of subsurface
water to the soil surface is unable to supply water at the potential evaporation rate. During
stage 2, the soil surface appears partially dry and a portion of the evaporation occurs from
below the soil surface. The energy required for subsurface evaporation is supplied by the
transport of heat from the soil surface into the soil profile. The evaporation rate during
stage 2 drying decreases as soil water content decreases as shown in Figure 6.4. The
evaporation rate can therefore be expressed as being proportional to the water remaining
in the evaporation layer relative to the maximum depth of water that can be evaporated
from the same soil layer during stage 2 drying. The background of this procedure is the
same as for the computation of the evaporation coefficient Ke in the dual crop coefficient
approach dealt with in Chapter 7, where further details are provided. The maximum total depth of water that can be evaporated from the surface soil layer
is termed “total evaporable water” or TEW. In turn, the maximum total depth of water
that can be evaporated during stage 1 is termed “readily evaporable water” or REW,
which is discussed in Chapter 7. If the evaporation rate during stage 2 drying is assumed to be linearly proportional to
the equivalent depth of water remaining in the evaporation layer, as shown in Figure
6.4, then the average soil water evaporation rate during stage 2 can be estimated as

6.2.9 Total evaporable water
The value for TEW is the maximum depth of water that can be evaporated from the
soil following wetting. The value for TEW is governed by the depth of the soil profile
contributing to soil water evaporation and by the soil water holding properties within
the evaporating layer. In addition, the value for TEW is affected by the unsaturated
hydraulic conductivity, by the presence of a hydraulically limiting layer beneath the
evaporating layer, and by the conduction of sensible heat into the soil to supply energy
for subsurface evaporation. An approximation for the maximum value of TEW for
initial periods having ETo ≥ 5 mm d-1 is:

6.3.1 Illustration of the climatic effect
As discussed in Chapter 5, the effect of the difference in aerodynamic properties
between the grass reference surface and agricultural crops is not only crop specific but
also varies with the climatic conditions and crop height (Figures 5.2 and 5.4). More arid
climates and conditions of greater wind speed will have higher values for Kc mid. More
humid climates and conditions of lower wind speed will have lower values for Kc mid. These variations are caused by the effects of greater aerodynamic roughness for many

progressively reduced when crop height increases, and that Kc mid increases are larger
when wind speed is higher. As an example, expected variations for Kc mid for wheat in
response to regional climatic conditions are presented in Box 6.2. 6.3.2 Adjustment of Kc mid for climate

Equation 6.16 is valid for vegetable and field crops with mean plant heights up to around
3 m. For plant heights shorter than 0.1 m, vegetation will behave aerodynamically
similar to grass reference and Equation 6.16 should not be applied. In case of fruit trees
and vines, the correction for climate is less necessary unless transfers of Kc mid values are
done for very different climates because orchard architecture and crop training play a
large role in plant's aerodynamic behaviour. Example values for h are listed in Tables
6.1 – 6.3 for various crops but the mean plant height can vary greatly with crop cultivar
and cultural practices. Therefore, wherever possible, h should be obtained from general
field observations. However, the presence of the 0.3 exponent in Equation 6.16 makes
the equation relatively insensitive to small errors in the value used for h. Generally, only
a single value for h is used in Equation 6.16 to represent the mid-season period. Example
6.6 compares applications of Equation 6.16 for the same crop in different climates. 6.3.3 Adjustment for frequency of wetting
Kc mid is less affected by wetting frequency than is Kc ini, as vegetation during this
stage is generally near full ground cover so that the effects of surface evaporation on
Kc are smaller. For frequent irrigation of crops (more frequently than every 3 days)
and where the Kc mid of Tables 6.1 – 6.2 is less than 1.0, the value can be replaced by
approximately 1.1-1.3 to account for the additional combined effects of continuously
wet soil, evaporation due to interception (sprinkler irrigation) and roughness of the
vegetation, especially where the irrigation system moistens an important fraction of
the soil surface (fw > 0.3). 6.4 CROP COEFFICIENT FOR THE END OF THE LATE SEASON
STAGE (Kc end)
Typical values for the crop coefficient at the end of the late season stage, Kc end, are
listed in Tables 6.1 – 6.5 for various agricultural crops and land covers. The values given
for Kc end reflect crop and water management practices particular to those crops and
vegetation. If the crop is irrigated frequently until harvested fresh, the topsoil remains
wet and the Kc end value will be relatively high. On the other hand, crops that are
allowed to senesce and dry out in the field before harvest receive less frequent irrigation
or no irrigation at all during the late season stage. Consequently, both the soil surface
and vegetation are dry and the value for Kc end will be relatively small (Figure 6.6). Where the local water management and harvest timing practices are known to deviate
from the typical ones, the user should make adequate adjustments to the values for
Kc end. Some guidance on the adjustment of Kc values for wetting frequency is provided
in Chapter 7. For premature harvest, the user can construct a Kc curve using the Kc end
value provided in Tables 6.1 – 6.5 and a late season length typical of a normal harvest
date; and then the user should terminate the constructed curve early, corresponding
to the time of the early harvest. The Kc end values in Tables 6.1 – 6.5 are typical values
expected for the average Kc end under the standard climatic conditions.

6.5.1 Annual crops
Only three-point values for Kc are required to describe and to construct the Kc curve. The
curve such as that shown in Figure 6.7 is constructed using the following steps:
1. Divide the growing period into four general growth stages that describe crop
phenology or development (initial, crop development, mid-season, and late season
stage), determine the lengths of the growth stages, and identify the three Kc values
that correspond to Kc ini, Kc mid and Kc end from Tables 6.1 – 6.5. 2. Adjust the Kc values to the frequency of wetting and/or climatic conditions of the
growth stages as outlined in the previous section. 3. Construct a curve (following Chapter 5) by connecting straight line segments
through each of the four growth stages. Horizontal lines are drawn through Kc ini in
the initial stage and through Kc mid in the mid-season stage. Diagonal lines are drawn
from Kc ini to Kc mid within the course of the crop development stage and from Kc mid
to Kc end within the course of the late season stage (Figure 6.7). 4. Consider a downward adjustment to the Kc values in cases of inadequate soil water
and consequent water stress, as well as in case of stress due to salinity, lack of
fertility and inadequacy of other crop practices, as indicated early in this chapter
or as described in Chapters 8 and 9. FIGURE 6.7

6.5.3 Kc mid when effects of individual cutting periods are averaged
The user may wish to average the effects of cuttings for a forage crop over the course
of the growing season. When cutting effects are averaged, then only a single value for
Kc mid and only a single Kc curve need to be employed for the whole growing season. When this is the case, a “single” Kc curve is constructed as in Figure 6.7, where only one
midseason period is considered for the forage crop. The Kc mid for this total midseason
period must average the effects of grazing or hay cuttings. The value that is used for
Kc mid is therefore an average of the Kc curve for the time period starting at the first
attainment of full cover and ending at the beginning of the final late season period,
often near dormancy or frost. The value used for Kc mid under these averaged conditions
may be only about 80 percent of the Kc value that represents full ground cover as in
Figure 6.8. For example, for alfalfa hay, the average, full-season Kc mid often is 1.05,
whereas the Kc mid for an individual cutting period is 1.20. 6.6 CALCULATING ETc
The Kc value for any period during the growing period can be graphically or numerically
determined from the crop coefficient curve. Once the Kc values have been derived, the
crop evapotranspiration, ETc, can be calculated by multiplying the Kc values by the
corresponding ETo values. 6.6.1 Graphical determination of Kc
Weekly, ten-day or monthly values for Kc are necessary when ETc calculations are
made on weekly, ten-day or monthly time steps. A general procedure is to construct
the Kc curve, overlay the curve with the lengths of the weeks, decades or months, and
to derive graphically from the curve the Kc value for the period under consideration
(Figure 6.7). Since all decades have a duration of 10 days, adopting decades as time
periods facilitates the derivation of Kc and introduces little error in the calculation of
ETc. The constructed Kc curve in Figure 6.9 relative to a dry bean crop (detailed in Box
6.3), was used to construct the curve in Figure 6.10. This curve has been overlaid with
the lengths of the decades. Kc values of 0.15, 1.19 and 0.35 and the actual lengths for
growth stages equal to 25, 25, 30 and 20 days were used. The crop was planted at the
beginning of the last decade of May and was harvested 100 days later. BOX 6.3

6.8.1 Thermal lengths of the crop growth stages
The construction of the crop coefficient curve requires the estimation of the lengths of
the four stages that connect or represent the three Kc values. These stages are the initial
(ini), development (dev), mid-season (mid) and late-season (end) as in Figure 6.7 and
are defined in Chapter 5. In the absence of limiting factors such as water or nutrients, a crop’s development
essentially depends on the temperature accumulation over time. Thus, the use of
thermal time or growing degree days (GDD) to estimate the crop growth stage lengths
has the merits of allowing one to adequately extrapolate from one year to the next,
to diverse locations, and to take into consideration the impacts of climate change,
particularly in temperature, on crop growth cycles. The use of GDD is important for
studies relating to the assessment of climate change impacts on water and irrigation
requirements. Therefore, in this updated publication, the use of GDD to determine the
lengths of crop growth stages and the shape of the seasonal Kc curve is provided rather
than static stage lengths as provided in the 1998 FAO56 publication. Stage lengths,
expressed in days, are available in the previous version of these guidelines. [TABLE 1]
