6. ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc)
The time of emergence of vegetation and the time of effective full cover can be estimated
using sophisticated plant growth models or by cumulative GDD regression equations. While those models should be verified or validated for the local area or for a specific
crop variety using local observations, the use of generalized GDD is a more simplified
but reliable method that can be applied using simple computer software or spreadsheets. Crop growth and development of the Kc curve is assumed to occur on any day when
the mean air temperature exceeds a lower temperature threshold termed the base
temperature (Tbase). The value of Tbase depends on the crop and variety. In conjunction
with Tbase, when the mean daily air temperature exceeds an upper temperature threshold
(Tupper), crop development is assumed to be limited to the GDD below that limit. Thus,
the estimation of the GDD for a certain crop is based upon the daily average between
the daily maximum and minimum temperatures and values for Tbase and Tupper as follows:

The cumulative GDD that defines the length of the crop stages and the crop season are
shown in Table 6.11 for various annual and perennial crops:
•  GDDini
cumulative growing degree days from the planting of the annual crop
or greenup of the perennial crop until the start of the development
period, thus the length of the initial period;
•  GDDdev
cumulative growing degree days from the start of the development
period until the beginning of the midseason period, thus the length of
the development period;
•  GDDmid
cumulative growing degree days from the start of the midseason
period to its end, i.e., length of the midseason period;

•  GDDlate
cumulative growing degree days from the end of the midseason
period until harvest, full maturity or plant death, i.e., length of the
late season period;
•  Total GDD total cumulative growing degree days, from planting or greenup until
harvest or end of the growing season, thus crop season length. The length for each of the four growth stage periods is determined by summing GDD
on a daily basis, using Equations 6.23. The number of days occurring can represent the
length of the stage in days. The rate at which vegetation cover develops and the time at which it attains effective full
cover are affected by weather conditions in general and by mean daily air temperature in
particular. Therefore, the length of time between planting and effective full cover will vary
with climate, latitude, elevation, and planting date. It will also vary with cultivar (crop
variety). Generally, once the effective full cover for a plant canopy has been reached, the
rate of further phenological development (flowering, fruit development, ripening, and
senescence) is more dependent on plant genotype and less dependent on weather. The end of the mid-season and beginning of the late season is usually marked by
senescence of leaves, often beginning with the lower leaves of plants. The length of
the late season period may be relatively short (less than 10 days) for vegetation killed
by frost (for example, maize at high elevations in latitudes > 40°N) or for agricultural
crops that are harvested fresh (for example, table beets and small vegetables). Moisture
stress or other environmental stresses will usually accelerate the rate of crop maturation
and can shorten the mid and late season growing periods, however affecting yields. Information in Table 6.11 refers to trusted observations only. It is possible to find
more GDD in the literature for a large number of crops, but it is often not clear
which values of Tbase and Tupper temperatures were used as compared to those in Table
6.10, what specific GDD calculations were applied, or if the crop growth stages
were defined according to those in FAO56 as adopted in the current study. To avoid
such problems, GDD values in Table 6.11 were recalculated from literature sources
containing trusted observations and data analyses. Users of Table 6.11 are encouraged
to, first, perform their own observations using the Tbase and Tupper temperatures in
Table 6.10 or, secondly, to directly use data from Table 6.11 for the crops listed, or,
thirdly and indirectly, by comparing the considered crop with another, selected by
the user, listed in Table 6.11. Table 6.11 summarises GDD data that are based on published and refereed literature
sources. That Table is complemented by Table 6.12 that lists approximate minimum and
maximum values for GDD that do not appear in Table 6.11. The GDD values in Table
6.12 are associated with the range of original growth stage lengths reported in the original
Table 11 of the 1998 FAO56 publication. Table 6.12 can be used as a general indication of
expected ranges in values for GDD. The values for GDD in Table 6.12 were developed
by associating general climatic and cultural regions listed for the crops in the original
Table 11 of the 1998 publication with specific representative locations on the globe. The
representative locations were then used to calculate GDD values that are associated with
the lengths of stages in the original table. The calculation of associated GDD used the
ERA5 (fifth generation ECMWF atmospheric reanalysis of the global climate) gridded
weather data set using normal air temperature over the 1991-2020 period. The minimum
and maximum GDD values or the “common” GDD values should be considered to
be only approximate values and can serve as a starting point and perhaps as bounds on
locally determined values or for new values to be found in the literature.

6.8.2 Converting the thermal time of the growth stages into calendar time
Once the planting date has been determined for annual crops, the length of the growth
stages in thermal time can be converted to an equivalent length in days. A graphic showing the transformation of GDD into lengths of growth stages, in days,
is shown in Figure 6.12. When using a spreadsheet, the GDD can be accumulated from
the date of planting and a lookup type of function can be employed to select the date for
each stage. Figure 6.12 applies the procedure for transforming GDD values into lengths
for growth periods for a crop of maize near Holdrege, NE. USA., using air temperature
data from 2017. The estimated planting date occurred relatively soon after the beginning
of the rapid accumulation of GDD in the spring. Harvest (end) occurred right before a
transition to cold periods where there was little additional accumulation of GDD. Figure 6.13 shows an example of the variation in lengths of the growth period of
a maize cultivar for several locations and for different sowing dates. The figure
represents the average length of the crop cycle using a weather data set of at least 10
years. This example clearly shows the advantage of using GDD instead of time for
establishing the duration of the crop stages, particularly in locations that experience
greater temperature variability. FIGURE 6.12

7. ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke)
ETc and dual crop coefficient
(Kc = Kcb + Ke)
This chapter, complementing Chapter 6, deals with the calculation of crop
evapotranspiration (ETc) under standard, non-stressed cropping conditions where no
limitations are placed on crop growth or evapotranspiration. This chapter presents the
procedure for predicting the effects of specific wetting events on the value of the crop
coefficient Kc. The solution consists of splitting Kc into two separate coefficients, one for
crop transpiration, i.e. the basal crop coefficient (Kcb), and one for soil evaporation (Ke):
ETc = (Kcb + Ke) ETo
(7.1)
The dual crop coefficient approach is more complicated and more computationally
intensive than the single crop coefficient approach (Kc) dealt with in Chapter 6. The
procedure is conducted on a daily basis and is intended for applications using computers. It is recommended that the approach be followed when improved estimates for Kc are
needed, for example, to schedule irrigations for individual fields on a daily basis, mainly
in case of incomplete cover crops, or to increase accuracy in hydrologic studies. The calculation procedure for crop evapotranspiration, ETc, consists of:
1. identifying the lengths of crop growth stages, and selecting the corresponding basal
Kcb coefficients;
2. adjusting the selected Kcb coefficients for climatic conditions during the respective
crop growth stage;
3. constructing the basal crop coefficient curve (allowing one to determine Kcb values
for any day or timestep during the crop season);
4. determining daily the soil evaporation coefficient Ke values for surface evaporation;
and
5. calculating ETc as the product of ETo and (Kcb + Ke). 7.1 TRANSPIRATION COMPONENT (Kcb ETO)
7.1.1 Basal crop coefficient (Kcb)
The basal crop coefficient (Kcb) is defined as the ratio of the crop evapotranspiration
over the grass reference evapotranspiration (ETc/ETo) when the soil surface is dry but
transpiration is occurring at a potential rate, i.e. water is not limiting transpiration
(Figure 5.3). Therefore, “Kcb ETo” represents primarily the transpiration component of
ETc and Kcb is often called transpiration coefficient. The Kcb ETo does include a small,
residual diffusive evaporation component supplied by soil water below the dry surface
and by soil water from beneath dense vegetation. As the Kc values of Chapter 6 include averaged effects of evaporation from the soil
surface, the Kcb values lie below the Kc values as illustrated in Figure 5.7 and a separate
table for Kcb is required. Recommended values for Kcb are listed in Tables 7.1 to 7.3 for
the same crops listed in Tables 6.1 to 6.3. Values tabulated in Tables 7.1 to 7.3 do not
include the influence of mulches, which are dealt with in Chapter 10. Chapter 7

As with Tables 6.1 to 6.3, the values for Kcb in Tables 7.1 to 7.3 represent Kcb for
a standardized sub-humid climate and with moderate wind speed. For specific
adjustment in climates where RHmin differs from 45 percent or where the wind speed
is larger or smaller than 2 m s-1, the Kcb mid must be adjusted. In addition, Kcb end values
larger than 0.45 are also adjusted. Adjustment is made using the following equation:

The soil evaporation coefficient, Ke, describes the evaporation component of ETc. Where the topsoil is wet, following rain or irrigation, Ke is maximal. Where the soil
surface is dry, Ke is small and even zero if no water remains near the soil surface for
evaporation. Two calculation procedures are presented, the FAO56 original and the
skin layer evaporation approach, which consists of a refinement of the former to
increase accuracy, mainly for small wetting depths. 7.2.1 FAO 56 original calculation procedure
Where the soil is wet, evaporation from the soil occurs at the maximum rate. However,
the crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke) can never exceed a maximum value, Kc max. This
value is determined by the energy available for evapotranspiration at the soil and plant
surfaces, thus (Kcb + Ke ≤ Kc max), or Ke ≤ (Kc max – Kcb). When the topsoil dries out less water is available for evaporation and a reduction in
evaporation begins to occur in proportion to the amount of water remaining in the
surface soil layer, or:
Ke =Kr (Kc max - Kcb) ≤ few Kc max
(7.3a)
or
Ke = min [Kr (Kc max – Kcb), few Kc max]
(7.3b)

Stage 1: energy limiting stage
At the start of a drying cycle, following heavy rain or irrigation, the soil water content
in the topsoil is at field capacity and the amount of water depleted by evaporation,
De, is zero. During stage 1 of the drying process, the soil surface remains wet and
it is assumed that evaporation from soil exposed to the atmosphere will occur at the
maximum rate limited only by energy availability at the soil surface. This stage holds
until the cumulative depth of evaporation, De, is such that the hydraulic properties of
the upper soil become limiting, and water cannot be transported to the soil surface at a
rate that can supply the potential demand. During stage 1 drying, Kr = 1.0. The cumulative depth of evaporation, De, at the end of stage 1 drying is REW (readily
evaporable water, which is the maximum depth of water that can be evaporated from
the topsoil layer without restriction during stage 1). The depth normally ranges from
5 to 12 mm and is generally highest for medium and fine textured soils. Typical values

In crops with incomplete ground cover, evaporation from the soil often does not occur
uniformly over the entire surface but is greater between plants where exposure to
sunlight occurs and where more air ventilation is able to transport vapour from the soil
surface to above the canopy. This is especially true where only part of the soil surface
is wetted by irrigation. It is recognized that both the location and the fraction of the soil surface exposed
to sunlight change to some degree with the time of the day and depending on row
orientation. The procedure presented here predicts a general averaged fraction of the
soil surface from which the majority of evaporation occurs. Diffusive evaporation from
the soil beneath the crop canopy is very small and assumed to be largely included in
the basal Kcb coefficient. Where the complete soil surface is wetted, as by precipitation or sprinkler, then the
fraction of soil surface from which most evaporation occurs, few, is essentially defined as
(1−fc), where fc is the average fraction of soil surface covered by vegetation and (1−fc) is the
approximate fraction of soil surface that is exposed (Example 7.3). However, for irrigation
systems where only a fraction of the ground surface is wetted, few must be limited to fw, the
fraction of the soil surface wetted by irrigation (Figure 7.3). Therefore, few is calculated as:
few = min (1 - fc, fw)

for fw should be based on a weighted average of the fw for precipitation (fw = 1) and the

7. ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke)
7.2.2 Calculation procedure using the skin layer approach
The use of the fraction of the time step calculation (day or hour) that resides in stage 1
evaporation, Astage 1, is an extension to the original FAO 56 approach to provide more
precise definition of the transition from stage 1 to stage 2 drying during a time step. The improved definition can be important when using daily calculation time steps,
especially for coarse soils having small REW. The skin layer approach improves daily
estimates for Ke when the depths of wetting events are small. Small depths of wetting
occur when precipitation or sprinkler irrigation events are less than about 10 mm. If
small wetting events occur when the total 100 to 150 mm deep soil evaporation layer
is dry (De, i ~ TEW), then much of the added water remains close to the top of the soil
evaporation layer and tends to evaporate quickly. The original procedure implicitly
assumes that small water additions are mixed throughout the soil evaporation layer. As a result, the original procedure tends to extend the evaporation of the added water
over a number of days at a relatively low rate due to small values calculated for Kr. In
contrast, the skin evaporation extension retains water close to the surface in the REW
zone, so the Es rate is generally higher in value and shorter in time. The skin evaporation
extension tends to reproduce the relatively short-lived and higher magnitude Stage 1
spikes of Es and Ke that are observed in field monitoring. It is important to note that the skin evaporation extension and the original Ke
computation procedure will generally produce similar total depths of evaporation over
an extended period. This is because both methods adhere to a water balance of the
topsoil and to the conservation of mass. The difference is in the duration and magnitude
of Ke. These differences in daily estimates may not matter when estimating total water
consumption (ET) over extended periods. The skin evaporation extension may be most
important when comparing ET estimates to ground or remote sensing observations
where the timing and magnitude of evaporation on a specific day is important. The skin
evaporation extension can be applied to daily or hourly calculation timesteps. As for the original calculation procedure, Kc max is determined by the energy available
for evapotranspiration at the soil and plant surfaces, thus resulting Kcb + Ke ≤ Kc max
or Ke ≤ Kc max − Kcb. When the topsoil dries out, less water is available for evaporation
and a reduction in evaporation begins to occur in proportion to the amount of water
remaining in the surface soil layer, or:
Ke = Kr (Kc max - Ks Kcb) ≤ few Kc max

7.2.3 Daily calculation of Ke
Limits on De, i
By assuming that the topsoil is at field capacity following heavy rain or irrigation, the
minimum value for the depletion De,i is zero. As the soil surface dries, De,i increases
and in the absence of any wetting event will steadily reach its maximum value TEW
(Equation 7.5). At that moment no water is left for evaporation in the upper soil layer,
Kr becomes zero, and the value for De,i remains at TEW until the topsoil is wetted once
again. The limits imposed on De,i are consequently:
0 ≤ De, i ≤ TEW
(7.15)
Initial depletion
To initiate the water balance for the evaporating layer, the user can assume that the
topsoil is near field capacity following a heavy rain or irrigation, i.e. De,i−1 = 0. Where
a long period of time has elapsed since the last wetting, the user can assume that all
evaporable water has been depleted from the evaporation layer at the beginning of
calculations, i.e. De, i−1 = TEW = 1 000 (θFC − 0.5 θWP) Ze. Precipitation and runoff
Pi is equivalent to daily precipitation. Daily precipitation in amounts less than about
0.2 ETo is normally entirely evaporated and can usually be ignored in the Ke and water
balance calculations. However, small amounts of precipitation are also correctly dealt
with by Equation 7.11 – 7.15. Light precipitation events will generally have little or no
runoff. The amount of rainfall lost by runoff depends on: the intensity of rainfall; the
slope of land; the soil type, its hydraulic conditions and antecedent moisture content;
and the land use and cover. For general situations where many irrigated fields have small
slopes, ROi can be assumed to be zero or can be accounted for by considering only a
certain percentage of Pi. This is especially true for the water balance of the topsoil layer,
because almost all precipitation events that would have intensities or depths large enough
to cause runoff would probably still replenish the water content of the topsoil layer to
field capacity. Therefore, the impact of the runoff component can be ignored. Irrigation
Ii is generally expressed as a depth of water that is equivalent to the mean infiltrated
irrigation depth distributed over the entire field. Therefore, the value Ii/fw is used to
describe the actual concentration of the irrigation volume over the fraction of the soil
that is wetted (Figure 6.3). Evaporation
Evaporation beneath the vegetation canopy is assumed to be included in Kcb and is
therefore not explicitly quantified. The computed evaporation is fully concentrated in
the exposed, wetted topsoil. The evaporation Ei is given by Ke ETo. The Ei/few provides
for the actual concentration of the evaporation over the fraction of the soil that is both
exposed and wetted. Transpiration
Except for shallow rooted crops (i.e. where the depth of the maximum rooting zone is <
0.5 to 0.6 m), the amount of transpiration from the evaporating soil layer (Tew) is small
and can be ignored (i.e. Tew = 0). In addition, for row crops, most of the water extracted
by the roots may be extracted from beneath the vegetation canopy. Therefore, Tew from
the few fraction of soil surface can be assumed to be zero in these cases.

7.2.4 Daily water balance calculation
The daily water balance calculation for the surface layer, even for shallow rooted crops,
is not usually sensitive to extractions for transpiration from the surface layer (Tew) for
the first 3-5 days following a wetting event. Tew can, therefore, generally be ignored. The effects of the reduction of the water content of the evaporating soil layer due to Tew
can be accounted for if needed by decreasing the value for Ze, for example from 0.15 to

In making calculations for the Kcb + Ke procedure, for example when using a spreadsheet,

7. ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke)
The sequential procedure for calculating crop evapotranspiration is presented in Box
7.1. Dual crop coefficient case studies for a dry bean crop at Kimberly, USA, for a
pea crop for industry at Alpiarça, Portugal, and a super-high density (hedgerow) olive
orchard at Viana do Alentejo, Portugal, are presented with summaries of calculation
procedures in Boxes 7.2, 7.3 and 7.4. BOX 7.1
Calculating ETc
The calculation procedure lends itself to application by computer, either in the form
of electronic spreadsheets (as calculated for Example 7.9) or in the form of structured
programming languages. The calculation procedure consists of determining:
a. Reference evapotranspiration, ETo: Estimate ETo using the procedure given
in Chapter 4.
b. Growth stages: Determine the locally adjusted lengths of the four growth stages
by performing field observations (for general information on cumulative growing
degree days used to estimate growth stage lengths, consult Table 6.11):
• initial growth stage: Lini [days];
• crop development stage: Ldev [days];
• mid-season stage: Lmid [days]; and
• late season stage: Llate [days].
c. Basal crop coefficient, Kcb: Calculate basal crop coefficients for each day of the
growing period:
• select Kcb ini, Kcb mid and Kcb end from Tables 7.1 through 7.3;
• adjust Kcb mid and Kcb end to the local climatic conditions (Equation 7.2); and
• determine the daily Kcb values
◊ initial growth stage:
Kcb = Kcb ini,
◊ crop development stage:
from Kcb ini to Kcb mid (Equation 6.20),
◊ mid-season stage:
Kcb = Kcb mid,
◊ late season stage:
from Kcb mid to Kcb end (Equation 6.20).
d. Evaporation coefficient, Ke: Calculate the maximum value for Kc, i.e. the upper
limit Kc max (Equation 7.4), and determine for each day of the growing period:
• the fraction of soil covered by vegetation, fc (Tables 7.1-7.3, Table 7.7 or
Equation 7.8);
• the fraction of soil surface wetted by irrigation or precipitation, fw (Table 7.6);
• the fraction of soil covered by vegetation, fc (Tables 7.1-7.3, Table 7.7 or
Equation 7.8);
• the fraction of soil surface wetted by irrigation or precipitation, fw (Table 7.6);
• the fraction of soil surface from which most evaporation occurs, few (Equation 7.7);
• the cumulative depletion from the REW layer, DREW, and from the evaporating
soil layer, De, determined by means of a daily (or shorter) soil water balance of
the topsoil (Equation 7.14 and 7.15);
• the corresponding evaporation reduction coefficient, Kr (Equation 7.12); and
• the soil evaporation coefficient, Ke (Equation 7.3).
e. Crop evapotranspiration, ETc: Calculate ETc = (Kcb + Ke) ETo (Equation 7.1).

8. ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions
ETc under soil water and salinity
stress conditions
Forces acting on the soil water decrease its potential energy and make it less available
for plant root extraction. When the soil is wet, the water has a high potential energy, is
relatively free to move and is easily taken up by the plant roots. In dry soils, the water
has a low potential energy and is strongly bound by capillary and absorptive forces to
the soil matrix and is less easily extracted by the crop. When the potential energy of the soil water drops below a threshold value, the crop is
said to be water stressed. The effects of soil water stress are described by multiplying
the basal crop coefficient by the water stress coefficient, Ks:
ETc  act= (Ks Kcb+Ke ) ETo
(8.1)
For soil water limiting conditions, Ks < 1. Where there is no soil water deficit, Ks = 1. Ks describes the effect of water stress on crop transpiration. Where the single crop
coefficient is used, the effect of water stress is incorporated into Kc as:
ETc  act = Ks Kc ETo = Kc  act ETo
(8.2)
Salinity also decreases the potential energy of the soil water and makes water more
difficult to be extracted by the plant roots. Thus Equations 8.1 and 8.2 also apply
when salinity of the soil and the irrigation water affect extraction by the roots, with Ks
becoming a salinity and water stress coefficient, i.e. salinity and water stress combine
in Ks < 1 as developed later in this chapter. Because the water stress coefficient impacts
only crop transpiration, rather than evaporation from soil, the application of Ks
using Equation 8.1 is generally more accurate than its application using Equation 8.2. However, in situations where evaporation from soil is not a large component of ETc,
the use of Equation 8.2 will provide quite reasonable results. 8.1 SOIL WATER AVAILABILITY
8.1.1 Total available water (TAW)
Soil water availability refers to the capacity of a soil to retain water available to plants. After heavy rainfall or irrigation, the soil will drain until field capacity is reached. Field capacity is the amount of water that a well-drained soil should hold against
gravitational forces, or the amount of water remaining when downward drainage has
markedly decreased. In the absence of water supply, the water content in the root
zone decreases as a result of water uptake by the crop. As water uptake progresses, the
remaining water is held to the soil particles with greater force, lowering its potential
energy and making it more difficult for the plant to extract it. Eventually, a point is
reached where the crop can no longer extract the remaining water. The water uptake
becomes zero when wilting point is reached. Wilting point is the water content at which
plants will permanently wilt. As the water content above field capacity cannot be held
Chapter 8

against the forces of gravity and will drain, and as the water content below wilting
point cannot be extracted by plant roots, the total available water in the root zone is
the difference between the water content at field capacity and wilting point:
TAW = 1000 (θ FC - θ WP) Zr
(8.3)
where TAW
the total available soil water in the root zone [mm],
θFC
the water content at field capacity [m3 m-3],
θWP
the water content at wilting point [m3 m-3],
Zr
the rooting depth [m]. TAW is the amount of water that a crop can extract from its root zone, and its magnitude
depends on the type of soil and the rooting depth. Typical ranges for field capacity
and wilting point are listed in Table 7.5 for various soil texture classes. Ranges of the
maximum effective rooting depth for various crops are given in Tables 6.1 through 6.3. 8.1.2 Readily available water (RAW)
Although water is theoretically available in the root zone until the wilting point is
attained, the crop water uptake is reduced well before the wilting point is reached. Where the soil is sufficiently wet, the soil supplies water fast enough to meet the
atmospheric demand of the crop, and water uptake equals ETc. As the soil water
content decreases, water becomes more strongly bound to the soil matrix and is more
difficult to extract. When the soil water content drops below a threshold value, soil
water can no longer be transported quickly enough toward the roots to respond to the
transpiration demand and the crop begins to experience stress. The fraction of TAW
that a crop can extract from the root zone without suffering water stress is the readily
available soil water:
RAW = p TAW
(8.4)
where RAW
the readily available soil water in the root zone [mm],
p
average fraction of total available soil water (TAW) that can be
depleted from the root zone before moisture stress (reduction in ET)
occurs [0-1]. Values for p are listed in Table 8.1 through 8.4 respectively for vegetable, field, woody
fruit and grass crops. The factor p differs from one crop to another. The factor p
normally varies from 0.20 for very shallow rooted plants at high rates of ETc (> 8 mm
d-1) to 0.70 for deep rooted plants at low rates of ETc (< 3 mm d-1). A value of 0.50 for p
is commonly used for many field crops, a lower value is often used for vegetable crops,
and a higher value is used for woody crops with large roots and to grasses, generally
less susceptible to water stress. For many woody crops there is little information and,
thus, indicative values are given for each group. The p value is small for frequent and
very frequent irrigation, and larger for surface irrigation where time intervals between
irrigation events are large. Therefore, the values of p listed in Table 8.1 through 8.4 are
for large time intervals between irrigation events, thus for surface irrigation. Users may
reduce the tabulated p values for the irrigation method that they are using. The fraction p is a function of the evaporation power of the atmosphere. At low rates
of ETc, the p values listed in Table 8.1 through 8.4 are higher than at high rates of ETc. For hot dry weather conditions, where ETc is high, p maybe 10-25 percent less than
the tabulated values in Table 8.1 through 8.4, and the soil is still relatively wet when

p = pTable + 0.04 (5 − ETc)

Expressing the tolerance of crops to water stress as a function of the fraction (p) of
TAW is only an approximation. The rate of root water uptake is, in fact, influenced
more directly by the potential energy level of the soil water (soil matric potential and
the associated hydraulic conductivity) than by water content alone. As a certain soil
matric potential corresponds in different soil types with different soil water contents,
the value for p is also a function of the soil type. Generally, it can be stated that for fine textured soils (clay) the p values listed in Table
8.1 can be reduced by 5-10 percent, while for more coarse textured soils (sand), they
can be increased by 5-10 percent. RAW is similar to the term Management Allowed Depletion (MAD) often used
in irrigation management practice. However, values for MAD are influenced by
management and economic factors in addition to the physical factors influencing p. Generally, MAD < RAW where there is risk aversion or uncertainty, and MAD > RAW
where plant moisture deficit is an intentional part of soil water management.

8.2 WATER STRESS COEFFICIENT (KS)
The effects of soil water stress on crop ET are described by reducing the value for the
crop coefficient. This is accomplished by multiplying the crop coefficient by the water
stress coefficient, Ks (Equations 8.1 and 8.2). Water content in the root zone can also be expressed by the root zone depletion, Dr, i.e.
the water consumed relative to field capacity. At field capacity, the root zone depletion
is zero (Dr = 0). When soil water is consumed by evapotranspiration the depletion
is increasing, and stress will be induced when Dr reaches RAW. When the root zone
depletion exceeds RAW (the water content drops below the threshold θt), the root zone
depletion is high enough to limit evapotranspiration to less than potential values and
the crop evapotranspiration begins to decrease in proportion to the amount of water
remaining in the root zone (Figure 8.2 and Example 8.2). [TABLE 1]

8.3 SOIL WATER BALANCE
The estimation of Ks requires a daily water balance computation for the root zone. Schematically (Figure 8.4), the root zone can be presented by means of a container
in which the water content may fluctuate. To express the water content as root
zone depletion is useful. It makes the adding and subtracting of losses and gains
straightforward as the various parameters of the soil water budget are usually expressed
in terms of water depth. Rainfall, irrigation, and capillary rise of groundwater towards
the root zone add water to the root zone and decrease the root zone depletion. Soil
evaporation, crop transpiration and percolation losses remove water from the root
zone and increase the depletion. The daily water balance, expressed in terms of depletion at the end of the day is:

8.3.1 Limits on Dr,i
In Figure 8.4 it is assumed that water can be stored in the root zone until field capacity is
reached. Although following heavy rain or irrigation the water content might temporally
exceed field capacity, the total amount of water above field capacity is assumed to be
lost the same day by deep percolation, following any ET for that day. By assuming
that the root zone is at field capacity following heavy rain or irrigation, the minimum
value for the depletion Dr,i is zero. As a result of percolation and evapotranspiration,
the water content in the root zone will gradually decrease and the root zone depletion
will increase. In the absence of any wetting event, the water content will steadily reach
its minimum value θWP. At that moment no water is left for evapotranspiration in the
root zone, Ks becomes zero, and the root zone depletion has reached its maximum value
TAW. The limits imposed on Dr,i are consequently 0 ≤ Dr,i ≤ TAW. 8.3.2 Initial depletion
To initiate the water balance for the root zone, the initial depletion Dr,i-1 should be
estimated. The initial depletion can be derived from measured soil water content by:
Dr , i-1 = 1000 (θFC - θ i-1) Zr
(8.8)
where θi-1 is the average soil water content for the effective root zone. Following heavy
rain or irrigation, the user can assume that the root zone is near field capacity, i.e. Dr,i-1 ≈ 0. 8.3.3 Precipitation (P), runoff (RO) and irrigation (I)

balance calculations especially when the single crop coefficient approach is being used. Ii is equivalent to the mean infiltrated irrigation depth expressed for the entire field
surface. Runoff from the surface during precipitation can be predicted using standard

8.3.4 Capillary rise (CR)
The amount of water transported upwards by capillary rise from the water table to the
root zone depends on the soil type, the water table depth below the ground surface
(WTD), the crop evapotranspiration and the wetness of the root zone. However, CR
is primarily influenced by WTD as explained in Box 8.1. The wetness of the root zone is represented by the actual soil water storage in the root
zone (Wa). When WTD is close to the root zone, especially if ETc act is high, upward
fluxes are expected to occur even when the soil water storage is close to field capacity. Under such WTD and ETc act conditions, CR fluxes are important, especially in silty soils. These fluxes depend mainly on WTD and may start at different water table depths and
various values of soil water storage, depending on the soil type. This storage is termed
the critical soil water storage (Wc) [mm] and varies between the soil water storage at
field capacity and the storage when the soil water content corresponds to the depletion
fraction p for no stress (Table 8.1). The critical soil water storage may be calculated as:
Wc = a1 WTDb1
(8.9)
where WTD
water table depth [m],
a1
soil water storage for the maximum root depth at field capacity [mm],
b1
adjustment parameter depending on soil physical characteristics,
namely soil texture [-] (Table 8.5). ETc act progressively depletes the soil water storage, and the upward fluxes attain a
maximum value, called the potential capillary flux (CRmax), which is mainly dependent
on WTD and less dependent on ETc act. For shallow water table depths (WTD ≤ 3 m), a
steady soil moisture profile is formed when CRmax is reached and the soil water storage
assumes an almost constant value, termed the steady soil water storage (Ws), that is
almost independent of ETc. In contrast, when the water table is deeper (WTD > 3 m), the
upward flow may no longer be sufficient to sustain ETc act, which continuously decreases
due to increased soil water deficit. Under such conditions steady soil water storage (Ws)
varies with ETc act and CRmax is only reached when the soil water storage is low. The
Ws, which is the total water stored in the root zone [mm], primarily depends upon the
groundwater depth and therefore may be approximated similarly to Wc (Equation 8.9) as:

CRmax no longer increases. This critical WTD (WTDc), corresponds to the water table
depth when CR reaches the virtually constant value CRmax, i.e., the maximum potential
groundwater contribution. It has been observed that the critical water table depth
mainly depends on the ETc act:

Where the soil water depletion is smaller than RAW, the crop evapotranspiration
equals ETc = Kc ETo or as ETc = (Kcb + Ke) ETo. As soon as Dr,i exceeds RAW, the crop
evapotranspiration is reduced and ETc can be computed from Equation 8.1 or 8.2. 8.3.6 Deep percolation (DP)
Following heavy rain or irrigation, the soil water content in the root zone might exceed
field capacity. In this simple procedure it is assumed that the soil water content is at
θFC within the same day of the wetting event, so that the depletion Dr, i in Equation 8.7
becomes zero. Therefore, following heavy rain or irrigation:

drainage when actual soil water storage is initially above the water storage at field

8.4 FORECASTING OR ALLOCATING IRRIGATIONS
Irrigation is required when rainfall is insufficient to compensate for the soil water used as
evapotranspiration. The primary objective of irrigation is to apply water at the right time
and in the right amount. The timing and depth of future irrigations can be planned by
calculating the soil water balance of the root zone on a daily basis (Equation 8.7). To avoid
crop water stress, irrigations should be applied before or at the moment when the readily
available soil water is depleted so that Dr,i is always ≤ RAW. To avoid deep percolation losses
that may leach valuable nutrients out of the root zone, the net irrigation depth should be
smaller than or equal to the root zone depletion (Ii ≤ Dr,i) unless leaching of salts is needed. Example 8.3 illustrates the application of a water balance of the root zone to predict

Salts in the soil water solution can reduce evapotranspiration by making soil water
less "available" for plant root extraction. Salts have an affinity for water and hence
additional force is required for the crop to extract water from a saline soil. The
presence of salts in the soil water solution reduces the total potential energy of the
soil water solution. In addition, some salts may cause toxic effects in plants and can
reduce plant metabolism, growth and yield. A function is presented hereafter that
predicts the reduction in evapotranspiration caused by the salinity of soil water. The
function is derived by combining yield-salinity equations from the FAO Irrigation
and Drainage Paper No29 with yield-ET equations from FAO Irrigation and Drainage
Paper No33. The resulting equation provides a first approximation to the reduction in
evapotranspiration expected under various salinity conditions. 8.6.1 Salinity impacts and crops tolerance
There is evidence that crop yield and transpiration are not as sensitive to low osmotic
potential as they are to low matric potential. Under saline conditions, many plants
are able to partially compensate for the low osmotic potential of the soil water by

soil solution and by synthesizing organic osmolytes. Both of these reactions reduce the
impact of osmotic potential on water availability. However, the synthesis of organic
osmolytes does require the expenditure of metabolic energy. Therefore, plant growth is
often reduced under saline conditions. The reduced plant growth impacts transpiration
by reducing ground cover, and a further reduction in transpiration is sometimes
additionally caused by partial stomatal closure. Other impacts of salts in the soil include direct sodium and chloride toxicities and
induced nutrient deficiencies. These deficiencies reduce plant growth by reducing the
rate of leaf elongation, the enlargement, and the division of cells in leaves. The modality
depends on the method of irrigation. With sprinkler irrigation, adsorption of sodium and
chloride through the leaf can result in toxic conditions for all crop species. With surface
or trickle irrigation, direct toxic conditions generally occur only in vine and tree crops;
however, high levels of sodium can induce calcium deficiencies for all crop species. Since salt concentration changes as the soil water content changes, soil salinity is normally
measured and expressed on the basis of the electrical conductivity of the saturation
extract of the soil (ECe). The ECe is defined as the electrical conductivity of the soil water
solution after the addition of a sufficient quantity of distilled water to bring the soil
water content to saturation. ECe is typically expressed in deciSiemens per meter (dS m-1). Under optimum management conditions, crop yields remain at potential levels until a
specific, threshold electrical conductivity of the saturation soil water extract (ECe threshold)
is reached. If the average ECe of the root zone increases above this critical threshold
value, the yield is presumed to begin to decrease linearly in proportion to the increase
in salinity. The rate of decrease in yield with increase in salinity is usually expressed as a
slope, b, having units of % reduction in yield per dS m-1 increase in ECe. All plants do not respond to salinity in a similar manner; some crops can produce acceptable
yields at much higher soil salinity levels than others. This is because some crops are better
able to make the needed osmotic adjustments that enable them to extract more water from
a saline soil, or they may be more tolerant of some of the toxic effects of salinity. Salt tolerance for many agricultural crops is provided in the FAO Irrigation and
Drainage Papers No. 33 and 48. The ECe threshold and slope b from these and other
sources are listed in Tables 8.8 through 8.11, respectively for vegetable, field, fruit tree
and vine, and grass and forage crops. The data serve only as a guideline - tolerance
vary depending on climate, soil conditions and cultural practices. Crops are often less
tolerant during germination and seedling stage. As can be observed from the data in
these Tables, there is an 8 to 11-fold range in salt tolerance of agricultural crops. The
effect of soil salinity on yield and crop evapotranspiration is hence crop specific. The ECe threshold and b parameters in Tables 8.8 through 8.11 were determined primarily
in research experiments using nearly steady-state irrigation where soil water contents
were maintained at levels close to field capacity. However, under most types of irrigation
scheduling for sprinkler and surface irrigation, the soil water content is typically depleted
to well below field capacity, so that the EC of the soil water solution, ECsw, increases prior
to irrigation, even though the EC of the saturation extract does not change. The increased salt concentration in the soil water solution reduces the osmotic potential
of the soil water solution (it becomes more negative), so that the plant must expend more
metabolic energy and may exert more mechanical force to absorb water. In addition, the
metabolic and toxic effects of salts on plants may become more pronounced as the soil
dries and concentrations increase.

8. ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions
Increased evaporation (Ke) under high frequency irrigation of the soil surface may
counteract reductions in Kc caused by stress due to high ECe of the root zone. Under
these conditions, the total Kc and ETc are not very different from the non-saline,
standard conditions under less frequent irrigation, even though crop yields and crop
transpiration are reduced. Because of this, under saline conditions, the Ks reducing
factor should only be applied with the dual Kc approach. The effects of soil salinity and water stress are generally additive in their impacts on
crop evapotranspiration. Therefore, the same yield-ET functions may hold for both
water shortage induced stress and for salinity induced stress. 8.6.2 Yield-Salinity relationship
A widely practiced approach for predicting the reduction in crop yield due to salinity
has been described in the FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No29. The approach
presumes that, under optimum management conditions, crop yields remain at potential
levels until a specific, threshold electrical conductivity of the soil water solution is
reached. When salinity increases beyond this threshold, crop yields are presumed to
decrease linearly in proportion to the increase in salinity. The soil water salinity is
expressed as the electrical conductivity of the saturation extract, ECe. In equation form,
the salinity response function is a linear equation. The procedure of FAO Irrigation
and Drainage Paper No29 is followed:

8. ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions
Limitations
Because the impact of salinity on plant growth and yield and on crop evapotranspiration
is a time-integrated process, generally only the seasonal value for Ky is used in predicting
the reduction in evapotranspiration. For many crops, the seasonal Ky is nearly 1.0
(Table 8.7). For crops where Ky is unknown, the user may assume Ky = 1 in Equations
8.19 and 8.25, or may select a Ky relative to a crop type that has similar behaviour. Equations 8.19 and 8.25 are suggested as approximate estimates of salinity impacts on
ET, and represent the general effects of salinity on evapotranspiration as occurring over
an extended period of time (as measured in weeks or months). These equations are not
expected to be accurate for predicting ETc act for specific days. Nor do they include
other complicating effects such as specific ion toxicity. Application of Equations 8.19
and 8.25 presumes that the ECe represents the average ECe for the root zone. The equations presented may not be valid at high salinity, where the linear relationships
between ECe, crop yield and Ks may not hold. The use of Equations 8.19 and 8.25
should usually be restricted to ECe < ECthreshold + 50/b. In addition, care is required
when the equations predict Ya = 0 before Ks = 0 when Ky > 1 and vice versa. As indicated earlier, a reduction in ETc in the presence of soil salinity is often partially
caused by reduced plant size and fraction of ground cover. These effects are largely
included in the coefficient values. Therefore, where plant growth is affected by salinity,
Equations 8.19 and 8.25 are applied and no other reductions in Kc are required. 8.6.4 Application
Under steady state conditions, the value for ECe can be predicted as a function of
EC of the irrigation water (ECiw) and the leaching fraction, using a standard leaching
formula. For example, the FAO-29 leaching formula LR = ECiw / (5 ECe – ECiw)
predicts the leaching requirement when approximately a 40-30-20-10 percent water
extraction pattern occurs from the upper to lower quarters of the root zone prior
to irrigation. ECiw is the electrical conductivity of the irrigation water. From this
equation, ECe is estimated as:

9. Actual crop ET (ETc act) by agricultural and natural vegetation
Actual crop ET (ETc act) by
agricultural and natural vegetation
Actual crop ET (ETc act) refers to both agricultural and natural vegetation including nonpristine agricultural vegetation. The latter is defined, in the usage here, as vegetation
having less than perfect growing conditions or stand characteristics (i.e. relatively poor
conditions of density, height, leaf area, fertility, vitality and biomass yield) as compared
to “pristine” maximal yield conditions. Non-typical cropping conditions are also
included and refer to types or arrangements of agricultural crops that are not listed or
described in Tables 6.1 to 6.4 and 7.1 to 7.3. However, non-typical cropping conditions
are mainly dealt with in Chapter 10. The approach whereby a crop is characterized by a crop coefficient, Kc, and the crop
evapotranspiration is given by the product of Kc and the reference evapotranspiration
ETo, provides a simple and convenient way of also characterizing the evapotranspiration
from natural vegetation and for diverse non-typical cultivation practices. This chapter presents procedures for estimating actual Kc and Kcb values for natural
vegetation and for agricultural vegetation independent of having Kc and Kcb values
available. The section on estimating crop coefficients from fraction of ground cover
and crop height is particularly important because it focuses on the estimation of ETc act
aimed at its use in irrigation scheduling and water management in real time. 9.1 CALCULATION APPROACH, GENERAL ASPECTS
The first step in the Kc ETo approach is the estimation of lengths of crop growth
stages, which also applies to natural vegetation (Tables 6.4 and 6.5). The next step is the
development of crop coefficient curves that represent the ratios of ETc to ETo during
the various growth stages of the vegetation as described in Chapters 5 and 6. 9.1.1 Initial growth stage
The procedure to estimate crop coefficients for the initial growth stage for agricultural
non-pristine and natural vegetation is identical to that described for agricultural crops
in Chapter 6 (single crop coefficient Kc ini) or Chapter 7 (dual crop coefficient, Kcb ini
+ Ke). The crop coefficient during this stage is primarily determined by the frequency
with which the soil is wetted. 9.1.2 Mid and late season stages
The Kc act during the mid-season period (Kc mid act and Kcb mid act), and to a lesser extent
the Kc act during the late season period, differ from those described in previous chapters
6 and 7. As the ground cover for non-pristine vegetation is often reduced, the Kc act is
affected to a large extent by the frequency of precipitation and/or irrigation and by
the amount of leaf area and ground cover. Natural vegetation, mainly when sparse, is
affected by the frequency of precipitation and the Kc act is dependent on the amount of
leaf area and ground cover. Dual crop coefficient approach
The determination of Kc for non-pristine and natural vegetation should ordinarily
follow the approach described in Chapter 7 whereby separate transpiration (Kcb) and
Chapter 9

evaporation (Ke) coefficients are used. The effects of evaporation from the soil surface
can be directly estimated as such. Two procedures that can be used to adjust the basal crop coefficient (Kcb mid act) for sparse
vegetation are presented in this section. In these approaches, Kcb mid act is estimated either
from LAI or from the effective ground cover and height. After the determination of Kcb mid act, the soil evaporation coefficient, Ke, should be
determined as described in Chapter 7 to obtain the crop coefficient for the mid-season
stage: Kc mid act = Kcb mid act + Ke. Even where the estimated Kcb mid act is small, the total Kc mid act
(= Kcb mid act + Ke) following precipitation may sometimes be as high or higher than the Kc
for pristine vegetation due to soil evaporation from among sparse vegetation. Single crop coefficient approach
When the single crop coefficient Kc of Chapter 6 is used, the average effects of soil
wetting are incorporated into a general mean Kc. Some guidelines for the estimation of
Kc act are given in the following sections. The single crop coefficient can also be derived
from the adjusted Kcb by considering the frequency of soil wetting, i.e., Kc mid act = Kcb mid act
+ 0.05 for infrequent wetting and Kc mid act = Kcb mid act + 0.10 for wettings of up to once a
week. For more frequent wettings, the dual crop coefficient approach should be used. Alternatively, the procedure for adjustment for sparse vegetation described below in the
next section can be used. Then, Kc min can be set equal to Kc ini, where Kc ini is estimated
as described in Chapter 6 because Kc ini incorporates the effects of soil evaporation and,
therefore, may serve as a lower limit on the estimate for Kc mid. 9.1.3 Water stress conditions
Where rainfall or irrigation is low, water stress might be induced and the
evapotranspiration will drop below the standard crop evapotranspiration, ETc. The
reduction in the value for Kc under conditions of low soil water availability is then
determined using the stress coefficient Ks as described in Chapter 8. Similarly, when
water stress is induced by salinity, then Kc act is also determined using the salinity stress
coefficient Ks described in Chapter 8 (Equations 8.20 and 8.25). 9.2 MID-SEASON STAGE–ADJUSTMENT FOR SPARSE VEGETATION

9. Actual crop ET (ETc act) by agricultural and natural vegetation
9.4 ESTIMATION OF CROP COEFFICIENTS FROM GROUND
COVER AND HEIGHT
A popular and generally successful method for estimating Kc is to base the estimate on
the fraction of ground covered by vegetation and the height of the vegetation. These
two parameters are the primary characteristics of vegetation that control the rate of
ETc act in terms of its ratio to the grass reference ETo. This method, referred to as the
Allen and Pereira (A&P) approach, is explained hereafter in Equations 9.8-9.14. 9.4.1 Concepts
For expanses of vegetation large enough that an equilibrium boundary layer is
established, so that general one-dimensional equations such as the Penman-Monteith
apply, a maximum upper limit on ET is established according to the law of conservation
of energy. Thus, for expanses of vegetation larger than about 500 to 2 000 m2, the Kc
will have upper limits of 1.2-1.3 for the grass reference. However, under conditions of
"clothesline effects" (where vegetation height exceeds that of the surroundings) or "oasis
effects" (where vegetation has higher soil water availability than the surroundings), peak
Kc may attain larger values. Caution is required when extrapolating ET measurements
from small plots to large stands because the resulting ET may be overestimated. An upper energy-constrained limit on Kc is the maximum value for Kc (Kc max) following
rain or irrigation, which is governed by the amount of energy available for evaporation. The Kc max varies with climate, ranging from about 1.05 to 1.30:

9. Actual crop ET (ETc act) by agricultural and natural vegetation
9.4.3 Parameterization of the ground cover fraction and height approach
The application of the A&P approach requires that parameters fc, fraction of ground
cover, and h, crop height, are observed or estimated from remote sensing, and that
appropriate values for ML, representing the intensity of canopy shading and limitations
on root and stem fluxes, and Fr, the effect of increased stomatal control, are adequately
selected. The parameter Fr is used in the calculation of Kcb full (Eqs. 9.11 and 9.12) and
ML is used in the computation of the density coefficient Kd (Equation 9.13). Both Kd
and Kcb full are used when computing Kcb for any crop or natural vegetation, with or
without active ground cover (Equations 9.9 and 9.10). It has been shown that Fr plays a
primary role in the estimation of Kcb and Kc, particularly for trees and vines that exercise
substantial control over stomatal conductance, even under well-watered conditions. To support the application of the A&P approach for most applications to compute
Kcb A&P, a selection of Fr and ML values has been performed through a numerical search
of parameter values that tend to cause Kcb A&P to match the tabulated Kcb values in
Chapter 7 (Kcb TAB). The procedure consists of:
1. Selecting initial values for Fr [0.25 to 1.0] and ML [1.00 to 2.00]. Fr is likely to be
close to 1.0 when the crop has young and very green leaves, particularly annual
crops, and close to 0.50 during the late season of deciduous woody fruit crops and
annual crops that are harvested dry. ML is close to 1.00 under dry crop conditions
and close to 2.0 when the crop is not stressed; in addition, ML is close to 2.0 when
the canopy is less transparent to radiation. Alternatively, the parameters in Tables
9.1 to 9.4 are considered. 2. Computing crop Kcb A&P with observed/known values of fc eff and h and using the
selected initial values for Fr and ML, and then comparing the resulting Kcb A&P with
the target value, which is commonly the standard tabulated value (Kcb target = Kcb TAB)
for the same crop (Tables 7.1 to 7.3), or with a Kcb target < Kcb TAB when the crop is
known to be cultivated somewhat far from pristine conditions. 3. Repeating the computations using an iterative numerical search where the initial
Fr values are progressively changed, but constrained by the limits of Fr, while
comparing the successive values of Kcb A&P with Kcb target values for the same crop,
progressively decreasing the differences between both values until differences are
negligible. The value for Fr needs to be progressively modified until the computed
Kcb A&P effectively represents the crop under study. 4. When a Fr value is selected, the calculations are performed with the Fr value
obtained in the previous calculation set, but now changing ML within its selected
interval aiming at minimizing the difference between Kcb A&P and Kcb target. 5. If increasing or decreasing ML leads to increases in the difference between Kcb A&P
and Kcb TAB, then the last value for ML is retained, as well as the Fr used in the
calculation; however, if the difference decreases, a new run must be performed until
an ML value is found that minimizes that difference. The value selected for Fr in
Step 3 remains fixed throughout Steps 4 and 5, but it may be required to reapply
the numerical search, focusing on Fr. 6. The procedure ends when the difference Kcb A&P - Kcb target is minimized and values for
both ML and Fr selected are within the respective intervals. These values can then be
used with Eq. 9.9, 9.11, and 9.13 to calculate values for Kcb mid act for any fraction of cover. Tables 9.1 to 9.4 propose values for the parameters of the A&P approach. Tables 9.1 and
9.2 present ML and Fr that are able to produce Kcb A&P = Kcb TAB for vegetable and field crops
for mid-season and end-season, i.e., for most of the crop seasons. Table 9.3 presents ML
and Fr for Kcb A&P for fruit trees, shrubs and vines targeting Kcb TAB ± 5%. Table 9.4 refers to
grasses.

10. ETc act under various crop management practices
ETc act under various crop
management practices
This chapter discusses various types of factors that may cause the values for Kc act and
ETc act to deviate from the standard Kc and Kcb values described in Chapters 6 and
7. These factors refer to the effects of surface mulches, intercropping, small areas of
vegetation and estimation of Kc or Kcb for periods under conditions of frozen soil as
well under non-active cover. This chapter is intended to serve as a resource for situations where cultivation practices
are known to deviate from those assumed in Tables 6.1 to 6.4 and 7.1 to 7.3 and where
estimates of Kc act and ETc act are still necessary. This chapter is by no means exhaustive;
its intent is to show some of the procedures that can be used to make adjustments to
Kc to account for deviations from standard conditions. 10.1 EFFECTS OF SURFACE MULCHES
Mulches are frequently used in vegetable production to reduce evaporation losses from
the soil surface, to accelerate crop development in cool climates by increasing soil
temperature, to reduce erosion, or to assist in weed control. Mulches may be composed
of organic plant materials, or they may consist of plastic sheets or films. 10.1.1 Plastic mulches
Plastic mulches generally consist of thin sheets of polyethylene, or a similar material
placed over the ground surface, especially along the plant rows. Holes are cut into the
plastic film at plant spacings to allow the plant vegetation to emerge. Plastic mulches
can be transparent, white, or black. Colour influences albedo, mainly during the early
stages of the crop. However, as the intention is to use a simple procedure for adjusting
Kc for mulched crops, only generalized recommendations are given here. The published
literature offers contradictory information on impacts of plastic mulches on Kc and ET. However, it appears likely that black plastic increases the soil temperature more than
transparent plastic, so that transparent plastic may cause slightly smaller differences in
Kc relative to not adopting any type of mulching. Plastic mulches can substantially reduce the evaporation of water from the soil surface. The impact of plastic mulch is likely more evident under trickle irrigation systems. Associated with the reduction in evaporation, however, there may occur a general
increase in transpiration from the vegetation caused by the transfer of both sensible and
radiative heat from the surface of the plastic cover to adjacent vegetation. Even though
the transpiration rates under mulch may increase by an average of 10-30 percent over
the season as compared to no mulch, the Kc values may decrease by an average of
10-30 percent due to a 30-80 percent reduction in soil evaporation. Ranges in observed
reductions in Kc are given in Table 10.1 for three groups of crops: field crops referring
to cereals, cotton and sugar cane; vegetable crops comprised of various species, and
fruit tree and vine crops, namely apricot and pear orchards, and grape vineyards. Table
10.2 presents the percentage of reduction Kc in relation to the type of mulch which
complements the information provided in Table 10.1. Chapter 10

10. ETc act under various crop management practices
When estimating basal Kcb for mulched crops, less adjustment is normally needed to
the Kcb curve, likely being half the order of reduction in overall Kc, as it is generally
understood that the “basal” evaporation of water from the soil surface that is associated
with the standard Kcb value is less with a plastic mulch, though the transpiration is
likely increased. The effect on Kcb can be greater with low density crops, e.g. with
tree orchards and vine crops. Local calibration of Kcb (and Kc) for use with mulch is
encouraged, namely using soil water balance models and computing soil evaporation Ke. Where calculating the soil evaporation coefficient Ke with plastic mulch (Example 10.1),
the fw should represent the relative equivalent fraction of the ground surface that can
contribute to evaporation through the vent holes in the plastic cover and to the fraction
of surface that is wetted and is not covered by the mulch. The effective area of vent
holes is normally two to four times the physical area of the vents (or even higher) to
account for vapour transfer from under the sheet. EXAMPLE 10.1
Effects of surface mulch
A plastic mulch is placed over cucumbers under drip irrigation. The mulch is clear
plastic covering the entire field surface, with small openings at each plant. Adjust both
the single and basal Kc values for this crop to reflect the presence of the mulch. From Table 6.1, Kc ini, Kc mid and Kc end for fresh market cucumbers have values equal
to 0.60, 1.00 and 0.75. As the plastic mulch is continuous with only small vents at each plant, the Kc ini
is assumed to be only 0.10 (this value should be adjusted upward if precipitation
occurs). The Kc mid and Kc end values are estimated as:
Kc mid = 0.85 (1.0) = 0.85
Kc end = 0.85 (0.75) = 0.64
where the 0.85 multipliers are derived from Table 10.1 and reflect an assumed 15
percent reduction in ETc due to the mulch, assuming an approximately weekly
irrigation frequency. From Table 7.1, the values for Kcb ini, Kcb mid, and Kcb end are 0.15, 0.95 and 0.70 for
this same cucumber crop. The Kcb ini is assumed to be similar to the Kc ini for mulched
cover and is therefore set equal to 0.10. The Kcb mid and Kcb end values are estimated to
be reduced by near 10 percent so that:
Kcb mid = 0.90 (0.95) = 0.85
Kcb end = 0.90 (0.7) = 0.63
These basal values are similar to the adjusted values for Kc. This is expected as
evaporation from the mulch covered surface can be ignored. Additional adjustment
to these Kc values to account for climate is necessary using Eq. 6.16 and 7.1. The values for mean Kc and Kcb are similar with values of 0.10 for the initial stage, 0.85
for the mid-season stage and 0.64 at the end of the late season stage.

10.1.2 Organic mulches
Effects of organic mulches are considered through the differences between mulched
and non-mulched Kc as in Table 10.1 and 10.2. Organic mulches are often used with
orchard production and with row crops under reduced tillage operations. Organic
mulches may consist of unincorporated plant residues or foreign material imported
to the field such as straw. The depth of the organic mulch and the fraction of the
soil surface covered can vary widely. These two parameters will affect the amount of
reduction in evaporation from the soil surface, with Kc differences increasing when
larger amounts of mulch are used, namely straw mulch, as well as when the percentage
of ground coverage is larger. A general rule when applying Kc from Tables 6.1, 6.2 and 6.3, and when applying the
dual Kcb + Ke method, is to reduce the amount of soil water evaporation by about 5
percent for each 10 percent of soil surface that is effectively covered by an organic
mulch. For example, if 50 percent of the soil surface were covered by an organic crop
mulch of high density, then the soil evaporation would be reduced by about 25 percent. In the case of Kc ini, which represents mostly evaporation from soil, one would reduce
Kc ini by about 25 percent. For less dense mulches, this percentage should be reduced
by 5 or 10 percent. In the cases of Kc mid and Kc end, one may reduce these values by 25
percent of the difference between (Kc mid − Kcb mid) and (Kc end − Kcb end) from Tables 6.1,
6.2 and 6.3 and Tables 7.1, 7.2 and 7.3. Generally, the differences between values in
these Tables are only 5 - 10 percent for mid- and late-season, so that the adjustment to
Kc mid and Kc end to account for an organic mulch may not be very large. However, one
may instead consider utilizing information in Table 10.1 and 10.2. When applying the dual crop coefficient approach (Kc = Kcb + Ke) with a separate water
balance of the surface soil layer, the magnitude of the evaporation component (Ke ETo)
should be reduced by about 5 percent for each 10 percent of soil surface covered by the
organic mulch. Kcb is not changed. These recommendations are only approximate and attempt to account for the effects of
partial reflection of solar radiation from residue, micro advection of heat from residue
into the soil, lateral movement of soil water from below residue to exposed soil, and
the insulating effect of the organic cover. As these parameters can vary widely, local
observations and measurements are required if more precise estimates are required. 10.2 INTERCROPPING
Intercropping refers to the situation where two different crops are grown together
within one field. For the estimation of the crop coefficient, a distinction is made
between (see Figure 10.1):
•  contiguous vegetation, where the canopies of the two crops intermingle at some
height (e.g. corn and beans intercropping);
•  overlapping crops, where the canopy of one crop is well above that of the other
so that the canopies cannot be considered to be contiguous (e.g. date trees
overlapping pomegranate trees at an oasis); and
•  border crops, where tall crops such as windbreaks border fields of shorter crops,
or high trees border a field crop.

10.2.1 Contiguous vegetation, single Kc
Where the taller crop has canopy foliage that extends down to the same elevation as
that of the top of the shorter crop, the vegetation canopy can be considered to be
contiguous. For example, in Africa and South America, maize and beans are frequently
intercropped as contiguous vegetation, with one row of maize planted per one or
more rows of beans. Another example is the cultivation of five to seven rows of wheat
intercropped with three rows of maize in many areas of China. Case of single Kc for similar fractions of ground covered by both crops
Where the leaf area or fraction of ground covered by the vegetation (fc) is similar
for each crop, the Kc in Tables 6.1 to 6.3 and Tables 7.1 to 7.3 for the taller crop (if
this Kc is higher) can be taken to represent the entire field. The taller crop will act in
some sense as a clothesline so that Kc (and ETc) for the taller crop per unit of ground
area is increased over that given in Tables 6.1 to 6.3 and Tables 7.1 to 7.3. However,
the Kc (and ETc) for the shorter crop will be reduced due to the windbreak effect
by the taller crop. As a result, the Kc for the field as a whole may be similar to the
weighted average of the Kc values for the two crops from Tables 6.1 to 6.3 and Tables
7.1 to 7.3, or, the total Kc may more closely follow the Kc predicted for a field sown
entirely to the taller crop (Kc field ≈ Kc taller crop). Yields for the shorter crop may be
reduced relative to those for single cultivar production due to the effects of shading
by the taller crop and the competition for soil water.

10.3 OVERLAPPING VEGETATION
Where intercropping entails overlapping of another crop's spacing, the canopy of one
crop is well above the other. This is the case, for example in southern California, where

Where tall crops such as windbreaks or date palms border fields of shorter crops, the
upper storey of the taller crop can intercept extra sensible heat energy from the air
stream. Under these conditions, the Kc is weighted according to the areas for each crop. However, prior to the weighting, the Kc for the border crop, if taller than the field
(interior) crop, should be adjusted for a potential clothesline impact. 10.5 Kc FROM SMALL AREAS OF VEGETATION
Natural vegetation and some subsistence agriculture frequently occurs as small groups
or stands of plants. The value for Kc for these small stands depends on the type and
condition of other vegetation surrounding the small stand. In the majority of cases for natural vegetation or for non-pristine agricultural vegetation,
the value for Kc must adhere to upper limits for Kc of approximately 1.20-1.30, when the
areal expanse of the vegetation is larger than about 2 000 m2. This is required because
ET from large areas of vegetation is governed by one-dimensional energy exchange
principles and by the principle of conservation of energy. ET from small stands
(< 2 000 m2) may be impacted by advected energy from beyond the stand and will
adhere to these same principles and limits only where the vegetation height, leaf area,
and soil water availability are similar to that of the surrounding vegetation. 10.6 Kc DURING NON-GROWING PERIODS
This section describes procedures for estimating ETc and crop coefficients during
non-growing periods. Non-growing periods are the periods during which the crop is
dormant. Generally, the non-growing periods refer to periods of frost and continuously
frozen conditions in case of annual crops and to the dormancy periods in the case of
perennials, namely the evergreen trees and shrubs.

10.6.1 Annual winter crops
The type and condition of the ground surface during non-growing periods largely
influences the range for ETc. Where the surface is covered by nearly dead vegetation,
or some type of organic mulch or crop residue, then the Kc will be similar to that for
agriculture that uses a surface mulch. Where the surface is covered by weed growth or
growth of “volunteer” plants, then the Kc will vary according to the leaf area or fraction
of ground covered by the vegetation and by the availability of soil water. Where the
surface is snow covered or frozen, then the Kc is difficult to predict and a constant value
for Kc may have to be assumed (Box 10.4). Where the ground is left mostly bare following harvest, then the Kc following harvest
will be strongly influenced by the frequency and amount of precipitation or irrigation
when a post-harvest leaching irrigation is applied. Kc for bare soil may be estimated
as Kc = Kc ini where Kc ini is computed using the procedure proposed in Chapter 6. However, as for the wheat case in North China Plain (Box 10.4), if the post-harvest
period is wet and Kc is then high, a Kc n-gro of around 0.25-0.50 may be selected. Where a daily soil water balance is applied, the user may elect to apply the dual Kcb
approach (Chapter 7), preferably using a simulation computer model. If the topsoil
layer dries to very low water contents during periods having no precipitation, the
daily water balance calculation with Kcb not far from 0 will generally provide accurate
estimates of ETc during the non-growing periods. BOX 10.3
