10.7 STRATEGIES, METHODS AND TECHNOLOGIES TO ACHIEVE
WATER SAVINGS
In recent decades, research has produced a variety of strategies, methods, and
technologies to reduce non-beneficial water use on farms for adaptation to the rising
occurrence of water scarcity, agricultural droughts, and multi-sectoral rivalry for
water, all which are increased by climate change. Adopting consumptive water-saving
practices (WSET), i.e. that refer to ETc act requires accurate determination of crop water
requirements using the FAO56 methods (Kc ETo) under various water availability
and management techniques, as described in the previous chapters. However, the
non-consumptive water-saving practices (WSDP+RO), that refer to controlling deep
percolation (DP) and runoff (RO) at farm and off-farm, generally originate WSDP+RO
> WSET. Both DP and RO refer to excess irrigation water applied relative to ETc and
to limitations of the irrigation technologies and of the irrigators. In fact, water-saving
practices must base not only on well-known net crop irrigation requirements but also
on the availability of appropriate irrigation technologies and management. This section, therefore, outlines ideas and methods for reducing non-beneficial
consumptive and non-consumptive water use, mainly referring to ET, DP and RO
(NBWUET and NBWUDP+RO) while maintaining high crop water productivity on
farms. These achievements tipically require maintaining high levels of water use for
transpiration and managing the irrigation systems targeting ETc. In particular, this
section describes water-saving routines linked to irrigation scheduling and management
for irrigation systems, crop and soil management, mulching, remote sensing techniques,
plant conditioners, and micro-climate adaptation. Controlling non-beneficial offfarm water use and non-consumptive farm water use imply different management
and technological issues not dealt with in FAO56 but that are closely associated with
the on-farm water management techniques and practices previously referred to and
described hereafter. Off-farm reductions in water consumption include the adoption of
modernized irrigation water collection, transport and distribution to farms and fields,
and the use of automation for improving those related functions not described herein. All of these practices require an assessment of the local and regional hydrology to
determine their overall impacts on reductions in water use. It is important to distinguish between water “use” and water “consumption” when
assessing impacts of irrigation on the fresh water resource. Water consumption is the
conversion of liquid water to vapour via the ET process, while the term water use
describes the total extraction of water from the environment and used as irrigation water. Water use includes both the consumed part of the extracted water and the non-consumed
part. In other words, water use consists of the consumptive use and the non-consumed
part, that remains on the land surface but does not infiltrate into the irrigated field, and
that stored below the surface. The first is runoff and the second is deep percolation as
referred to before. If the non-consumed component flows back to a surface stream or to
an underlying aquifer, then it remains as part of the freshwater system and is available
for later reuse. However, if the non-consumed component flows into a saline sink such
as the ocean or brackish ground water, then it is no longer part of the freshwater system
and is considered to be consumed. What is commonly considered to be “water savings’
is the difference between the common total water use, beneficial or not, and the water
use when the irrigator manages water to avoid excess ET, or DP or RO.

10. ETc act under various crop management practices
10.7.1 Water-saving of consumptive water use (WSET)
Irrigation scheduling and management
The main aim of irrigation management and scheduling may differ from an area to
another or from a farm to another depending on the WS purpose. The aim of the farmer
is to maximize the net economic benefit by increasing yield and/or reducing costs. This
may often be achieved by maximizing the beneficial consumption water use (ETc act)
and actual yield (Ya). As there is a strong relation between crop transpiration (Tc) and
CO2 assimilation (gas exchange through stomata), higher Ya is achieved at the expense
of more water transpired, mainly when aiming at little or no water stress. Chapter 8
develops the bases for irrigation scheduling and describes yield-water computations. Practical issues for determining crop coefficients under field practices and management
are dealt with in Chapter 9. Under conditions of water scarcity, the objective of irrigation management may be to
optimize crop water productivity (WPET), i.e. the marketable yield per unit of water
consumed if such a solution is economically appropriate. This involves knowing the
economic water productivity ratio (EWPR), which is the ratio of the value of the
marketable yield to the unit cost of water applied. In some instances, the goal of
maximizing the economics of production may be achieved by inducing controlled crop
water stress to reduce vegetative growth and to optimize the quality of marketable
yields, including eustress as previously defined (“good stress”), especially in some fruit
tree crops and vineyards. To reduce water consumption and optimize global WP and farm returns, an irrigation
schedule must be planned, where such a plan may or not include deficit irrigation,
depending upon the crop and water availability. For annual crops, optimizing WP
must include selection of the best planting date according to the local climate and/or
the foreseen weather conditions ahead of planting. That selection requires knowledge
of the relationships between evapotranspiration or transpiration deficit and yield
decrease (Equations 8.18 and 8.19, and Chapters 8 and 9). Using irrigation scheduling
modelling, irrigation events may be planned using short and medium range weather
forecasts, which are produced by various international organizations, e.g. ECMWF,
the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, WAMIS, the World
AgroMeteorological Information Service, or the Weather Prediction Center, USA
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Irrigation scheduling with the
FAO56 methodologies requires appropriate selection of Kc and Kcb values tabulated
in Chapters 6 and 7, and revised in their application depending on various specific
conditions including planting density and water and salinity stressors as discussed in
Chapters 8 and 9, as well as in the previous sections of this current chapter. Assuming that the tabulated Kc and Kcb are likely representing the upper maximum
or near-maximum values since they refer to pristine conditions, those values may
be difficult or unreasonable to achieve in common practice where it is essential to
achieve water savings. The same upper limits apply to the field attainment of crop
coefficients: Tabulated Kc and Kcb should represent reference values relative to those
observed from field data and can be useful to verify data quality and data handling
approaches, and thus to question results when locally observed values are well above
or well below the tabulated values. Limited deficit irrigation (DI) is specifically introduced into the irrigation practice to
allow some degree of crop water stress and Ya reduction, with a goal to reduce soil
evaporation (Es) and water and chemical losses, whilst maintaining transpiration at
levels that produce economically viable yields. Deficit irrigation can be considered to

be a water-saving strategy where soil water depletion in the root zone goes below the
optimum yield threshold and therefore transpiration decreases. Irrigation is applied up
to a certain level below field capacity so that occasional rainfall can replenish the soil
water storage capacity. Less frequent irrigation can reduce evaporation from the soil
surface. However, the uneven distribution of rainfall and variable weather conditions
pose a risk that may lead to Ya losses larger than desired or planned. To be a sustainable
practice, reduction of water consumption in deficit irrigation should be proportionally
higher than the reduction in Ya, so that WPET (kg m-3) is optimized, and EWPR is
always positive (above the economic feasibility threshold, EWPR>1.0). Published research has provided inconsistent evidence on performance of deficit
irrigation as a water-saving and economic strategy. In general, during years of water
shortage, farmers may choose to adopt deficit irrigation schedules for their less
profitable and more water-stress tolerant crops. To be economically viable, the cost
of reduction of water use should be higher than the cost of reduction of the market
value of Ya. This may be difficult to achieve or manage, depending on the degree of
deficits. Therefore, deficit irrigation is not always the preferred option by farmers due
to the increased risk of both Ya and monetary losses. Reducing the irrigated area may
be a preferred solution, e.g. decreasing the irrigable area having annual crops in favour
of watering of perennial crops. However, exceptions include the adoption of eustress
in perennial crops where lower Ya results in better quality fruit and higher profits, as
for grapevine where beneficial effects such as decreased berry size or increased sugar
content may lead to great benefit since wine quality may be improved. Deficit irrigation can be implemented by applying a fixed water reduction strategy
throughout the cropping season or targeted to some non-critical phenological stages in
relation to water stress. Two main types of DI may be considered:
•  regulated deficit irrigation (RDI) that targets certain phenological stages during
which plants are less sensitive to water stress;
•  partial root-zone drying (PRD), mostly used in fruit trees and vine crops, which
targets the production of the plant hormone abscisic acid (ABA), which reduces
leaf expansion and stomatal conductance by stressing one portion of the roots,
whilst the other portion of the roots sustains transpiration. Nevertheless, published research findings on RDI and PRD are not always consistent. Some results suggest that deficit irrigation and associated practices such as RDI and
PRD may only be acceptable in reducing capital and operating costs of irrigation and to
improve yield quality when carried out with using precision irrigation (timing, amount
and placement) based on the knowledge of crop responses to water stress, which vary
with crop and, often, with cultivar. Consequently, water-yield models, such as that
described in Chapter 8, are often crop and crop cultivar specific. Deficit irrigation is a highly complex practice that involves many variables. Its application
must focus on overcoming the uncertainty of outcomes. In general, the applicability of
deficit irrigation depends on site-specific conditions, crop types and related cultivars,
and climatic variables (e.g., rainfall distribution and reference ET levels). Given the large
variety of conditions and factors affecting crop water demand, yields and economic
return, optimization modelling and decision-support tools are useful aids to design the
most appropriate strategies for specific sites and for specific crops. Among such models
are those used to derive various Kc and Kcb values tabulated in Chapters 6 and 7, e.g. CROPWAT, SIMDualKc and AquaCrop. These tools allow one to consider diverse
criteria, primarily economic (maximizing profits), and select the irrigation scheduling
and management issues that better lead to water-savings and to control environmental

10. ETc act under various crop management practices
impacts (minimizing leaching of nitrates and chemicals, controlling groundwater
depletion and quality degradation). The FAO56 approach is used in such modelling
applications and may be able to determine the effects of deficit irrigation on crop yield,
non-beneficial crop water use, WPET and EWPR. Crop and soil management
The planting date of annual crops likely impacts the amounts of beneficial and nonbeneficial crop water use, namely the consumptive use, due to differences in responses to
climatic factors, mainly the timing and distribution of rainfall. Anticipating or delaying
planting dates is commonly done in relation to soil conditions for seeding and planting
machines to move on the soil more easily and favouring the emergence of the new plants. But when farmers have predictive information on weather conditions, mainly rainfall,
that adjustment of dates refer to the increased use of rainfall during the first periods of
crop growth. This adjustment of the planting date is generally done using any kind of
simulation tools that are able to predict the soil water content and ETc act, therefore the
gain in water availability. Adjusting that planting date requires that rainfall predictions are
available to support farmers decisions. The availability of adequate Kc is also paramount. Research has confirmed that the response of crops to water stress depends on critical
periods in their phenological stages. Under conditions of water scarcity, irrigation
during sensitive phenological stages (e.g. reproductive stage in wheat and maize) is
favoured ahead of irrigation during less sensitive stages (e.g. vegetative stage). Again,
this is favoured when SWB models are used based upon weather predictions. Crop and
soil monitoring are also required. Optimal crop growth and Tc may be reduced under conditions of limited supply of
nutrients, fertilization and/or water, or under salinity conditions. This effect on ETc act
can be accounted for in the FAO56 approach either by reducing Kc and Kcb coefficients
empirically, or by adding the water stress coefficient (Ks) as described in previous
chapters. Nutrient or other shortage effects manifest through a reduction in plant
growth and canopy cover, and therefore a field can experience an increase in Ke due to
more soil exposure. When irrigation is insufficient, fertilization should be reduced to
avoid decreasing the osmotic potential. Plant density and canopy size of perennials affect the utilization of resources. Reducing
stand density makes more resources (e.g. water, nutrients) available to individual
plants, in particular under rainfed agriculture. However, reduced plant density and
canopy size are likely to increase Es, thus increasing non-beneficial water use, i.e. Es increases in detriment of Tc. In general, drier conditions are more suited to lower
planting densities for perennials. Canopy cover is used in FAO56 guidelines to estimate
the split of ET into Es and Tc, because it approximates the ratio of radiation intercepted
by the canopy and incoming solar radiation. Thus, Chapter 9 provides a guideline for
the estimation of Kcb from the effective fraction of ground cover, fc eff, and crop height,
i.e. the A&P approach. This approach has been successfully applied to vegetable, field
and tree crops and respective indicative parameters are tabulated in Chapter 9 to ease its
application. The approach is particularly applicable to tree and shrub crops planted in
rows given the large number of combinations of canopy sizes and densities (pruning),
plant densities, row distances and orientations, wetted areas of micro-irrigation, etc. This type of modelling may be applied at the stage of planning and design of the
cropping and irrigation system in order to provide for minimizing non-beneficial water
consumption to assess different combinations of canopy management (pruning) and
irrigation systems (e.g. drip vs micro-sprayers). However, the A&P approach, coupled
with the dual Kc procedure, is mainly useful when applied to established orchards and
vines to support planning and management of irrigation scheduling.

Inter-cropping (described in an earlier section of this chapter) and agro-forestry systems are
popular practices to optimize the use of resources (water, nutrients and radiation energy). A higher WPET can be achieved in agro-forestry systems compared to mono-cropping
because soil water between tree rows is consumed by inter-crop Tc rather than by Es. Soil management practices that may modify the volume of water infiltrated and
stored in the soil, thereby affecting the ratio of Es and Tc, are usually related to tillage
(e.g. conservation or no-tillage), land preparation (land levelling or tilling ridge and
furrows), or in-field rainwater harvesting. Soil additives and conditioners are materials
used to increase the soil water and nutrient retention capacity or to reduce Es. Many
of these practices affect particularly the topsoil, which is the most dynamic soil layer
in terms of mass and energy exchanges and may therefore impact Kc by decreasing Ke. Less frequent irrigations reduce Es compared to frequent irrigations, but they may
increase the risk of crop water stress and favour Ya reduction when ETo is high. The
frequency of irrigation wetting depends on various factors, namely the storage capacity
of the soil, the type of irrigation system and the ET rate. Soil evaporation is site-specific
depending upon climate through ETo, the frequency of soil wetting, the use of mulches,
and the fraction of ground shadowed by the canopy, which depends upon the crop
density and the crop growth stage. Es can be quantified through the partitioning of ET
for the considered crop, namely using the dual Kc approach. Es is limited by the shading
of the crop canopy, which corresponds to limitations imposed to the available energy
for evaporation at the soil surface. This approach is valid for all irrigation methods that
wet the soil surface and is in proportion to the wetted fraction, as occurs for furrow
irrigation, particularly, when alternate furrows are adopted. As previously described in the current chapter, mulching is an old practice of covering
the soil surface to reduce soil evaporation and surface runoff, regulate soil temperature,
suppress weeds, improve soil health, and therefore improve crop growth. Different
materials can be used for mulching, such as bark chips, straw, grass or other plant material,
stones or plastic sheets, and humic substances. A wide variety of environmental and
management factors have been reported in literature relative to the complex crop growth
response to various types of mulch. Effects of mulches are greater at earlier crop stages,
when the soil is yet bare or only partially covered by the crop canopy. As a result, those
are periods when crop coefficients greatly can vary with the frequency of wettings and soil
wetness. Kc can be estimated according to the previous mulching section of this chapter. Only used in high-tech farming, plant conditioners include anti-transpirants, biostimulants and plant growth regulators. They are mainly applied to regulate harvesting
dates of market produces, and to mitigate effects of environmental stresses. Although
plant conditioners do not directly reduce non-beneficial water use, NBWUET, they
affect Tc or the Tc/ETc ratio and, therefore, their effects need to be considered when
estimating total water consumption and in implementing irrigation scheduling. The
use of plant conditioners does not change the standard Kc and Kcb coefficients but
may act similarly to the stress coefficients in defining their actual values (Kc act and
Kcb act). They may affect soil evaporation when plant conditioners decrease (or increase)
the crop cover fraction due to their effects on plants. Anti-transpirants may act by
reducing stomatal conductance and then the reduced Kcb may be assessed using the Fr
factor described in the A&P approach (Chapter 9). These types of conditioners may
become more and more prevalent in the future as research develops means to reduce
transpiration from plants while sustaining inflow of carbon dioxide.

10. ETc act under various crop management practices
Various practices may be used to condition micro-climate to reduce water losses and
improve WSET through Tc. A typical case is sheltered or protected cultivation. However, as
it happens with tunnels, the FAO PM-ETo does not apply since the aerodynamic conditions
are changed and do not respect the Penman-Monteith assumptions. Windbreaks, such as
trees, may mitigate extreme winds and affect micro-climatic variables such as net radiation
(by increased shading), temperature, humidity, heat and evaporation fluxes resulting in
changes in evaporative demands and water vapour fluxes. The effects of tree windbreaks
depend on surface roughness, height, orientation and porosity. Warmer, more humid and
less windy conditions usually occur in the protected crop areas. Lower wind speed and more
humid conditions reduce vapor pressure deficit and crop ET, mostly without decreasing
dry matter assimilation. Reduction of sensible heat fluxes and surface resistances, on the
other hand, would most likely favor transpiration and dry matter assimilation. Higher Yact
can therefore be expected in sheltered areas except when crops compete for resources with
the windbreak plants (e.g. competition for water and nutrients). Generally, the trees in
windbreaks are more tolerant of water shortage than agricultural crops and therefore can
be irrigated less or not at all. Partial stomatal closure of the windbreak trees will cause a
larger proportion of total available energy to be transformed into sensible heat rather than
into evapotranspiration and total water consumption. As a result, total ET over large area
of windbreaks and agriculture can be reduced. 10.7.2 Water-saving of non-consumptive water use (WSDP+RO)
Farm irrigation systems
Irrigation methods can be broadly classified as surface, sprinkler and micro-irrigation. This section focuses on water-saving practices that are typical for each irrigation
method and applicable on farms. It should be born in mind that costs and benefits
play a major role when assessing respective water-saving issues because economic
returns of irrigation tend to decrease when water-saving practices are adopted. Water
consumption and use under different irrigation methods show sometimes contrasting
outcomes, depending on the type of crop, canopy cover, soil properties (mainly relative
to infiltration), land slope, irrigation wetted area, and irrigation management. Surface irrigation systems can have high performance when precise laser levelling is
adopted, inflow rates are adequate and non-erosive, and discharge applications are well
controlled. These rules apply to either basin, border or furrow irrigation. Precise land
levelling for basin, furrow and border irrigation is usually fundamental for efficient
application with surface irrigation methods. When applied water creates ponds on the
land surface before infiltrating into the soil, it not only leads to increased evaporation
losses but decreases distribution uniformity (DU) of the infiltrated water. As a result,
there will be parts of the field receiving less and parts receiving excessive water. If only
the average depletion is replaced, then field-average ET will be decreased due to water
stress on the under-irrigated portion of the field and field-average yields will decrease. To compensate for the less irrigated zones where the crop experiences stress, the farmer
may tend to apply water in excess, thus promoting high deep percolation. Several
authors reported that adopting precision land levelling in basin irrigation with controlled
inflow rates and respective application time duration, reduced water application by
nearly 40 percent relative to using less cared applications. However, the overall water
consumption (evaporation and transpiration) may be similar but the cumulative soil
evaporation may be less because the land surface is then usually wetted less frequently
and transpiration increases because the canopy is increased and Es is reduced.

Equipment for precise control of applied flow rates and volumes is rare where surface
irrigation is traditional. The use of hand held equipment is not precise in control
and largely depends upon the ability of the irrigant, which is another cause of nonuniformity of infiltrated volumes and, consequently, another reason why farmers may
tend to apply excess water. In fact, the lack of precision control equipment makes it
difficult to adopt precise scheduling in terms of managing discharge rates and volumes. For example, findings report a reduction in water application of up to 45% when surgeflow on alternate furrows is used, namely due to runoff control due to using automated
gated pipes. Adopting alternate furrow irrigation may additionally reduce consumptive
water use through reduced water application and less soil evaporation with little
reduction in yield and increased WPET as compared to conventional furrow irrigation. Achieving appropriate inflow control requires mechanization of water distribution to
basins, borders or furrows, preferably automation and remote control. Thus, changing
from traditional surface irrigation to modern practices requires investments that may
be economically unsatisfactory. However, research has been declining and automated
surface irrigation systems are not available in countries where traditional irrigation is
predominant. In many regions, the trend has been to replace surface irrigation with
sprinkler or micro-irrigation, which equipment is supported by strong markets as
compared to those for surface irrigation equipment. Rice is traditionally cultivated in flooded paddy fields where the basins’ water depth
is around 5 to 10 cm. Basins are surrounded by soil bunds that avoid RO. This water
plays a large role: providing for crop ET, controlling impacts of temperature on the
crop and controlling weed growth. When land levelling is improved, the flooding depth
may be reduced to about 5 cm, which may decrease deep percolation (DP). When the
climate is favourable, intermittent (nearly daily) flooding may be practiced with the soil
water kept near saturation, thereby further decreasing DP. When infrequent irrigation
by surface, sprinkler or micro-irrigation is practised with aerobic rice production, both
DP and Es may decrease, however depending upon soil and land surface conditions. It is important to note that water-savings primarily refer to a reduction in DP and likely
to little reduction to evaporation and the non-beneficial water consumption fraction. In other words, water use is reduced, but water consumption may be only slightly
reduced. However, the standard Kc values change with the adopted management of the
rice crop as tabulated in Chapter 6. As stated, net crop water requirements decrease
from conventional flooding to flooding with dry seeding, flooding with anticipated
cutoff and, finally, to aerobic rice. The adoption of different, specific Kc values is a
condition for better achieving water saving. Sprinkler irrigation systems may be stationary or continuous moving. The former
includes portable and solid set systems and side roll. Continuous moving wheeled
laterals are automated and include center-pivots, linear-move systems, travelling gun
sprinklers and side-move systems. A primary objective of sprinkler systems is high
water distribution uniformity throughout the irrigated field. Thus, potential watersaving practices aim at maintaining high DU when adopting sprinkler flow rates that
favour water infiltration, spacing among sprinklers that provide for a good distribution
of water throughout the field, low variability of pressure and discharge if the field is
sloping, system maintenance and design for controlling wind effects. If irrigation scheduling is appropriate in terms of the crop and soil water contents
dynamics, these characteristics lead to high ratios of requirement to water applied, i.e.,
water application efficiencies. Sprinkler systems perform best when the soil infiltration
is high, and wind speed is low. Sprinkler system design, mainly referring to the

10. ETc act under various crop management practices
selection of sprinklers sizes and spacing, pressure, flow rates, water application depths
and diameters of piping, is fundamental to ensure uniform distribution of pressure and
flow rates, and to reduce evaporative losses. Practices and design to improve water infiltration and thereby reduce runoff require
appropriate sprinkler selection. Because water applied by large sprinkler systems wets
the entire ground surface, non-beneficial consumption of water can be substantial
under high wind and high evaporative demand of the atmosphere. Wind-induced
evaporation of spray may be highest when drops are small, and when the canopy
cover is low and risers are high above the ground surface. Evaporation of spray can
be reduced by placing nozzles closer to or even inside the plant canopy, using larger
drop sizes and attempting to irrigate when wind speeds are low. Modern sprinkler
systems, such as center-pivot and linear moving laterals, are often designed to apply
small irrigation depths to avoid runoff. As a result, they must irrigate more frequently,
thereby increasing total evaporation losses from soil. The more frequent irrigation
reduces the risk of crop stress, but at the expense of increased Es. The dual Kc procedure
can be used to estimate the increases in Ke and Es under frequent irrigation. Figures 6.1
and 6.2 can be used to estimate the increase in Kc under low vegetation cover. Micro-irrigation systems include high-tech methods having large capital and maintenance
investment. Systems are low-pressure and include surface and subsurface drip irrigation
for row crops and orchards, micro-sprinklers and micro-sprayers for horticulture
and under-tree irrigation, and bubblers for orchards. These irrigation systems wet a
limited portion of the ground, targeting the crop root zone, mainly in case of orchards
and vines. The limited wetting of the surface reduces the soil evaporation impact due
to high frequency irrigation, thus providing for high WSET by reducing NBWUET. Achieving good performance with micro-irrigation systems requires good design, which
complexity may be overcome using decision support and design models. WS practices
resulting from good design aim at improving water application control, the emission
uniformity (EU), and the management of irrigation, as well as automation and control. The benefits of drip irrigation compared to surface and sprinkler irrigation include
reduced water application, controlled operational water losses, less labour, low or no
runoff and reduced energy consumption and pumping costs per unit area, as well as
improved management of water, fertilization and pesticides for a range of high-profit
crops. Micro-sprinklers and micro-sprayers have similar benefits, but the wetting
pattern is wider and may be affected by wind. However, for under-tree irrigation,
wind drift and Es may be less than for field crops. Despite advantages, managing drip
or micro-spray irrigation systems for peak performance is very demanding, including
when automation is adopted. High-tech micro-irrigation methods may not be economically feasible under all
conditions since, for field crops, economic returns tend to decrease when more
precision water-saving techniques are adopted. Benefits are generally greater for
irrigating tree and vine crops having a better developed root system compared to
annual crops. Water can be easily applied near the root zone of tree and vine crops, and
it may be easier to apply deficit irrigation, in particular partial root-zone drying. Soil
evaporation is controlled because the soil is only partially wetted near the crops, and
often under the shadow of the crop canopy. When subsurface drip is applied, ground
surface wetting occurs only by capillarity from the buried emitters. Drip irrigation,
and border and basin irrigation, have advantages over sprinkler systems in saline
environments by avoiding the wetting of the plant canopy. Drip irrigation can have
reduced accumulation of salts in the root zone due to near continuous irrigation and
therefore better suitability for salt sensitive crops.

In summary, the impact of the irrigation system type on consumptive water losses through
evaporation and transpiration is controlled by the irrigation frequency, the fraction of soil
surface wetted, the characteristics of spray drops and their evaporation in the case of sprinkler
irrigation, and the wetting of the crop canopy in the case of sprinkler irrigation. These impacts
can be generally quantified using the dual Kc approach. Differently, the processes of deep
percolation and runoff, mainly depend upon the irrigation design and management, thus only
indirectly from ET and Kc. However, the appropriate selection of Kc values permits the use of
equipment and management tools that contribute to control DP and RO. Off-farm irrigation systems
Water collection, transportation and distribution to farms may be a source of water losses
in case of open channel conduits, much less when pipe systems are used. The latter respond
quickly to management, and farmers may often receive water on demand, thus producing
only minimal losses and causing adequate implementation and adoption of irrigation water
distribution on demand. Gravity canal systems have a demanding operation and regulation
to control discharges to low order canals or to distributors. Then, since it is difficult to
operate on-demand, thus often producing supplies with discharges and pressure heads that
vary and cause difficulties to the irrigation scheduling by the farmers and consequent losses. In addition, gravity systems respond slowly to regulation and management operative
orders. Modern canal automation and permanent hydraulic monitoring, as well as distant
command of gates, associated with using simulation of aggregated ETc act demands, allow
an important water saving and appropriate delivery of water to the farms, thus producing
WS at farm and off-farm. 10.7.3 Remote sensing techniques for irrigation crops monitoring
Remote sensing (RS) data and methodologies have been increasingly used for estimating
parameters related to crop water requirements, namely Kc and Kcb as for many cases
collected to build their tabulated values. By providing the spatial distribution of vegetation
and ET, RS provides for a better understanding of within- and among fields variability,
which is important to support irrigation management ranging from local farmers up to offfarm irrigation systems’ managers. The increased number of satellite missions, improved
sensor technology, enhanced spatial, temporal and spectral resolutions of data, and easier
data access have all encouraged the use of RS for irrigation management. A description of
RS-based techniques is provided in Chapter 1. RS estimates are valuable for assessing the
occurrence of water shortage or poor distribution or other impacts caused by poor nutrient
availability or salinity. The vegetation-based and thermal-based RS methods work well
together as compliments in estimating both potential (standard) Kcb and actual Kc act. Overall, the accurate estimation of Kcb, Kc act and actual crop ET can be assisted by
RS Improved estimation improves irrigation management and contributes both to the
convergence of actual Kc and Kcb values towards better knowledge of standard values
and to their distribution in space. Improved knowledge of Kc aids in achieving larger
WPET and water savings, and minimizing non-beneficial water uses associated with
over-irrigation. For successful application of RS, the availability of cloud-free satellite,
UAV and/or manned aircraft images with an adequate temporal resolution of at least
one clear image every 15 days is needed throughout the irrigation season. An important
example of application of RS for irrigation management is SIMS, Satellite Irrigation
Management Support. SIMS adopts the A&P approach to compute Kc and Kcb, using
the fraction of ground cover estimated from RS. The model is used to support irrigation
scheduling of perennials and annuals in California. The model is currently integrated
with other RS irrigation management models in OpenET, which is aimed at RS advising
on irrigation scheduling in the West of USA and assessing performance of RS viewed
fields.

Annex 3

A3.1 COMPLETING A DATA SET
Quite often data sets containing a weather variable Yi observed at a given station are
incomplete due to short interruptions in observations. Interruptions can be due to a large
number of causes, the most frequent being the breakage or malfunction of instruments
during a certain time period. When data are missing, it may be appropriate to complete
these data sets from observations Xi from another nearby and reliable station. However, to use portions of data set Xi to insert in data set Yi, both data sets Xi and Yi
must be homogeneous. In other words, they need to represent the same conditions
throughout time. The procedure for completing data sets must be applied after a test
for homogeneity and any needed correction for non-homogeneity have been performed. The data completion procedure proposed herein consists of using an appropriate
regression analysis. The procedure for inserting data of a nearby station into an incomplete data set can be
summarized as follows:
1. Select a nearby weather station for which the data set length covers all periods for
which data are missing. 2. Characterize the data sets from the nearby station, Xi, and of the station having
missing data, Yi, by computing the mean and the standard deviation sx for the
nearby weather station data set (Xi):

Weather data collected at a given weather station during a period of several years may
be non-homogeneous when the data presents a sudden change in its mean and variance
in relation to the original values. This phenomenon may occur due to several causes,
some of which are related to changes in instrumentation and observation practices, and
others which relate to modification of the environmental conditions of the site, such as
rapid urbanization or, on the contrary, perhaps development of irrigation in the area.

Annex 3: Statistical analysis of weather data sets
Changes relative to data collection may be caused by:
•  change in grass vegetation cover, its watering and management;
•  change in location of the weather station, or in type of shelters;
•  significant change in type of vegetation surrounding the weather station;
•  change in type of sensor or instrument;
•  change of observer and/or the timing of observations; and
•  deterioration of sensors, or poor management of instruments leading to the
malfunctioning of mechanical parts of instruments. These changes cause observations made prior and after the change to belong to
statistically different populations. Quite often, the occurrence of such changes and the
dates when they occurred are not known, making it necessary to access whether a given
data set can be considered homogeneous and, if not, to identify the sub-data series and
perform the required corrections. Procedures indicated hereafter are simple, well proven in practice and rely upon the
statistical comparison of two data sets, one considered homogeneous and consisting
of observations Xi performed in a nearby weather station, the other being the one
under analysis and consisting of the observations Yi of the same weather variable
(Tmax, Tmin, u2, RHmax, Rs, etc). Both sets Xi and Yi should be collected at two stations
that are in the same climatic region, have the same time length of observations and
presenting the same trends in time despite the space variability when short time scales
(daily, or 10-day) are utilized. A3.2.1 Method of Cumulative Residuals
When relating two weather data sets from two weather stations, where the first is
homogeneous, the data set of the second station can be considered homogeneous
if their cumulative residuals from its linear regression with the first data set are not
biased. The bias hypothesis can be tested for a selected probability p by verifying
whether the residuals are contained within an ellipse which axis and depend on the
probability p used to test the hypothesis. The magnitudes of and also depend on the
size of the data set and on the standard deviation of the sample being tested. This test uses the residuals of the linear regression of Y on X as described herein
before. The residuals should follow a normal distribution with mean zero and standard
deviation sy,x, i.e. the error Ԑi ∈ N (0,sy,x). Thus, the residuals εi must be independent
random variables, i.e., they should exhibit homoscedasticity. The procedure for analysing the homogeneity of a weather data set Yi of a given
weather station can be summarized as follows:
1. Select a reference weather station inside the same climatic region that is known to
have a homogeneous data set Xi of the same weather variable. As an alternative,
construct a “regional” homogeneous data set by averaging the observations at
several weather stations in the same region. 2. Organize both data sets with their values xi and yi (i = 1, 2,..., n) in chronological
order, where the initial timing and the time increment are identical for both data sets. 3. For both data sets, compute the mean and standard deviation (Eq. A3.1 to A3.4) for
the homogeneous variable (xi) and for the variable to be tested (yi).

4. Calculate the regression line between the two variables yi and xi and the associated
correlation coefficient (Eq. A3.5 to A3.8). The regression equation among the full
data sets (subscript f) is expressed as:
ŷi = af + bf xi (i = 1, 2, ..., n)
(A3.11)
Whenever possible, plot xi, yi and the regression line to visually verify whether
the homoscedasticity hypothesis can be accepted (see Figure A3.1), i.e., when the
deviations of yi to the regression estimates ŷi are within the same range for all xi,
thus when those deviations are not increasing (or decreasing) when the values of
xi are increasing. FIGURE A3.1

The double-mass technique is also useful for assessing homogeneity in a weather data
set. As with the method of cumulative residuals discussed above, the double-mass
technique requires data sets from two weather stations, where Xi (i = 1, 2,...,n) is a

chronologic data set for a given weather variable observed for a certain time length at
a “reference” station which is considered to be homogeneous, and where Yi is a data
set of the same variable, with the same time length, observed at another station and for
which homogeneity needs to be analysed. In the double-mass technique, starting with the first observed pair of values X1 and Y1,
cumulative data sets are created by progressively summing values of Xi and Yi to verify
whether the long-term trends in variation of Xi and Yi are the same. Thus, the following
cumulative variables are obtained:

The graphical application of the double-mass analysis is done by plotting all coordinate
points xi and yi (Figure A3.5). The plot is then visually analysed to determine whether

As global agricultural systems face increasing pressure from
climate variability, water scarcity, and the growing demand for
food, there is a critical need for updated, science-based tools
that support efﬁcient and sustainable water use in agriculture. The original FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 56,
published in 1998, set a global standard for computing crop
evapotranspiration and estimating crop water requirements. Its methodologies have become integral to irrigation planning,
agricultural water management, and policy development
worldwide. However, advancements in data science, sensor technology, and
climate modeling—coupled with emerging challenges such as
